lessons.title: What Simulation and Modeling Are
lessons.content:
Imagine you want to know whether a new flyover in Dhaka will really cut traffic jams. You could build it, wait two years, spend thousands of crores of taka and then find out. Or you could build a pretend version of the roads, cars and signals inside a computer, let millions of pretend cars drive on it, and see what happens in a few days. That second idea is the whole subject of this course. Pilots do the same thing in a flight simulator: they can crash a hundred times and nobody gets hurt. Simulation lets us crash ideas safely.

System: Let us start with three words that the whole course stands on. A system is the real thing we care about: a group of parts that work together for some purpose. A tea stall with one cashier and a line of customers is a system. So is a bank branch, a hospital emergency room, a mobile network, a garment factory line, or the spread of flu in a school. A system lives inside an environment, which is everything outside it that still pushes on it. For the tea stall, the weather and the office closing time are part of the environment, because they change how many customers come.

Model: A model is a simplified description of a system that keeps the parts that matter for our question and throws away the rest. If our question is how long customers wait at the tea stall, the model needs the arrival of customers, how long the cashier takes, and the line. It does not need the colour of the cups or the name of the cashier. A good model is not the most detailed one. It is the simplest one that still answers the question correctly. A map is a good everyday example: a Dhaka bus route map leaves out every building, and that is exactly why it is useful.

Simulation: A simulation is running a model over time to imitate how the real system would behave. The model is the recipe; the simulation is actually cooking it and tasting the result. We feed the model inputs, such as 30 customers per hour, let the computer play out what happens minute by minute, and collect outputs, such as average waiting time. Then we change something, say add a second cashier, run it again and compare. Banks, Carson and Nelson, the authors of a classic textbook, define simulation as the imitation of the operation of a real-world process or system over time.

Why not just try it for real: Experimenting with the real system is often impossible, dangerous, too slow or too costly. You cannot test a new hospital emergency layout by letting real patients wait longer. You cannot run a nuclear reactor to failure to learn how it fails. You cannot wait thirty years to see if a pension plan runs out of money. And a new runway at Hazrat Shahjalal airport cannot be built three different ways to pick the best. A computer model can be built three ways in a month.

Time compression: One huge gift of simulation is that it can squeeze time. A whole year of a bank branch, with thousands of customers, can be simulated in a few seconds because the computer skips straight from one interesting moment to the next. The opposite also works: a chemical reaction that takes a millionth of a second can be stretched out and watched step by step. Either way, we see behaviour we could never watch comfortably in real life.

What-if questions: Managers love simulation because it answers what-if questions. What if customer arrivals grow by 20 percent during Eid shopping? What if one machine in the garment line breaks down twice a week? What if we change the traffic signal from 60 seconds green to 45 seconds? Each question becomes one more run of the model with one input changed. This is much cheaper than a real trial, and you can try ideas that would be crazy to try for real.

Why not just use a formula: Sometimes a formula is enough, and then you should use it. For a very simple line with random arrivals and one server, queuing theory (lessons 16 to 18) gives exact answers with a pocket calculator. But real systems quickly become messy: customers who leave when the line is long, cashiers who take tea breaks, rush hours, machines that break, priority patients. The formulas either do not exist for such cases or need assumptions that are false. Simulation does not care how messy the rules are. If you can describe the rules step by step, the computer can play them out.

When simulation is the right tool: Simulation is a good choice when the system is too complex for formulas, when experimenting on the real system is impossible or risky, when you want to compare several designs before building any, when you need to understand how parts interact, and when you need to train people (pilots, surgeons, power plant operators) without real danger. It is also used to check that a new analytic formula is right: if the simulation and the formula agree, both are more believable.

When simulation is NOT the right tool: Banks and his co-authors list clear cases where you should not simulate. If common sense solves the problem, do not simulate. If an exact formula solves it, use the formula. If doing the real experiment is easier and cheaper, just do it. If the cost of the study is more than the savings it could bring, skip it. If there is no data and no expert who can guess the numbers, the model will be built on air. If there is not enough time or money to finish properly, a half-done simulation can mislead more than no simulation. And if nobody can check the model against reality, be very careful about trusting it.

Advantages in one place: New policies, layouts and rules can be tested without disturbing the real system. Hardware designs and factory layouts can be tested before buying anything. Time can be compressed or expanded. Bottlenecks, the slowest part that holds everyone else up, become visible. You learn which inputs matter most. And the animated version of a model is a great way to convince a manager, because people trust what they can watch.

Disadvantages in one place: Building a good model takes skill and training; two people can build very different models of the same system. Results are often hard to interpret because the outputs are random: one run might say average wait is 6 minutes and the next run 9 minutes, so you must learn output analysis (lesson 24). Simulation can be expensive in time. And it gives you the answer to the question you asked, under the rules you coded; it does not tell you the best answer automatically unless you add optimisation on top.

Deterministic or random: Some simulations have no randomness, such as a ball falling under gravity: the same start always gives the same result. Most simulations in this course are stochastic, meaning randomness is built in, because real arrivals, service times and breakdowns are random. That is why the first part of the course spends real time on probability, random numbers and how to turn them into realistic random times. Lesson 2 makes these categories precise.

A short history: In 1777 the French scientist Buffon dropped needles on a floor with parallel lines and showed the chance of a needle crossing a line is connected to pi; it is one of the oldest random experiments used to estimate a number. In the 1940s, scientists working on the Manhattan Project, including Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann, used random sampling on early computers to study how neutrons travel through material; they named the method Monte Carlo after the famous casino. In the early 1960s Geoffrey Gordon at IBM created GPSS, one of the first languages made only for simulation. Today we have tools like Arena, AnyLogic, SimPy in Python and NetLogo, and huge simulations of weather and climate run on supercomputers.

Where simulation is used today: Factories simulate production lines before buying machines. Hospitals simulate emergency rooms and vaccine centres. Airports simulate check-in counters and security lines. Telecom companies simulate networks with tools like ns-3 before rolling out new towers. Banks run Monte Carlo simulations to estimate risk. Weather offices run physics models of the atmosphere every day. Video games run a physics simulation many times a second. Self-driving car companies drive billions of simulated kilometres. And during COVID-19, epidemic models helped governments estimate hospital bed needs.

Real-life example 1, a tea stall near a university: Rahim bhai runs a tea stall near Dhaka University. Between 4 and 6 pm students arrive about once a minute, and he takes on average 50 seconds per cup. Students complain that the line is too long. Should he hire a helper? Step one, he writes down the arrival times and serving times for an afternoon. Step two, a student builds a model: random arrivals, one server, a line. Step three, the computer simulates 100 afternoons with one server and 100 afternoons with two. Step four, the result says average wait drops from about 7 minutes to under 1 minute with a helper. Step five, Rahim bhai compares the helper's wage with the extra sales from students who stop walking away. A clear decision, made without risking a single real afternoon.

Real-life example 2, planning a vaccination centre: During a vaccination campaign, an upazila health office must decide how many registration desks and how many vaccination booths to open. Too few and hundreds of people stand in the sun for hours; too many and nurses sit idle. A simulation model takes the expected arrivals per hour, the time to check an NID and register, the time to vaccinate and the 15-minute observation area, and tries different numbers of desks and booths. The model quickly shows where the bottleneck is. Often it is not the vaccination booth everyone expected but the registration desk, a surprise that is cheap to discover on a computer and expensive to discover on the day.

The course map: The course moves in four big steps. First, foundations: systems and models, the steps of a simulation study and a probability review (lessons 1 to 6). Second, randomness: making random numbers, testing them and turning them into realistic random times (lessons 7 to 10). Third, the main kinds of simulation: Monte Carlo (11 and 12), discrete-event simulation by hand and in code (13 to 15), queuing theory to check our simulators (16 to 18), inventory (19), continuous simulation (20), system dynamics and agent-based models (21). Fourth, trusting the results: input modeling (22), verification and validation (23), output analysis (24) and a capstone (25).

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up model and simulation; remember the model is the description and the simulation is running it. Another mistake is thinking a more detailed model is always better; extra detail costs time, needs data you may not have, and can hide errors. A third is trusting a single run of a random simulation. Typical exam questions are: define system, model and simulation; list advantages and disadvantages of simulation; state when simulation is not appropriate; and give three areas where simulation is used, with an example of each.

Recap: A system is the real thing, a model is a simplified description of it, and a simulation runs that model over time to imitate the system. We simulate when real experiments are impossible, risky, slow or costly, and when formulas cannot handle the messy rules. We do not simulate when common sense or a formula already answers the question, when data is missing, or when the study costs more than it saves. Next lesson we open up a system and name its parts: entities, attributes, events, state and resources.
key_points: A system is the real thing; a model is a simplified description that keeps only what matters for the question.
A simulation runs a model over time to imitate the real system and produce outputs like waiting time.
Simulate when real experiments are impossible, risky, slow or costly, or when formulas cannot handle the rules.
Do not simulate when common sense or an exact formula is enough, data is missing, or the study costs more than it saves.
Simulation compresses time, answers what-if questions and reveals bottlenecks.
Outputs of random simulations vary from run to run, so they need careful analysis.
Monte Carlo was named in the 1940s Manhattan Project; GPSS was one of the first simulation languages.
lessons.tip: For every system you see this week, ask yourself one question: if I had to model this, what is the one output I care about? That habit of choosing the question first is half of good modeling.
lessons.task: Stand near a shop counter, tea stall or bus stop for 15 minutes. Write down the time each person arrives and the time each person leaves. Then write two lines: what parts would a model need, and what details would you leave out?

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a model?
options: A simplified description of a system that keeps what matters for the question
quiz.explain: A model keeps the important parts for the question and drops the rest, like a bus route map.

quiz.q: What is a simulation?
options: Drawing a diagram of a system
Running a model over time to imitate a system
quiz.explain: Simulation is the imitation of a real process over time by running the model.

quiz.q: In which case should you NOT use simulation?
options: An exact formula already answers the question cheaply
The real system is too dangerous to experiment on
You want to compare three factory layouts before building
The rules are too messy for formulas
quiz.explain: If a formula or common sense answers it, simulation just adds cost.

quiz.q: Why can a year of a bank branch be simulated in seconds?
options: The computer runs a real bank faster
Customers are removed from the model
The simulation jumps from one interesting moment to the next, skipping empty time
Banks are open only one hour
quiz.explain: Time compression comes from jumping directly between events.

quiz.q: The name Monte Carlo for random-sampling methods came from...
options: A famous casino, chosen by 1940s scientists
quiz.explain: Ulam and von Neumann's group named it after the Monte Carlo casino because the method relies on chance.

lessons.title: Systems, Components and Types of Models
lessons.content:
When a doctor examines a patient, she does not just say the person looks unwell. She names parts: heart rate, temperature, blood pressure. Naming the parts is what lets her reason clearly. Modeling works the same way. Before we can simulate a bank, a bus route or a hospital, we must name its parts using a small, shared vocabulary. This lesson gives you that vocabulary and then sorts models into types, so that when you meet any new system you can quickly say what kind of model it needs.

System and environment again: A system is a collection of parts that interact to reach some purpose. Everything outside the system that still affects it is the environment. The line between them is the system boundary, and drawing it is your first modeling decision. For a bank branch study, is the ATM outside the door part of the system? If your question is about teller waiting times and ATM users never come inside, put it outside the boundary. If many customers who find the ATM broken walk in to the teller, the ATM matters and should move inside. There is no single right boundary; there is a boundary that fits your question.

Entity: An entity is an object of interest in the system, something we want to track. In a bank, customers are entities. In a factory, each shirt moving down the line is an entity. In a computer network, each data packet is an entity. Some entities move through the system and then leave, such as customers; these are often called transient or temporary entities. Others stay for the whole run, such as the tellers or machines; these are often called permanent entities or resources.

Attribute: An attribute is a property of an entity. A customer may have attributes like arrival time, type of service wanted (cash deposit, account opening) and priority (normal or VIP). A shirt may have its size and colour. Attributes travel with the entity and let the model treat different entities differently. For example, a hospital model may use the attribute severity to decide which patient the doctor sees first.

Activity: An activity is a period of time of known length, once it starts. Serving a customer for 4 minutes, cutting fabric for 90 seconds, or a bus driving from Farmgate to Mohakhali for 12 minutes are activities. The length may be fixed or random, but in the model we know it at the moment the activity begins, because we draw it from a distribution or a table. Activities are the busy times of the system.

Delay: A delay is also a period of time, but its length is not known in advance; it depends on what else happens in the system. A customer waiting in the line is in a delay: nobody can say how long she will wait until the customers in front of her are served. Textbooks sometimes call this a conditional wait, as opposed to the unconditional wait of an activity. Keeping activities and delays apart helps you design the model: activities come from data, delays come out of the simulation as results.

Event: An event is an instant when something happens that may change the state of the system. Arrival of a customer is an event. Service completion is an event. A machine breaking down is an event. Events take zero time; they are moments, not durations. An activity starts with one event and ends with another. Some events come from inside the system and are called endogenous, like a service finishing. Others come from the environment and are called exogenous, like a new customer arriving from the street.

State and state variables: The state of a system is the collection of variables that describe everything we need to know about the system at a given moment to continue the simulation. For a one-teller bank, two numbers may be enough: number of customers in line, and whether the teller is busy or idle. These are the state variables. When an event happens, some state variables change. A customer arrives: if the teller is idle, she becomes busy; otherwise the line grows by one. Choosing state variables is a key skill: too few and the model cannot continue correctly; too many and it becomes slow and confusing.

Resource: A resource is something that entities need and that is limited. Tellers, doctors, beds, machines, parking slots and phone lines are resources. When an entity wants a resource that is busy, it must wait in a queue. Resources usually have a capacity, such as 3 tellers, and a state, such as busy, idle or broken. Much of what managers want to know is about resources: how busy they are (utilisation) and whether adding one more would help.

A worked naming exercise: Take a petrol pump in Uttara. Entities: cars and motorbikes. Attributes: vehicle type, amount of fuel wanted, payment method. Resources: four nozzles and one cashier. Activities: filling fuel, paying. Delays: waiting for a free nozzle. Events: vehicle arrives, filling starts, filling ends, payment ends, vehicle leaves. State variables: number of vehicles waiting, status of each nozzle, status of the cashier. Environment: road traffic outside, time of day, fuel price news. Writing such a list before coding is the cheapest way to catch a forgotten part.

Kinds of models by form: Models can be physical, like a small scale model of a bridge in a wind tunnel or a clay model of a river delta used to study flooding. They can be mathematical, written with equations, like a formula for average waiting time. Among mathematical models, some can be solved directly by algebra or calculus; we call those analytic. When the equations are too hard to solve directly, we use numerical methods or simulation. A simulation model is a mathematical and logical model that we evaluate by running it, step by step, on a computer.

Static vs dynamic: A static model has no time in it. It represents the system at one moment, or a situation where time does not matter. Estimating the chance that three dice add up to more than 15, or estimating pi by throwing random dots, are static simulations; these are usually called Monte Carlo simulations (lessons 11 and 12). A dynamic model shows how a system changes over time, like a bank over a working day or a population over 20 years. Most of this course is about dynamic models.

Deterministic vs stochastic: A deterministic model contains no random parts. Given the same inputs, it always gives the same outputs. A dental clinic where patients arrive exactly at their appointment times and each check-up takes exactly 20 minutes is deterministic. A stochastic model has at least one random input. In a walk-in clinic, arrivals and treatment times are random, so outputs are random too. This has a big consequence: a single run of a stochastic model gives one random sample of the output, not the answer. You need many runs and statistics, which we study in lesson 24.

Continuous vs discrete systems: In a continuous system, state variables change smoothly over time. The water level in a tank that is filling, the temperature of a cup of tea that is cooling, and the speed of a car on a highway are continuous. In a discrete system, state variables change only at separate points in time. The number of customers in a bank jumps from 3 to 4 when someone arrives and back to 3 when someone leaves; between events nothing changes. Few systems are purely one or the other, but usually one view fits the question better.

Continuous vs discrete models: The model does not have to match the system's nature exactly. Traffic is made of discrete cars, but if you study traffic on a whole motorway, treating it as a continuous flow, like water in a pipe, may be simpler and accurate enough. On the other hand, a continuous chemical process may be modelled as discrete steps if you only care about when a tank becomes full. Choose the model type that answers your question most simply. Discrete-event models are covered in lessons 13 to 15; continuous models in lesson 20.

Putting the categories together: Every model gets three labels. A bank with random arrivals studied over a day: dynamic, stochastic, discrete. A cup of tea cooling, described by Newton's law of cooling: dynamic, deterministic, continuous. Estimating the chance of winning a dice game by rolling virtual dice a million times: static, stochastic, and the time question does not even arise. The most common model in this course is the discrete-event stochastic dynamic model, usually shortened to discrete-event simulation or DES.

Open and closed systems: A small extra idea is whether entities come from an outside population that is effectively endless, called an open system, or circulate among a fixed group, called a closed system. A bank serving the public is open. A computer lab with 30 students who keep sending print jobs to one printer is closed: at most 30 jobs can ever wait, and when many are waiting, fewer new jobs are created. This changes how arrivals behave, and we will meet it again as finite vs infinite calling population in lesson 16.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka city bus route: Suppose BRTC wants to know how many buses to run on a route. Entities: passengers and buses. Passenger attributes: boarding stop and destination stop. Bus attributes: capacity of 50 seats and current load. Resources: buses themselves, and road space. Events: passenger arrives at stop, bus arrives at stop, bus departs, passenger alights. Activities: driving between stops, boarding. Delays: waiting at the stop, waiting in traffic. Model type: dynamic, stochastic, discrete. Output measures: average waiting time at stops and how full buses are.

Real-life example 2, a water reservoir: A water treatment plant fills a reservoir from the river and the city draws water from it. The main state variable is the water volume, which changes smoothly as inflow and outflow rates change. Rainfall and city demand are random, so the model is stochastic. Time matters, so it is dynamic. Volume changes smoothly, so it is continuous. Questions like will the reservoir run dry in April if rainfall is 30 percent below normal are answered by running this continuous model many times with different random rainfall.

Common mistakes: Students often confuse an event with an activity; remember an event is an instant, an activity is a duration. Another mix-up is calling every waiting time an activity; waiting in line is a delay because its length is not known in advance. Some think a stochastic model gives a fixed answer; it gives a random output. And many forget to draw the boundary and end up modeling the whole city when the question was about one counter.

What exams ask: Define entity, attribute, activity, event, state and resource with one example each. Classify a given system (bank, traffic light, epidemic) as discrete or continuous, static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic. List the components of a given system in a table. Explain the difference between endogenous and exogenous events. Explain why a discrete model can be used for a continuous system or the reverse.

Recap: A system sits inside an environment, separated by a boundary you choose. Its parts are entities with attributes, resources, activities of known length, delays of unknown length, and events that change the state variables. Models can be physical, analytic or simulation models, and each model is static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic, continuous or discrete. Next lesson shows the full journey of a simulation study, from the first question to the final recommendation.
key_points: The system boundary separates the system from its environment and depends on your question.
Entities are tracked objects; attributes are their properties; resources are limited things entities need.
An activity has a known length once it starts; a delay (like waiting in line) has a length decided by the simulation.
An event is an instant that may change state; endogenous events come from inside, exogenous from outside.
State variables are the minimum information needed to continue the simulation from any moment.
Every model is static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic, continuous or discrete.
The main model of this course is the dynamic, stochastic, discrete-event simulation (DES).
lessons.tip: Make a habit of the six-column table: entities, attributes, resources, activities, events, state variables. Fill it for any system before writing a single line of code.
lessons.task: Pick your home kitchen during dinner time or a school canteen. Write a table listing at least two entities, two attributes, one resource, two activities, one delay, three events and two state variables. Then label the model as static or dynamic, deterministic or stochastic, discrete or continuous.

quiz.q: A customer standing in a line whose wait depends on the people ahead is an example of...
quiz.explain: A delay has a length that is not known in advance and comes out of the simulation.

quiz.q: Which of these is an event?
options: The instant a machine breaks down
quiz.explain: Events are instants that may change the state; durations are activities.

quiz.q: A cup of tea cooling according to Newton's law of cooling is best described as...
quiz.explain: Temperature changes smoothly over time with no randomness in the basic law.

quiz.q: For a one-teller bank, which pair of state variables is usually enough?
options: Number in line and teller busy or idle
quiz.explain: These two describe everything needed to continue the simulation.

quiz.q: Why does a stochastic model need many runs?
options: Because the computer forgets the result
Because each run gives one random sample of the output, not the true answer
quiz.explain: Random inputs make outputs random, so we use statistics over many runs.

lessons.title: Steps in a Simulation Study
lessons.content:
Cooking biryani for a wedding is not just putting rice in a pot. You first ask how many guests are coming, then make a shopping list, buy ingredients, cook, taste, fix the salt, cook the big batch, serve, and finally check if everyone was fed. Skip the tasting step and you may serve 300 people salty rice. A simulation study is the same kind of journey. The coding part, which beginners think is the whole job, is only one step in the middle. This lesson walks through the classic 12 steps from the Banks, Carson, Nelson and Nicol textbook and shows them on a real-looking example.

Why a process at all: Many simulation projects fail not because the code is wrong but because the wrong question was answered, the data was poor, or the manager never believed the result. A clear process protects against these failures. It also tells everyone what to expect and when. Think of the 12 steps as a checklist that experienced modelers carry in their heads.

Step 1, problem formulation: Every study starts with a statement of the problem. Who has the problem, and what exactly is it? Bad statement: the pharmacy is slow. Good statement: during 10 am to 1 pm, patients at the outpatient pharmacy of our hospital wait on average more than 40 minutes for medicine, and the director wants it under 15 minutes. The modeler and the person who owns the problem must agree on this statement. Often the first statement changes as people talk; that is normal and healthy.

Step 2, setting objectives and overall project plan: Objectives are the questions the simulation must answer. For the pharmacy: how many counters are needed to keep average wait under 15 minutes? Would a separate counter for pre-paid prescriptions help? The project plan lists the alternative designs to be studied, the measures used to compare them (average wait, maximum queue length, staff idle time), who works on the study, how long it takes and what it costs. This is also the moment to ask whether simulation is the right tool at all, using the checklist from lesson 1.

Step 3, model conceptualisation: Here you build the model on paper before any code. Using the vocabulary of lesson 2, list entities (patients, prescriptions), resources (counters, pharmacists, the medicine store), events (arrival, start of service, end of service), activities (checking a prescription, picking medicine, billing) and the queue rules. Start with a simple model and add detail only where needed. Experienced modelers say: begin simple, then enrich. A flowchart showing the path of a patient is a good output of this step. It is also wise to show it to the people who work in the pharmacy, because they know rules you will never guess.

Step 4, data collection: Data collection runs side by side with model building, because the model decides what data is needed and the data often changes the model. For the pharmacy we need arrival times of patients, time per prescription broken into checking, picking and billing, number of items per prescription, staff break times and how often a medicine is out of stock. Some of this comes from the hospital computer log, some from a student with a stopwatch for a few days. Data collection usually takes a big share of the project time. Lesson 22 is all about turning this raw data into input models.

Step 5, model translation: Now the conceptual model becomes a computer program. You can use a general language like Python, C++ or Java, a library like SimPy, or a dedicated tool like Arena, AnyLogic or Simio. General languages give full control but take more code; dedicated tools are faster to build with, include animation and statistics, but cost money and limit unusual logic. For a student project, a Python program with a priority queue (lesson 15) is a fine choice.

Step 6, verified? Verification asks: does the program do what the conceptual model says? It is a debugging question. You trace a few customers by hand, check that nobody is served before arriving, check that the number in the queue never goes negative, run a simple case where the answer is known from a formula, and watch the animation for strange behaviour. If verification fails, go back to step 5 and fix the code. Lesson 23 covers techniques in detail.

Step 7, validated? Validation asks: is the model an accurate enough picture of the real system for our question? You compare the model's output for the current situation with real measurements. If the real pharmacy has 3 counters and patients really wait about 42 minutes, the model with 3 counters should give something close, say 38 to 46 minutes. If the model says 12 minutes, something important is missing. Maybe pharmacists actually leave the counter to fetch medicine from a back store. You then go back to steps 3 and 4. This loop of comparing and adjusting is called calibration.

Step 8, experimental design: Now you decide exactly which alternatives to simulate and how. For each design: how long is each run, how many independent runs (replications), do we need a warm-up period, and what random number streams do we use? A typical plan for the pharmacy: test 3, 4 and 5 counters, with and without a fast counter for pre-paid prescriptions, so 6 designs, each simulated for the 10 am to 1 pm peak on 20 independent days.

Step 9, production runs and analysis: Run the experiments and estimate the performance measures for each design, with confidence intervals so you know how precise each number is. Compare designs carefully: a difference of 2 minutes between two designs might be real, or just noise from randomness. Lesson 24 teaches how to tell.

Step 10, more runs? Look at the results and ask whether you need more replications to tighten confidence intervals, or new designs suggested by what you learned. Maybe 4 counters are almost enough, and 4 counters plus one floating helper at peak time becomes a new design worth testing. Simulation is iterative; good questions often appear only after the first results.

Step 11, documentation and reporting: There are two kinds of documentation. Program documentation explains the code, its assumptions and how to run it, so someone else can reuse or check it. Progress and final reports explain to decision makers what was studied, what was found, how sure we are, and what is recommended. A short, clear report with one chart and a table of designs with average wait and confidence intervals beats a hundred pages of output nobody reads.

Step 12, implementation: The real test is whether the recommendation is used and works. If the manager was involved in steps 1, 2 and 7, implementation is much more likely. After implementation, measure again: did average waiting time actually fall? If the real result differs a lot from the model's prediction, learn from it; the model may have missed something, and that lesson makes the next model better.

The four phases: These 12 steps are often grouped into four phases. Discovery or orientation is steps 1 and 2. Model building and data collection are steps 3 to 7. Running the model is steps 8 to 10. Implementation is steps 11 and 12. The arrows do not only go forward: verification failure sends you back to coding, and validation failure sends you back to conceptualisation and data. Real projects often loop between steps 3 and 7 three or four times before the model is good enough. That is not a sign of failure; it is how understanding grows. Plan time for these loops in step 2, because a schedule that assumes everything works the first time is the most common reason simulation projects run late.

Worked example, the whole pharmacy story in numbers: Data shows that at peak, about 120 prescriptions arrive per hour and one counter handles one prescription in 2 minutes on average, so one counter can do about 30 per hour. With 3 counters, the capacity is 3 x 30 = 90 per hour, which is less than 120. A line that receives more than it can serve grows without limit, which matches the angry complaints. Four counters give exactly 120 per hour, which still is not enough, because with random arrivals and random service times a system running at 100 percent of capacity also has an ever-growing queue. Five counters give 150 per hour, so counters are busy about 120 / 150 = 80 percent of the time. Simple arithmetic already says at least 5 counters are needed; the simulation then tells us how long the wait is with 5 and whether a fast counter helps further.

Why the arithmetic is not the end: That quick capacity check is valuable and you should always do it first. But it ignores the fact that some patients bring 12 items and some bring 1, that pharmacists take breaks, and that arrivals bunch up after the doctors' morning rounds. Those details decide whether the average wait with 5 counters is 6 minutes or 25 minutes. This is exactly where simulation earns its place.

Real-life example 2, a garment factory sewing line: A factory in Gazipur wants to raise output of a sewing line from 800 to 1,000 shirts per day. Problem formulation: where is the bottleneck? Objectives: which operation needs an extra machine or operator? Conceptual model: 12 operations in sequence, buffers between them, breakdowns. Data: time studies for each operation, breakdown records. Validation: the model with today's setup should produce about 800 shirts per day. Experiments: add a machine at each candidate operation in turn. Result: extra machine at collar attaching gives the biggest gain. Implementation: done, and output measured again after a month.

Common mistakes: Jumping straight to coding without a clear problem statement. Collecting data that is easy to get rather than data the model needs. Building every detail at once so nothing works for weeks. Skipping validation because the model looks impressive. Running each design once and comparing single numbers. Writing a report full of jargon that the decision maker cannot use. And keeping the client away until the end, so they never trust the result.

What exams ask: List and explain the steps of a simulation study, often with a flowchart showing the loops back from verification and validation. Explain the difference between verification and validation. Explain why data collection and model building overlap. Apply the steps to a given case such as a bank, hospital or traffic junction.

Recap: A simulation study is a journey of 12 steps: problem formulation, objectives and project plan, model conceptualisation, data collection, model translation, verification, validation, experimental design, production runs and analysis, more runs, documentation and reporting, and implementation. Coding is only one step. Simple capacity arithmetic first, simulation for the messy details, and involvement of the real owners of the problem from start to end. Next lesson we refresh the probability we need to describe randomness.
key_points: A simulation study has 12 steps; writing code is only step 5.
A sharp problem statement and agreed objectives come before any modeling.
Model conceptualisation and data collection go side by side and influence each other.
Verification checks the program matches the conceptual model; validation checks the model matches reality.
Experimental design fixes the alternatives, run length, number of replications and warm-up.
Do a quick capacity check first: if arrivals reach or exceed capacity, the line grows without limit.
Documentation, clear reporting and involving the decision maker make implementation likely.
lessons.tip: Before writing code for any project, write one sentence: who has the problem, what measure is bad, and what target would make them happy. If you cannot write it, you are not ready to model.
lessons.task: Choose a queue you know well (a bKash agent shop, a canteen, a photocopy shop). Write steps 1, 2 and 3 for it on paper: a one-line problem statement, two objectives with the measures you would compare, and a simple flowchart of a customer's path.

quiz.q: Which step asks whether the program correctly implements the conceptual model?
quiz.explain: Verification is about building the model right, like debugging.

quiz.q: Validation fails: the model says 12 minutes wait but reality is 42 minutes. What should you do?
options: Run the model once more and pick the closer result
Go back to conceptualisation and data to find what is missing
quiz.explain: Validation failure means the model misses something real, so revisit model and data.

quiz.q: Prescriptions arrive at 120 per hour and each counter serves 30 per hour. What is the minimum number of counters for a stable line?
quiz.explain: 4 counters give exactly 120 per hour, which is 100 percent load and still unstable; 5 give 150.

quiz.q: Why do data collection and model conceptualisation overlap?
options: Because both are done by the same computer
Because the model decides which data is needed and the data can change the model
quiz.explain: Each one shapes the other, so they run side by side.

quiz.q: In experimental design you mainly decide...
options: Which alternatives to run, run length, number of replications and warm-up
quiz.explain: Experimental design fixes how each design will be simulated.

lessons.title: Probability Review for Simulation
lessons.content:
Ask a tea stall owner how long it takes to make one cup and he will say about a minute. But it is never exactly a minute: sometimes 40 seconds, sometimes 90 when the kettle is empty. Ask when the next customer will come and he will laugh: who knows, maybe in 10 seconds, maybe in 5 minutes. Simulation must capture this kind of uncertainty honestly, and the language for uncertainty is probability. You studied it in Probability & Statistics (deep-cse-2-6). This lesson is a focused refresher: only the ideas a simulation builder uses every day, with the simulation reason for each.

Experiment and sample space: A random experiment is any action whose result we cannot predict exactly, like rolling a dice, timing a service or counting arrivals in an hour. The sample space is the set of all possible results. For one dice it is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. For a service time it is all positive real numbers. An event (in the probability sense, different from a simulation event) is a subset of the sample space, like rolling an even number, {2, 4, 6}, whose probability is 3/6 = 0.5.

Random variable: A random variable is a rule that attaches a number to each outcome of an experiment. The number of customers in an hour, the time a teller takes, the demand for rice tomorrow: all random variables. We write them with capital letters, like X, and a particular value with a small letter, like x. In simulation, almost every input is a random variable, and almost every output is a random variable too, which is why outputs change from run to run.

Discrete random variables: A discrete random variable takes separate values you can list, like 0, 1, 2, 3 customers. It is described by its probability mass function, PMF, written p(x) = P(X = x). The rules: each p(x) is between 0 and 1, and all of them add up to 1. Example: a small shop's daily demand for gas cylinders is 0 with probability 0.1, 1 with 0.3, 2 with 0.4 and 3 with 0.2. Check: 0.1 + 0.3 + 0.4 + 0.2 = 1. Good.

Continuous random variables: A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, like service time 2.37 minutes. The chance of any single exact value is zero, so we describe it with a probability density function, PDF, written f(x). Probability is the area under f(x) between two points: P(a <= X <= b) is the area from a to b. The total area is 1. Height of f(x) is not a probability; it can even be bigger than 1 if the interval is short. This confuses many students, so remember: in continuous land, probabilities are areas.

Cumulative distribution function: The CDF, F(x) = P(X <= x), works for both kinds. It starts at 0 on the far left, never goes down, and reaches 1 on the far right. For the gas cylinder demand: F(0) = 0.1, F(1) = 0.4, F(2) = 0.8, F(3) = 1.0. The CDF is the star of random variate generation (lesson 9): to create a random demand we pick a uniform random number R between 0 and 1 and find where it falls in these cumulative steps. R = 0.65 falls between 0.4 and 0.8, so demand is 2.

Expectation: The expected value E(X), also called the mean, is the long-run average. For a discrete variable, E(X) = sum of x times p(x). For a fair dice: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5. For the gas cylinders: 0 x 0.1 + 1 x 0.3 + 2 x 0.4 + 3 x 0.2 = 0 + 0.3 + 0.8 + 0.6 = 1.7 cylinders per day. You never sell 1.7 cylinders on a real day, but over 100 days you expect about 170. For a continuous variable, the sum becomes an integral of x times f(x).

Variance and standard deviation: The mean tells you the centre; variance tells you the spread. V(X) = E[(X - mean) squared], or the handy shortcut V(X) = E(X squared) - (E(X)) squared. For the dice, E(X squared) = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36) / 6 = 91 / 6, about 15.17, so V = 15.17 - 3.5 x 3.5 = 15.17 - 12.25 = 2.92 (exactly 35/12). Standard deviation is the square root, about 1.71. In simulation, spread matters as much as the mean: two cashiers who both average 2 minutes but one is steady and one swings between 30 seconds and 6 minutes create very different queues, as lesson 18 will show.

A continuous example, the uniform: The uniform distribution on [a, b] has a flat density f(x) = 1/(b - a). Its mean is (a + b) / 2 and its variance is (b - a) squared / 12. For a bus that arrives at a random moment between 2 and 8 minutes from now: mean 5 minutes, variance 36 / 12 = 3, and P(X <= 5) = (5 - 2) / (8 - 2) = 0.5. The special case on [0, 1], called U(0,1), is the raw material of every simulation; lesson 7 is about making it on a computer.

Independence: Two random variables are independent if knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Formally, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B). In basic queue models we assume that the gap between two arrivals is independent of the previous gap, and that service times are independent of arrival times. These assumptions make models simpler, but you must check them. In reality, a cashier under a long queue may work faster, so service time is not fully independent of queue length.

Conditional probability: P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B), the chance of A when we already know B happened. Simulation uses this all the time in branching logic: given the patient is an emergency case, 70 percent go to the resuscitation room. Writing such branch probabilities correctly is part of building the conceptual model.

Sum of random variables: The mean of a sum is the sum of the means, always: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y). The variance of a sum equals the sum of variances only if the variables are independent (or at least uncorrelated). If a patient spends a random registration time with mean 3 minutes and an independent random doctor time with mean 10 minutes, total mean is 13 minutes. This rule is used in project risk analysis (lesson 12) and in generating Erlang variables (lesson 10).

Law of large numbers: If you repeat an experiment many times and take the average, the average gets closer and closer to the true mean. Flip a fair coin 10 times and you may see 7 heads, a proportion of 0.7. Flip it 10,000 times and the proportion will almost surely be very close to 0.5. This law is the reason simulation works at all: we cannot compute the true average waiting time directly, so we generate many customers and many runs, and the average settles near the truth.

Central limit theorem: The average of many independent observations is approximately normally distributed, whatever the shape of the original distribution, as long as its variance is finite. If each replication of a bank simulation gives one average waiting time, then the average over 30 replications behaves roughly like a bell curve around the true mean. That is what lets us build confidence intervals for simulation output in lesson 24. The spread of that average shrinks like 1 over the square root of the number of observations, the same rule that governs Monte Carlo error in lesson 11.

Sample statistics: From simulation output we compute the sample mean, X-bar = sum of values / n, and the sample variance, S squared = sum of (value - X-bar) squared / (n - 1). The n - 1 instead of n makes S squared an unbiased estimate of the true variance. Example: replications give average waits 4, 6, 5, 7, 3 minutes. X-bar = 25 / 5 = 5. Deviations -1, 1, 0, 2, -2; squares 1, 1, 0, 4, 4; sum 10; S squared = 10 / 4 = 2.5; S is about 1.58. Notice the difference between S and the standard deviation of the mean: S describes how much single replications differ, while S divided by the square root of n, here 1.58 / 2.24, about 0.71, describes how much the average of five replications would wobble if we repeated the whole experiment.

Real-life example 1, a bKash agent shop: An agent in Mirpur records how many customers come between 6 and 7 pm over 50 evenings. The counts are a discrete random variable. She builds a frequency table, divides each count by 50 to get an estimated PMF, adds them to get the CDF, and computes the mean, say 22 customers, and the standard deviation, say 4.5. A simulation of her shop can now generate realistic evening loads, and she can see that on 1 evening in 10 or so she gets around 28 or more customers and needs her cousin to help.

Real-life example 2, cricket batting: A batsman's runs per innings is a random variable with a strongly skewed shape: many low scores, a few big ones. His average might be 35 but his median far lower. A simulation of a cricket series that only used the average 35 every innings would never produce a collapse or a century and would wrongly estimate the chance of winning. Modeling the whole distribution, not just the mean, is the lesson here, and it applies equally to service times and demand.

Common mistakes: Using only the mean and ignoring variance. Thinking a PDF value is a probability. Forgetting that the CDF never decreases. Assuming independence without checking. Dividing by n instead of n - 1 for sample variance. Believing that the law of large numbers works fast; with very skewed data you may need many thousands of observations before averages settle.

What exams ask: Given a PMF, check it is valid and compute the mean, variance and CDF. Given a simple PDF such as f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], find a probability by area (P(X <= 0.5) = 0.25) and the mean (2/3). State the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem and explain why they matter for simulation. Compute sample mean and variance of given simulation outputs.

Recap: Random variables describe uncertain inputs and outputs. Discrete ones use a PMF, continuous ones a PDF where probability is area, and both have a CDF that climbs from 0 to 1. Mean is the centre, variance the spread, and both matter. Independence is an assumption to check. The law of large numbers says averages of many runs approach the truth, and the central limit theorem lets us measure how close. Next lesson tours the specific distributions simulation uses most.
key_points: Almost every simulation input and output is a random variable, so outputs vary from run to run.
Discrete variables have a PMF; continuous ones have a PDF where probability equals area.
The CDF F(x) = P(X <= x) climbs from 0 to 1 and is the key to generating random values.
Mean is the long-run average; variance measures spread, and spread changes queues as much as the mean.
E(X+Y) = E(X) + E(Y) always; variances add only for independent (uncorrelated) variables.
The law of large numbers is why averaging many simulation runs approaches the true value.
The central limit theorem makes averages roughly normal, which allows confidence intervals.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see an average in a problem, immediately ask: and what is the spread? Training this reflex will save you from the most common modeling error.
lessons.task: Roll a dice (or use a phone dice app) 30 times. Compute the average after 5, 10, 20 and 30 rolls and write them down. Watch how the average moves toward 3.5. Then compute the sample variance of your 30 rolls and compare with 35/12, about 2.92.

quiz.q: For a continuous random variable, probability is given by...
options: The height of the PDF at one point
The area under the PDF between two points
quiz.explain: In continuous distributions, probabilities are areas under the density curve.

quiz.q: Demand is 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2. What is the mean demand?
Why does averaging many simulation runs get close to the true mean?
quiz.explain: The law of large numbers says long-run averages approach the expected value.

quiz.q: Sample values 4, 6, 5, 7, 3. What is the sample variance using n - 1?
quiz.explain: Squared deviations sum to 10; 10 / 4 = 2.5.

quiz.q: Uniform distribution on [2, 8]: what is the variance?

lessons.title: Distributions Used in Simulation
lessons.content:
A tailor in Gausia market keeps a few standard patterns: one for shirts, one for panjabis, one for kameez. When a customer comes, he does not invent a pattern from nothing; he picks the closest one and adjusts it to the measurements. Probability distributions are the modeler's standard patterns. Arrivals, service times, machine lifetimes, daily demand: each kind of randomness has a few well-known patterns that fit it well. Pick the right pattern, adjust its parameters to your data, and your model's randomness looks like reality. This lesson is the tailor's pattern book.

Why named distributions: You could always describe randomness with a raw table of observed values (an empirical distribution, discussed at the end). Named distributions are useful because they are compact (two numbers instead of a thousand), smooth out gaps in limited data, can produce values outside the range you happened to observe, and often come with a reason why they fit, such as the exponential for completely random arrivals. Knowing the reason behind each distribution is more valuable than remembering its formula.

Bernoulli: The simplest random variable: one trial with two outcomes, success (1) with probability p and failure (0) with probability 1 - p. Mean p, variance p(1 - p). In simulation it models yes/no branches: does this customer want a SIM card replacement (p = 0.15)? Is this item defective (p = 0.02)? Each time an entity reaches such a branch, the model draws a Bernoulli.

Binomial: Count the successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with the same p. P(X = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 - p)^(n - k). Mean np, variance np(1 - p). Example: a batch of 10 bulbs, each defective with probability 0.1. P(no defective) = 0.9^10, about 0.349. P(exactly one) = 10 x 0.1 x 0.9^9, about 0.387. Mean defects 1, variance 0.9. Use it for number of defective items in a lot, number of passengers who show up out of those who booked, or number of students who pass out of a class.

Geometric: Count the trials until the first success. With success probability p on each trial, P(first success on trial k) = (1 - p)^(k - 1) p, and the mean is 1/p. Example: a salesperson succeeds on 20 percent of calls. The chance the first sale is on the third call is 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.2 = 0.128, and on average she needs 1/0.2 = 5 calls. It is the discrete cousin of the exponential and also has the memoryless property.

Poisson: Counts how many events happen in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate. P(X = k) = e^(-lambda) lambda^k / k!, where lambda is the average count. Mean and variance are both lambda, a useful quick check on data. Example: a bKash agent gets on average 3 customers per 10 minutes. P(0 customers in 10 minutes) = e^(-3), about 0.050. P(exactly 2) = e^(-3) x 9 / 2, about 0.224. P(3 or more) = 1 - (0.050 + 0.149 + 0.224), about 0.577. Use it for counts of arrivals, phone calls, accidents, typos per page and defects per metre of cloth.

Uniform: Every value in [a, b] is equally likely. Mean (a + b)/2, variance (b - a)^2 / 12. Use it when you know only the minimum and maximum and nothing about which values are more likely, for example a train that is known to be between 0 and 10 minutes late. It is a weak assumption about the real world but the most important distribution in the computer, because every other random variable is built from U(0, 1) numbers.

Exponential: The time between completely random events. Density f(x) = lambda e^(-lambda x) for x >= 0, CDF F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x), mean 1/lambda, standard deviation also 1/lambda. Lambda is a rate, like 0.5 customers per minute, giving a mean gap of 2 minutes. P(gap > 2 minutes) = e^(-0.5 x 2) = e^(-1), about 0.368. Use it for interarrival times of independent customers, and sometimes for service times when most jobs are short and a few are long (call centre calls). Lesson 6 shows that Poisson counts and exponential gaps are two sides of the same coin.

The memoryless property: The exponential is the only continuous distribution with this property: P(X > s + t given X > s) = P(X > t). In words, if you have already waited s minutes for the next customer, the chance of waiting t more minutes is the same as if you had just started. Check with lambda = 0.5: P(X > 4 given X > 2) = e^(-2) / e^(-1) = e^(-1), same as P(X > 2). This makes exponential models mathematically easy, but be careful: a machine that wears out is NOT memoryless; an old machine is more likely to fail soon than a new one.

Normal: The bell curve, with mean mu and standard deviation sigma. About 68 percent of values fall within one sigma of the mean, 95 percent within two, 99.7 percent within three. If package weights are normal with mean 10 kg and sigma 2 kg, then about 68 percent weigh between 8 and 12 kg, and about 95 percent between 6 and 14 kg. Use it for measurement errors, heights and weights, and sums of many small effects (because of the central limit theorem). Warning: the normal allows negative values, so for service times with a small mean and large spread it can produce impossible negative times; truncate it or choose another distribution.

Triangular: Defined by a minimum a, most likely value c (the mode) and maximum b. Mean (a + c + b) / 3. When there is no data but an expert can say a task takes at least 2 hours, usually 4 hours and at most 9 hours, triangular(2, 4, 9) is a sensible guess, with mean 5 hours. The chance it takes at most 4 hours is (c - a) / (b - a) = 2/7, about 0.29. It is widely used in project planning and early-stage models (more in lesson 22).

Erlang and gamma: The sum of k independent exponential times each with mean 1/(k mu) follows an Erlang distribution with k phases and mean 1/mu. For example, a service with 3 steps (check, pack, bill), each exponential with mean 2 minutes, has total time Erlang with mean 6 minutes, and it is less variable than a single exponential with mean 6. Larger k means less variability; as k grows very large it becomes almost constant. The gamma distribution generalises Erlang to non-integer shapes. Both fit service and repair times that are made of several stages.

Weibull: Very popular for lifetimes and time to failure. It has a shape parameter beta and a scale parameter. When beta is less than 1, the failure rate decreases over time (early failures, like bad components failing in the first weeks). When beta equals 1, it becomes the exponential (constant failure rate). When beta is greater than 1, the failure rate increases (wear-out, like brake pads or bearings). This one parameter lets a reliability engineer describe the bathtub-shaped life of machines piece by piece.

Lognormal: If the logarithm of X is normal, X is lognormal. It is always positive and has a long right tail. It fits repair times, task times where most are moderate but a few take very long, incomes, and file sizes. It is a good alternative to a truncated normal for service times. The reason it appears so often is multiplication: when a time is the product of many small independent factors (a slightly slow worker, times a slightly hard job, times a slightly busy store), its logarithm is a sum of small effects, so by the central limit theorem the logarithm is close to normal.

Empirical distributions: When no named distribution fits, or for a quick start, use the data itself. For discrete data, the table of observed relative frequencies is the PMF. For continuous data, the observed values define a piecewise linear CDF between points. Empirical distributions reproduce the data's shape exactly, which is good, but they cannot produce values beyond the observed minimum and maximum, and they copy every accident of a small sample. Lesson 9 shows how to sample from them.

Which distribution for what: A practical cheat sheet. Count of arrivals in a period: Poisson. Time between random arrivals: exponential. Service time with several stages: Erlang or gamma. Service or repair time with a long tail: lognormal or Weibull. Time to failure of equipment: Weibull (or exponential for constant failure rate). Demand per day in small whole numbers: Poisson, binomial or an empirical table. Expert guess with no data: triangular or uniform. Measurement errors and sums of many effects: normal. Yes/no decisions: Bernoulli.

Real-life example 1, a mobile phone service centre: Customers arrive at random through the day at a rate of 12 per hour, so arrivals per 15-minute block are Poisson with lambda 3 and gaps are exponential with mean 5 minutes. A fixed repair has 3 stages (diagnosis, part replacement, testing) and is modelled as Erlang with 3 phases. Whether a phone is still under warranty is a Bernoulli with p = 0.4. The time until a repaired screen fails again is Weibull with shape greater than 1, because screens wear out. Four distributions, each chosen for a reason.

Real-life example 2, a grocery shop's daily rice demand: The shop owner in Khulna records daily sales of 25 kg rice bags for 60 days. Sales are whole numbers from 4 to 11 with a peak at 7. He compares the data with a Poisson with lambda equal to the sample mean. If the sample variance is close to the mean, Poisson is a good fit; if the variance is much larger (some days have weddings), he uses an empirical table instead. That choice feeds the inventory simulation of lesson 19.

Common mistakes: Using the normal for times that cannot be negative. Using the exponential for activities that clearly have a minimum time (nobody pays at a counter in 0 seconds). Confusing rate lambda with mean 1/lambda. Fitting a distribution only because it is famous. Forgetting that the Poisson's mean equals its variance and not checking this in data.

What exams ask: Write the PMF or PDF, mean and variance of common distributions. Compute Poisson, binomial or exponential probabilities with given numbers. Prove or explain the memoryless property. Say which distribution fits a given situation and why. Explain the relation between Poisson and exponential.

Recap: Distributions are standard patterns of randomness. Bernoulli, binomial, geometric and Poisson count things; uniform, exponential, normal, triangular, Erlang, Weibull and lognormal measure times and amounts. Each has a reason for fitting certain situations. Choose with the reason in mind, check against data, and remember an empirical table is always a fallback. Next lesson digs into the Poisson process, the standard model of random arrivals.
key_points: Named distributions are compact patterns of randomness; know the reason each one fits.
Poisson counts events in an interval; mean and variance are both lambda.
Exponential gaps between random events have mean 1/lambda and are memoryless.
Normal fits sums of many small effects but can give impossible negative times.
Triangular(min, mode, max) is the standard guess when only an expert's estimate exists.
Erlang (sum of exponential stages) is less variable; Weibull shape tells early failure vs wear-out.
Empirical distributions copy data exactly but cannot go beyond observed values.
lessons.tip: Make a one-page cheat sheet with three columns: distribution, what it models, and the one-line reason why. Revise the reason column, not just the formulas.
lessons.task: Count how many messages you receive on your phone in each of 20 ten-minute blocks. Compute the mean and the sample variance of the counts. If they are close, your messages behave a bit like a Poisson process; if the variance is much larger, think about why (group chats arrive in bursts).

quiz.q: An agent gets on average 3 customers per 10 minutes, Poisson. What is P(no customers in 10 minutes)?
Which distribution is memoryless among continuous distributions?
quiz.explain: Only the exponential has P(X > s + t given X > s) = P(X > t).

quiz.q: A Weibull lifetime with shape greater than 1 describes...
options: Wear-out, where failure rate increases with age
quiz.explain: Shape above 1 means older items fail more readily.

quiz.q: An expert says a task takes at least 2, most likely 4 and at most 9 hours. The usual choice is...
quiz.explain: Triangular uses exactly min, mode and max; its mean here is 5.

quiz.q: Why is the normal often a poor choice for short service times?
quiz.explain: With a small mean and large spread, the normal gives negative values, which are impossible for times.

lessons.title: The Poisson Process and Arrival Modeling
lessons.content:
Sit at a bKash agent shop on a weekday afternoon and watch people come in. Nobody coordinates with anybody. A garments worker comes to cash out, then a student sending money home, then two minutes of nothing, then three people almost together. Each person decides on their own, for their own reasons. When many independent people each make their own small decision to come, a beautiful mathematical pattern appears, called the Poisson process. It is the standard model of random arrivals in simulation and queuing theory, and almost every simulation you build will use it somewhere.

Counting process: Let N(t) be the number of arrivals from time 0 up to time t. N(0) = 0, N(t) only takes whole numbers, it never goes down, and it jumps by one each time someone arrives. A function like this is called a counting process. If you plot it, you get a staircase that rises one step at each arrival, with steps spaced unevenly. Different arrival patterns give differently shaped staircases; the Poisson process is the most random one possible at a given average rate.

The three assumptions: A counting process is a Poisson process with rate lambda if three things hold. First, arrivals come one at a time: two people never arrive at exactly the same instant. Second, the number of arrivals in any interval depends only on the length of the interval, not on when it starts (stationary increments): the next 10 minutes look statistically like any other 10 minutes. Third, the numbers of arrivals in non-overlapping intervals are independent (independent increments): a busy 10 minutes does not make the next 10 busier or quieter. These are assumptions about the world, and you must ask whether your system obeys them.

Why many independent customers give a Poisson process: Imagine 10,000 people in a neighbourhood, and each one has a tiny chance of visiting the agent in any given minute, independently. The count in a minute is binomial with huge n and tiny p. Mathematics shows that such a binomial is extremely close to a Poisson with mean np. This is why the Poisson process shows up in so many places: calls to a call centre, cars at a toll plaza at night, requests to a web server, radioactive decays. Many independent sources, each rarely active, add up to Poisson.

Result 1, counts are Poisson: In a Poisson process with rate lambda, the number of arrivals in any interval of length t follows a Poisson distribution with mean lambda t: P(N(t) = n) = e^(-lambda t) (lambda t)^n / n!. Example: the agent's customers arrive at lambda = 18 per hour = 0.3 per minute. In 10 minutes the expected count is 3. The chance of exactly 3 arrivals is e^(-3) x 27 / 6, about 0.224. The chance of 1 or fewer is e^(-3)(1 + 3), about 0.199.

Result 2, gaps are exponential: The time between consecutive arrivals, called the interarrival time, follows an exponential distribution with mean 1/lambda, and successive gaps are independent. Here the mean gap is 1 / 0.3, about 3.33 minutes. The chance that nobody arrives in the next 5 minutes equals the chance the gap exceeds 5 minutes: e^(-0.3 x 5) = e^(-1.5), about 0.223. Notice we got this both ways: as P(N(5) = 0) from the Poisson formula and as P(gap > 5) from the exponential. These are the same event seen from two sides.

Why this matters for simulation: Results 1 and 2 give us a very simple recipe for simulating Poisson arrivals. Start at time 0. Generate an exponential gap with mean 1/lambda (lesson 9 shows how: gap = -ln(1 - R) / lambda, where R is a uniform random number). The first arrival happens at that time. Generate another gap and add it to get the second arrival. Keep going. You never need to generate counts directly. Every discrete-event simulation from lesson 13 onwards uses this recipe for its arrival events.

A tiny worked trace: lambda = 0.3 per minute. Suppose the random numbers give gaps 1.2, 4.7, 0.4 and 6.1 minutes. Then arrivals happen at times 1.2, 5.9, 6.3 and 12.4 minutes. Notice the bunching: two people arrived within 0.4 minutes, then a long quiet stretch of 6.1 minutes. Beginners often think random means evenly spread; in fact true randomness looks clumpy. That clumping is exactly what creates queues even when the server is fast enough on average.

Memoryless arrivals: Because gaps are exponential, the process is memoryless. If no customer has come for 8 minutes, the next customer is not due; the expected remaining wait is still 3.33 minutes. Shopkeepers often feel someone must come soon after a long quiet spell. Under a Poisson model, that feeling is wrong. This property is also what makes the Poisson process easy to analyse in queuing theory (lesson 17).

Merging streams: If two independent Poisson streams with rates lambda1 and lambda2 arrive at the same place, the combined stream is a Poisson process with rate lambda1 + lambda2. If 10 cash-out customers and 8 send-money customers per hour arrive independently, total arrivals form a Poisson process with rate 18 per hour. This is why the many-independent-sources argument works: merging many small Poisson streams gives one big Poisson stream.

Splitting streams: Go the other way. If each arrival of a Poisson process with rate lambda is independently sent to type A with probability p and type B with probability 1 - p, then type A arrivals form a Poisson process with rate p lambda, type B with rate (1 - p) lambda, and the two are independent. If 30 percent of the agent's 18 customers per hour want cash-out, cash-out customers arrive as Poisson with rate 5.4 per hour. Splitting lets a model route customers to different counters while keeping each stream Poisson.

Non-stationary Poisson process: Real arrivals change with time of day. A bank is quiet at 10 am, busy at lunch, and very busy before closing. A non-stationary Poisson process (NSPP) has a rate lambda(t) that varies with time but keeps the other assumptions. The expected number of arrivals in an interval is the area under lambda(t) over that interval. If the rate is 10 per hour from 9 to 11 and 30 per hour from 11 to 1, the expected arrivals from 9 to 1 are 10 x 2 + 30 x 2 = 80. Ignoring this pattern and using a flat average of 20 per hour would hide the lunchtime queue completely.

Thinning, how to simulate an NSPP: A neat method by Lewis and Shedler. Let lambda-max be the highest rate, here 30 per hour. Generate candidate arrivals from an ordinary Poisson process with rate lambda-max. For each candidate at time t, keep it with probability lambda(t) / lambda-max and throw it away otherwise. In the 9 to 11 period the keep probability is 10 / 30 = 1/3, so about two candidates in three are discarded; from 11 to 1 every candidate is kept. The kept arrivals form exactly the NSPP we want. It wastes some random numbers but is simple and correct.

Batch arrivals: Sometimes people arrive in groups: a family at a restaurant, a busload at a tourist spot, a pallet of parcels at a sorting centre. The batches can arrive as a Poisson process while the batch size is a separate random variable, for example 1 person with probability 0.5, 2 with 0.3, 4 with 0.2. This is called a compound Poisson process. Modeling the group as a single arrival would underestimate the load on the server.

When arrivals are NOT Poisson: Scheduled arrivals, such as patients with appointments every 15 minutes or trains on a timetable, are far more regular than Poisson; model them as scheduled times plus a small random lateness. Arrivals that depend on the queue, like customers who see a long line through the window and walk past (balking), break the independence assumption; handle that with behaviour rules in the model. A small closed population, like 5 machines that can break, cannot generate Poisson arrivals because the rate falls as more machines are already broken. And bursty traffic, like social media notifications that trigger many app requests at once, needs other models.

Checking data for Poisson: Two quick checks. First, compare the mean and variance of counts per interval; for Poisson they should be about equal. Second, look at the interarrival times: a histogram should look like a decaying exponential curve, and the sample standard deviation should be close to the sample mean. Formal goodness-of-fit tests appear in lesson 22. Also check for time-of-day patterns before assuming a constant rate.

Real-life example 1, a toll plaza on the Padma bridge approach: At night, cars come from many independent drivers, so arrivals at the toll plaza are close to Poisson. Suppose the night rate is 120 cars per hour, so lambda = 2 per minute and the mean gap is 30 seconds. The chance that 5 or more cars arrive in a given 1-minute window can be computed from the Poisson formula with mean 2. A simulation of the plaza generates exponential gaps with mean 30 seconds, and splits cars into types (cars, buses, trucks) by probabilities to send them to the right booths. In the evening rush, the model switches to a non-stationary rate.

Real-life example 2, a food delivery app: A delivery platform in Dhaka sees orders rise sharply from 12:30 to 2 pm and from 8 to 10 pm. Modeling orders as an NSPP with an hourly rate profile from historical data lets the company simulate how many riders are needed in each hour. Splitting by area gives each zone its own Poisson stream. Without the time-varying rate, the simulation would recommend the same number of riders at 4 pm and 9 pm, a costly mistake.

Common mistakes: Assuming arrivals are Poisson because it is convenient, without checking. Using a constant rate when a strong daily pattern exists. Confusing the rate lambda (per minute) with the mean gap 1/lambda (minutes). Expecting random arrivals to be evenly spaced. Forgetting that merging only works for independent streams.

What exams ask: State the assumptions of a Poisson process. Show the relation between Poisson counts and exponential interarrival times. Compute probabilities of a number of arrivals in an interval, or of no arrival for some time. Explain merging and splitting with numbers. Describe how to generate Poisson arrivals in a simulation, and how thinning handles a time-varying rate.

Recap: A Poisson process models arrivals from many independent sources: one at a time, stationary and independent increments. Counts in time t are Poisson with mean lambda t; gaps are exponential with mean 1/lambda and memoryless. Merged independent Poisson streams add their rates; split streams stay Poisson. Real days need a non-stationary rate, simulated by thinning. Next lesson tackles the raw material behind every random gap: generating uniform random numbers on a computer.
key_points: A Poisson process assumes single arrivals, stationary increments and independent increments.
Arrivals in time t are Poisson with mean lambda t; gaps between arrivals are exponential with mean 1/lambda.
To simulate arrivals, keep adding exponential gaps to the clock.
Random arrivals bunch up; that clumping is what creates queues.
Merging independent Poisson streams adds rates; random splitting keeps each part Poisson.
Time-of-day patterns need a non-stationary Poisson process, simulated by thinning.
Appointments, queue-dependent behaviour, small populations and bursts are not Poisson.
lessons.tip: When you meet a new system, ask three questions out loud: do people arrive one at a time, does the rate change during the day, and do they decide independently? Those answers tell you whether a Poisson model is safe.
lessons.task: Record the exact times (to the second) of 20 arrivals at any place: cars passing your window, people entering a shop, messages in a busy group. Compute the 19 gaps, their mean and standard deviation. If the two are close and the gaps look clumpy, a Poisson model is reasonable.
