quiz.explain: Interarrival times of a Poisson process are independent exponentials with mean 1/lambda.

quiz.q: Two independent Poisson streams of 10 and 8 per hour merge. The combined stream is...
quiz.explain: Rates of independent Poisson streams add when merged.

quiz.q: Rate 0.3 per minute. What is P(no arrival in the next 5 minutes)?
Thinning is used to simulate...
options: A non-stationary Poisson process with a time-varying rate
quiz.explain: Generate at the maximum rate and keep each candidate with probability lambda(t)/lambda-max.

quiz.q: Which arrival pattern is NOT well modeled by a Poisson process?
options: Calls from thousands of independent customers
Cars at a toll plaza at night
Requests to a big web server
quiz.explain: Scheduled arrivals are much more regular than Poisson.

lessons.title: Random Number Generation
lessons.content:
A computer is the most obedient machine ever built. Give it the same instructions and the same starting data, and it will do exactly the same thing a billion times. So how can such a machine ever produce something random? The honest answer is that it usually does not. It produces numbers that only look random, from a clever formula, and for simulation that is not a weakness but a feature. This lesson explains how those numbers are made, why the formula matters so much, and how a bad formula once fooled scientists for years.

Why we need U(0,1): Every random thing in a simulation, from customer gaps to machine failures to rice demand, is built from one basic ingredient: random numbers that are uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, written U(0,1). Lessons 9 and 10 show how to turn U(0,1) numbers into exponential, normal or any other distribution. So if the U(0,1) numbers are bad, every random input in the model is bad, and every result is suspect. The random number generator is the foundation under the whole building.

What we want from them: Uniformity: in the long run, every equal-sized interval in [0,1) gets an equal share of numbers; if we cut [0,1) into 10 pieces, each should get about 10 percent. Independence: knowing past numbers should not help predict the next one; no patterns, no correlation. Practical needs: the generator must be fast, because big simulations use billions of numbers; it should have a very long period before repeating; it should not need much memory; and it must be reproducible, so the same seed gives the same stream.

True random vs pseudo-random: True random numbers come from physical processes, like radioactive decay, electronic noise or atmospheric noise. They are truly unpredictable but slow, hard to reproduce and need special hardware. Cryptography uses them for keys (deep-cse-6-2 covers secure randomness). Pseudo-random numbers come from a deterministic formula started from a seed. They are fast and reproducible, and if the formula is good, they pass statistical tests of randomness. Simulation almost always uses pseudo-random numbers, precisely because reproducibility lets us debug and compare designs fairly.

Why reproducibility is gold: Suppose your bank simulation shows a strange spike in waiting time at minute 347. If the random numbers were truly random, you could never see that run again to find the bug. With a pseudo-random generator, you reuse the same seed and the exact same customers arrive at the exact same times. Reproducibility also lets you compare two designs using the same customers, a powerful trick called common random numbers (lessons 12 and 24).

The midsquare method: One of the earliest ideas, proposed by John von Neumann around 1946. Take a 4-digit number, square it to get 8 digits (pad with zeros on the left), take the middle 4 digits as the next number, and divide by 10,000 to get a value in [0,1). Start with 5197: 5197 squared is 27008809; the middle 4 digits are 0088, so R1 = 0.0088. Square 0088: 00007744, middle 0077. Then 00005929 gives 0059, then 0034, then 0011, then 0001, then 0000, and from there it is stuck at zero forever. A different seed like 7182 behaves better for a while (5811, 7677, 9363, ...), but the method is known to fall into short cycles or zero. It is taught today mostly as a warning: a formula that looks random can collapse.

The linear congruential generator: The LCG, proposed by D. H. Lehmer in 1951 and still the classic textbook method, uses X(i+1) = (a X(i) + c) mod m, then R(i) = X(i) / m. Here X0 is the seed, a is the multiplier, c is the increment and m is the modulus. Mod m means the remainder after dividing by m, so every X is between 0 and m - 1. It needs just one multiplication, one addition and one remainder per number, which is why it was perfect for early computers.

Worked LCG, and a trap: Take X0 = 27, a = 17, c = 43, m = 100. X1 = (17 x 27 + 43) mod 100 = 502 mod 100 = 2, so R1 = 0.02. X2 = (17 x 2 + 43) mod 100 = 77, R2 = 0.77. X3 = (17 x 77 + 43) mod 100 = 1352 mod 100 = 52, R3 = 0.52. X4 = (17 x 52 + 43) mod 100 = 927 mod 100 = 27. But 27 is the seed! So the sequence 2, 77, 52, 27 now repeats forever. The period is only 4, although m = 100 allows up to 100 different values. Notice also that every R is a multiple of 0.01: an LCG can only produce values i/m, so m must be huge for the numbers to look continuous.

Full period, the Hull-Dobell conditions: An LCG with c not equal to 0 reaches its maximum period m, for every seed, if and only if three conditions hold. One, c and m have no common factor other than 1. Two, a - 1 is divisible by every prime factor of m. Three, if m is divisible by 4, then a - 1 is divisible by 4. In our example m = 100 has prime factors 2 and 5; a - 1 = 16 is divisible by 2 but not by 5, so condition two fails, and indeed the period was tiny.

A full-period worked example: Take m = 16, a = 5, c = 3, X0 = 7. Check: c = 3 and 16 share no factor; the only prime factor of 16 is 2 and a - 1 = 4 is divisible by 2; 16 is divisible by 4 and a - 1 = 4 is divisible by 4. All good. The sequence is 6, 1, 8, 11, 10, 5, 12, 15, 14, 9, 0, 3, 2, 13, 4, 7, then back to 6. All 16 values appear exactly once before repeating: full period. Compare a = 4, c = 2, m = 16, X0 = 7: the sequence is 14, 10, 10, 10, stuck forever, because a - 1 = 3 is not divisible by 2 and c = 2 shares the factor 2 with 16.

Multiplicative LCG: If c = 0, the generator is called multiplicative: X(i+1) = a X(i) mod m. It saves an addition but can never reach 0 (zero would stay zero forever), and its period depends on the seed. With m a power of 2, the best possible period is m/4, reached when the seed is odd and a is of the form 8k + 3 or 8k + 5. Worked: a = 13, m = 64. Seed 1 gives a period of 16 = 64/4 (13, 41, 21, ..., 1), seed 3 also gives 16, but seed 2 gives only 8 and seed 4 only 4. Seed choice matters here. When m is a prime number, the best multiplicative generators reach period m - 1; a famous one is the Lewis-Goodman-Miller minimal standard with m = 2^31 - 1 and a = 16807.

Seeds and streams: The seed is the starting value. Same seed, same sequence. In a good simulation, different random parts of the model use different streams: one stream for arrivals, one for service times, one for breakdowns. A stream is simply a long, non-overlapping section of the generator's sequence, started at a known seed. Separate streams mean that changing the service logic does not shift the arrival sequence, which keeps comparisons between designs clean.

The RANDU warning: In the 1960s and 70s, IBM computers widely used a multiplicative generator called RANDU with a = 65539 and m = 2^31. Single numbers looked fine. But if you take three consecutive numbers as a point (x, y, z) in a cube, all the points fall on only 15 parallel planes instead of filling the cube. Any simulation that used numbers in triples, such as a 3-D particle simulation, was quietly wrong. Many published results had to be rechecked. The lesson: a generator can pass simple tests and still hide structure. Every LCG has some lattice structure; good parameters make it extremely fine.

Modern generators: Today's tools usually use better generators. The Mersenne Twister (MT19937), from 1998, has a period of 2^19937 - 1 and is the default in Python's random module and many others; it is fast and statistically strong for simulation but not safe for cryptography. Newer families such as PCG and xoshiro are smaller and faster with excellent quality. Combined multiple recursive generators like L'Ecuyer's MRG32k3a are designed for simulation with many independent streams. For cryptography, use a cryptographically secure generator instead, such as Python's secrets module.

Practical rules: Do not write your own generator for real work; use a well-studied one from a good library. Always set and record the seed, so results can be reproduced. Use separate streams for separate random processes. Do not reseed with the time inside a loop, which can create overlapping or correlated sequences. Never use the low bits of a simple power-of-two LCG on their own, because they have very short periods. And remember that the C library rand() on some systems was historically weak.

Real-life example 1, a reproducible bank study: A student simulates a bank in Python with seed 2024 and reports average wait 6.8 minutes for 3 tellers. Her supervisor reruns the code with seed 2024 and gets exactly 6.8, so he trusts that the code is what she ran. Then they run 30 replications with seeds 1 to 30 to see the spread. Finally, they compare 3 and 4 tellers using the same seeds for arrivals, so both designs face exactly the same customers and the difference reflects only the extra teller.

Real-life example 2, lottery and games: A ludo app on a phone uses a pseudo-random generator to roll the dice. If the developer seeded it with the same value every time the app starts, every player would see the same sequence of rolls, which players would soon notice. Apps therefore seed from the clock or from system entropy. A government lottery, on the other hand, needs unpredictability that nobody can reproduce or guess, so it uses physical draws or cryptographically secure random sources, not a simple LCG.

Common mistakes: Assuming that a sequence that looks random is random. Choosing LCG parameters at random and getting a short period. Forgetting the period limit: an LCG with m = 100 can produce at most 100 values. Using the same stream for everything. Not recording the seed. Using a simulation-grade generator for passwords or keys.

What exams ask: Generate a few numbers with a given LCG and find its period. State and apply the Hull-Dobell conditions. Do the midsquare method for a few steps and explain its weakness. List the properties of a good generator. Explain the difference between true and pseudo-random numbers and why simulation prefers pseudo-random. Explain the role of the seed and streams.

Recap: Simulation needs U(0,1) numbers that are uniform and independent, generated fast, with a long period and reproducibly. Pseudo-random generators deliver this from a seed and a formula. The midsquare method collapses; the LCG X(i+1) = (a X(i) + c) mod m works well only with good parameters, checked by the Hull-Dobell conditions; RANDU shows hidden structure can lurk. Use a modern library generator, record seeds and use separate streams. Next lesson: how to test a stream of numbers for uniformity and independence.
key_points: Every random input in a simulation is built from U(0,1) numbers, so the generator is the foundation.
Good numbers are uniform and independent; good generators are fast, long-period and reproducible.
Pseudo-random numbers come from a formula and a seed; reproducibility is a feature for debugging and fair comparison.
Midsquare can collapse to zero; LCG X(i+1) = (a X(i) + c) mod m with R = X/m is the classic method.
Hull-Dobell: c and m coprime, a - 1 divisible by every prime factor of m, and by 4 if 4 divides m, give full period m.
RANDU's triples fell on 15 planes: passing simple tests does not prove quality.
Use a well-tested library generator, record seeds, and use separate streams; use secure generators for cryptography.
lessons.tip: When you meet a generator formula in an exam, always compute until the first repeat. Finding the period by hand once makes the Hull-Dobell conditions feel obvious.
lessons.task: On paper, run the LCG with m = 16, a = 5, c = 3 from seed 7 and confirm all 16 values appear. Then change a to 3 and run again from seed 7. Count the period and use the Hull-Dobell conditions to explain what changed.

quiz.q: LCG with X0 = 27, a = 17, c = 43, m = 100. What is X1?
Why does simulation usually prefer pseudo-random numbers over true random numbers?
options: They are reproducible and fast, which helps debugging and fair comparisons
quiz.explain: The same seed regenerates the same stream, which is gold for debugging and comparing designs.

quiz.q: For an LCG with m = 100, which Hull-Dobell condition does a = 17 break?
options: c and m must be coprime
a - 1 must be divisible by every prime factor of m (here 5)
quiz.explain: a - 1 = 16 is not divisible by 5, a prime factor of 100, so the period is not full.

quiz.q: What was wrong with RANDU?
options: Triples of consecutive numbers fell on only 15 planes
quiz.explain: Its hidden lattice structure broke simulations that used numbers in groups of three.

quiz.q: Midsquare starting from 5197 eventually...
quiz.explain: The sequence goes 0088, 0077, 0059, ..., 0001, 0000 and sticks at zero.

lessons.title: Testing Random Numbers
lessons.content:
Before a cricket match, the umpire checks the coin used for the toss. Nobody wants a coin that lands heads 70 percent of the time. Random number generators deserve the same check, only more carefully, because a simulation may use a billion numbers instead of one toss. Last lesson ended with RANDU, a generator that fooled people for years. This lesson gives you the standard tools to catch bad generators: tests for uniformity and tests for independence, each with a fully worked example you can repeat by hand.

What we test: A stream of numbers R1, R2, ..., RN should look like independent draws from U(0,1). That splits into two questions. Is the stream uniform, meaning numbers spread evenly over [0, 1)? Tests of this are called frequency tests. Are the numbers independent, meaning no pattern links one number to the next ones? Tests of this are called independence tests, such as the runs test and the autocorrelation test. A stream can pass one kind and fail the other: the sequence 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, ..., 0.9, 0.1, 0.2, ... is perfectly uniform and completely predictable.

Hypothesis testing in one paragraph: Each test sets up a null hypothesis H0, for example the numbers are uniformly distributed on [0, 1). We compute a test statistic from the data and compare it with a critical value from a table, chosen for a significance level alpha, often 0.05. If the statistic is beyond the critical value, we reject H0: the data looks too unlikely under H0. If not, we fail to reject H0. The level alpha is the probability of rejecting a good generator by bad luck (a Type I error). With alpha = 0.05, a perfect generator still fails about 1 test in 20. (deep-cse-2-6 covers hypothesis testing in full.)

Failing to reject is not proof: Passing a test only means this test could not find a problem with this sample. A bad generator can pass many tests, as RANDU did. That is why serious generators are put through large batteries of tests, such as Marsaglia's Diehard tests, the NIST statistical test suite and L'Ecuyer's TestU01 with its SmallCrush, Crush and BigCrush batteries. For our purposes, learning a few classic tests teaches the ideas behind all of them.

Chi-square frequency test, the idea: Divide [0, 1) into n equal classes. If N numbers are uniform, each class expects E = N/n numbers. Count the observed number O in each class. The statistic is chi-square = sum of (O - E) squared / E over all classes. If the numbers are uniform, this follows approximately a chi-square distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. A large value means the counts are too far from even. The rule of thumb is that each expected count should be at least 5.

Chi-square worked: Take N = 100 numbers and n = 10 classes, so E = 10 in each. Suppose the observed counts are 8, 12, 10, 9, 11, 7, 13, 10, 12, 8 (they add to 100). Differences from 10: -2, 2, 0, -1, 1, -3, 3, 0, 2, -2. Squares: 4, 4, 0, 1, 1, 9, 9, 0, 4, 4, total 36. Divide by E = 10: chi-square = 3.6. Degrees of freedom 10 - 1 = 9; the critical value at alpha 0.05 is 16.92. Since 3.6 is far below 16.92, we do not reject uniformity. A value like 25 would mean the counts are suspiciously uneven.

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, the idea: The KS test compares the empirical CDF of the sample with the uniform CDF F(x) = x. The empirical CDF S(x) is the fraction of sample values less than or equal to x; it climbs in steps of 1/N. The test statistic D is the largest vertical gap between S(x) and F(x). If D is bigger than the critical value for sample size N and level alpha, reject uniformity. KS works well for small samples and does not need classes.

KS worked: Take five numbers: 0.44, 0.81, 0.14, 0.05, 0.93. Sort them: 0.05, 0.14, 0.44, 0.81, 0.93. With N = 5, compute D+ = max of (i/N - R(i)): 0.20 - 0.05 = 0.15, 0.40 - 0.14 = 0.26, 0.60 - 0.44 = 0.16, 0.80 - 0.81 = -0.01, 1.00 - 0.93 = 0.07; maximum 0.26. Compute D- = max of (R(i) - (i - 1)/N): 0.05 - 0 = 0.05, 0.14 - 0.20 = -0.06, 0.44 - 0.40 = 0.04, 0.81 - 0.60 = 0.21, 0.93 - 0.80 = 0.13; maximum 0.21. D = max(0.26, 0.21) = 0.26. The table critical value for N = 5 and alpha = 0.05 is 0.565. Since 0.26 < 0.565, do not reject uniformity.

Chi-square or KS: Chi-square needs many numbers (enough so each class expects at least 5) and loses information by grouping. KS uses every value exactly and is more powerful for small samples, but in its basic form it is for continuous distributions with fully known parameters. For testing a generator with millions of numbers, chi-square with many classes is simple and fast. Both appear again in lesson 22, where we test whether real data fits a distribution.

Why independence needs separate tests: Imagine a generator that outputs 0.05, 0.15, 0.25, ..., 0.95 and then repeats. Every chi-square and KS test on it will look excellent, yet each number tells you exactly what comes next. If a simulation used such a stream for arrivals, gaps would rise steadily and then drop, a pattern no real queue has. Independence tests look for exactly this kind of hidden order.

Runs up and down, the idea: Write a + whenever a number is larger than the previous one and a - whenever it is smaller. A run is a block of identical signs in a row. A random sequence should have a moderate number of runs: too few means long rising or falling stretches (trends), too many means the numbers zigzag up-down-up-down too regularly. For N numbers, the expected number of runs up and down is (2N - 1)/3 and the variance is (16N - 29)/90; for N above about 20 the count is approximately normal.

Runs worked, counting: Take 0.12, 0.45, 0.33, 0.78, 0.81, 0.25, 0.60, 0.14. Signs: 0.45 > 0.12 is +, 0.33 < 0.45 is -, 0.78 is +, 0.81 is +, 0.25 is -, 0.60 is +, 0.14 is -. So the signs are + - + + - + -. Group them: (+) (-) (+ +) (-) (+) (-), which is 6 runs. For a test you need more numbers; this small one is only for practice in counting.

Runs worked, the test: A classic textbook example has N = 40 numbers with a = 26 runs. Expected runs = (2 x 40 - 1)/3 = 79/3, about 26.33. Variance = (16 x 40 - 29)/90 = 611/90, about 6.79, so the standard deviation is about 2.61. Z = (26 - 26.33)/2.61, about -0.13. At alpha 0.05 we reject only if Z is below -1.96 or above 1.96. Since -0.13 is well inside, we do not reject independence.

Runs above and below the mean, and run lengths: Other runs tests count runs of numbers above and below 0.5, or check the lengths of runs (how many runs of length 1, 2, 3 and so on) against what randomness predicts, using a chi-square test. A generator could have the right number of runs but too many long ones. Each test looks at a different possible flaw.

Autocorrelation test, the idea: Check whether numbers a fixed distance apart are related. For lag m, compare R(i) with R(i + m) across the sequence. If the generator is good, their correlation should be near zero. A simple estimator averages the products R(i) R(i + m), subtracts 0.25 (the value expected for independent uniforms), and turns the result into a Z statistic. A significant positive value means numbers m apart tend to be similar; a negative value means they tend to be opposite. Some generators show strong correlation at particular lags, which this test reveals.

Gap test and poker test, briefly: The gap test picks a digit, say 3, and records how many other digits appear between consecutive 3s; for random digits, gap lengths should follow a geometric distribution, checked with a KS or chi-square test. The poker test looks at groups of digits, like the three digits in 0.255, and checks how often all are different, exactly one pair appears or all three are the same, compared with the probabilities expected from random digits (0.72, 0.27 and 0.01 for three digits).

How many tests, and what failure means: In practice, run several tests on several long streams. If a generator fails one test once at alpha 0.05, rerun on fresh numbers; random failure happens 1 time in 20. If it fails repeatedly or fails dramatically, stop using it. A failure tells you the kind of flaw (uneven spread, trends, periodic correlation), which is useful when deciding whether that flaw matters for your simulation.

Real-life example 1, a student's homemade generator: A team building a ludo game for a class project writes its own LCG with m = 1,000. They generate 10,000 dice rolls and run a chi-square test over the 6 faces; it passes. Then they run a runs test on the underlying numbers and get Z = 4.1, a clear failure: the sequence rises and falls in a regular rhythm. They switch to the language's built-in generator, which passes both. The players will never know, but the AI opponent's test games now behave fairly.

Real-life example 2, auditing a lottery machine: A regulator wants to check that a digital raffle system used by a shopping mall in Dhaka is fair. They collect the drawn numbers from many draws and run frequency tests (are all numbers drawn equally often?) and independence tests (do certain numbers tend to follow others?). Passing does not prove fairness, but failing would be strong evidence of a problem. This is the same toolbox used on simulation generators.

Common mistakes: Testing only uniformity and ignoring independence. Using chi-square with tiny expected counts. Forgetting to sort the numbers before the KS test. Treating fail to reject as proof of randomness. Rejecting a generator after one failure at alpha 0.05. Mixing up the degrees of freedom: for n classes with nothing estimated from the data, use n - 1.

What exams ask: Perform a chi-square or KS test on given numbers and state the conclusion. Count runs up and down in a given sequence, compute expected value, variance and Z. Explain why both uniformity and independence tests are needed. Describe the autocorrelation, gap or poker test. Explain the meaning of significance level in this context.

Recap: Good random numbers must be uniform and independent. Chi-square and KS test uniformity; runs, autocorrelation, gap and poker tests look for dependence. Each test gives a statistic compared with a critical value; failing to reject is not proof of quality, and serious generators face whole batteries of tests. Next lesson takes our tested U(0,1) numbers and turns them into exponential, triangular and empirical random variables with the inverse transform method.
key_points: A random number stream must pass both uniformity (frequency) and independence tests.
Chi-square: sum (O - E)^2 / E over classes, compared with chi-square critical value with n - 1 degrees of freedom.
KS test: largest gap D between the sorted sample's empirical CDF and F(x) = x.
Runs up and down: expected (2N - 1)/3 runs, variance (16N - 29)/90, then a Z test.
Autocorrelation tests whether numbers m positions apart are related; gap and poker tests check digit patterns.
At alpha 0.05 a perfect generator still fails about 1 test in 20; failing to reject is not proof.
Serious generators are checked with test batteries such as Diehard, NIST and TestU01.
lessons.tip: Do one KS test and one runs test fully by hand with small numbers. Once you have computed D+ and D- yourself, exam questions on these tests become pure routine.
lessons.task: Use a calculator or phone to generate 30 random numbers (many calculators have a Ran# key). Count how many fall in [0, 0.5) and [0.5, 1), and count the runs up and down. Compare the run count with (2 x 30 - 1)/3, about 19.7.

quiz.q: Observed counts in 10 classes from 100 numbers give chi-square = 3.6. Critical value at alpha 0.05 is 16.92. Conclusion?
quiz.explain: 3.6 is below 16.92, so there is no evidence against uniformity, though that is not proof.

quiz.q: In the KS test, D is...
options: The largest gap between the empirical CDF and the uniform CDF
quiz.explain: D = max(D+, D-) measures the biggest vertical distance between the two CDFs.

quiz.q: The sequence 0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.9 repeated would most likely fail which test?
quiz.explain: It is perfectly uniform but highly predictable, which independence tests catch.

quiz.q: For N = 40 numbers, the expected number of runs up and down is about...
With alpha = 0.05, how often does a perfect generator fail a test by chance?
quiz.explain: The significance level is the probability of a Type I error.

lessons.title: Random Variate Generation I: The Inverse Transform
lessons.content:
Imagine a machine at a fair that gives you a ticket with a random number between 0 and 1. That is all it can do. But your simulation needs customer gaps that follow an exponential distribution, repair times from a table, task durations from an expert's triangular guess. How do you turn plain uniform tickets into all these shapes? This is called random variate generation: a random variate is one generated value of a random variable. The most important method, the one you should try first, is the inverse transform. It is simple, exact and works for both discrete and continuous distributions.

The idea in words: Every distribution has a CDF, F(x) = P(X <= x), that climbs from 0 to 1. Pick a uniform random number R between 0 and 1. Now go to the vertical axis of the CDF graph at height R, walk horizontally until you hit the curve, and drop down to the x-axis. The x where you land is your random variate. In formula terms, solve F(X) = R for X, so X = F-inverse(R). Steep parts of the CDF, where many probability is packed into a small range of x, catch many values of R; flat parts catch few. That is exactly how the variate ends up with the right distribution.

Why it works, simple proof: We want P(X <= x) = F(x). Since X = F-inverse(R) and F never decreases, X <= x happens exactly when R <= F(x). And for a uniform R, P(R <= F(x)) = F(x). So P(X <= x) = F(x). Done. This short argument is a classic exam question, so make sure you can write it.

The recipe, four steps: Step 1, write the CDF F(x) of the wanted distribution. Step 2, set F(X) = R, where R is U(0, 1). Step 3, solve the equation for X in terms of R. Step 4, generate R1, R2, R3, ... from the generator and compute X1, X2, X3, ... with the formula. Steps 1 to 3 are done once on paper; step 4 is the code.

Exponential, the most used case: The CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^(-lambda x) for x >= 0. Set 1 - e^(-lambda X) = R. Then e^(-lambda X) = 1 - R. Take the natural log: -lambda X = ln(1 - R). So X = -ln(1 - R) / lambda. Since 1 - R is also uniform on (0, 1), many programs use X = -ln(R) / lambda instead; both are correct, although the first form keeps the matching between small R and small X, which matters for tricks like antithetic variates (lesson 12).

Exponential worked: Customers arrive with rate lambda = 0.5 per minute, so mean gap 2 minutes. Take R = 0.10: X = -ln(0.90) / 0.5 = 0.1054 / 0.5, about 0.21 minutes. R = 0.55: X = -ln(0.45) / 0.5 = 0.7985 / 0.5, about 1.60 minutes. R = 0.83: X = -ln(0.17) / 0.5 = 1.772 / 0.5, about 3.54 minutes. Notice that R near 1 gives very long gaps; the exponential's long right tail comes from those rare large R values.

Uniform on [a, b]: The CDF is F(x) = (x - a) / (b - a) on [a, b]. Set (X - a) / (b - a) = R, so X = a + (b - a) R. A bus that comes uniformly between 2 and 8 minutes from now: with R = 0.35, X = 2 + 6 x 0.35 = 4.1 minutes. This is the simplest inverse and a good first check of any code.

Weibull: With scale alpha and shape beta, F(x) = 1 - e^(-(x / alpha)^beta). Solving gives X = alpha (-ln(1 - R))^(1/beta). For a bearing with scale 10 months and shape 2 (wear-out), R = 0.5 gives X = 10 x (ln 2)^(1/2), about 8.33 months. When beta = 1 this reduces to the exponential with mean alpha, a good self-check.

Triangular: For triangular(a, c, b) with minimum a, mode c and maximum b, the CDF has two pieces, one left of the mode and one right. Inverting each piece gives: if R <= (c - a)/(b - a), X = a + square root of (R (b - a)(c - a)); otherwise X = b - square root of ((1 - R)(b - a)(b - c)). Worked with triangular(2, 4, 9): the split point is (4 - 2)/(9 - 2) = 2/7, about 0.286. R = 0.2 is below it, so X = 2 + sqrt(0.2 x 7 x 2) = 2 + sqrt(2.8), about 3.67 hours. R = 0.7 is above it, so X = 9 - sqrt(0.3 x 7 x 5) = 9 - sqrt(10.5), about 5.76 hours.

Discrete distributions, table lookup: For a discrete variable, the CDF is a staircase. The inverse transform says: find the smallest value x such that F(x) >= R. Practically, build a table of cumulative probabilities and assign each value an interval of R. The gas cylinder demand from lesson 4 has values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2, so the cumulative values are 0.1, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0. Rule: R up to 0.1 gives demand 0; above 0.1 up to 0.4 gives 1; above 0.4 up to 0.8 gives 2; above 0.8 gives 3. With R = 0.07, 0.62, 0.91, 0.38 the demands are 0, 2, 3, 1.

The random-digit version used in hand simulations: Textbook hand simulations (lesson 14) often use 2-digit random numbers 01 to 100 (or 00 to 99) instead of decimals. Each value gets a range of digits proportional to its probability: demand 0 gets 01 to 10, demand 1 gets 11 to 40, demand 2 gets 41 to 80, demand 3 gets 81 to 100. It is the same table lookup, just with whole numbers. Make sure the ranges have exactly the right sizes, 10, 30, 40 and 20 here, and do not overlap.

Speeding up discrete lookup: With many values, searching from the first row every time is slow. Put the most likely values first, or use a binary search over the cumulative table, which takes about log2(n) comparisons. For huge tables, the alias method of Walker allows generation in constant time after a setup step; you only need to know it exists.

A discrete formula instead of a table, the geometric: Some discrete distributions have a direct inverse formula, so no table is needed. For the geometric (number of trials until the first success, with success probability p), F(k) = 1 - (1 - p)^k. The smallest k with F(k) >= R is X = ceiling of ln(1 - R) / ln(1 - p). Worked with p = 0.2 and R = 0.5: ln(0.5) / ln(0.8) = -0.693 / -0.223, about 3.11, and the ceiling is 4. Check: F(3) = 1 - 0.8^3 = 0.488, which is below 0.5, while F(4) = 1 - 0.8^4 = 0.590, which is above it, so 4 is right. A salesperson model can use this one line to decide how many calls the next sale takes.

Empirical continuous distributions: Suppose you measured repair times and grouped them: 0.25 to 0.5 hours in 31 percent of cases, 0.5 to 1.0 hours in 10 percent, 1.0 to 1.5 hours in 25 percent, 1.5 to 2.0 hours in 34 percent. Cumulative probabilities at the interval ends are 0.31, 0.41, 0.66 and 1.00. Assume values are spread evenly inside each interval, which makes the CDF a set of straight lines joining the points. To invert, find the interval where R falls, then interpolate linearly.

Empirical worked: R = 0.83 falls between 0.66 and 1.00, the interval 1.5 to 2.0 hours. Position inside: (0.83 - 0.66) / (1.00 - 0.66) = 0.17 / 0.34 = 0.5, halfway. So X = 1.5 + 0.5 x 0.5 = 1.75 hours. R = 0.20 falls in the first interval, between 0 and 0.31: X = 0.25 + (0.20 / 0.31) x 0.25, about 0.41 hours. This method reproduces the data's shape without assuming any named distribution.

When the inverse has no closed form: For some distributions you cannot write F-inverse with simple functions. The normal distribution is the famous case: its CDF has no closed-form formula. Gamma and beta distributions are similar. Options: use a very accurate numerical approximation of the inverse (libraries do this), solve F(X) = R numerically with a root-finding method from Numerical Methods (deep-cse-3-4), or use a different generation method entirely, like acceptance-rejection or Box-Muller, which are in lesson 10.

Advantages of the inverse transform: It is exact, not an approximation. It needs exactly one uniform number per variate, which makes synchronising random numbers across designs easy. It is monotone: a larger R always gives a larger X, which is what makes variance reduction tricks such as common random numbers and antithetic variates work well. And it makes generating from truncated distributions easy: to get values only in a sub-range, restrict R to the matching range of F.

Real-life example 1, a Dhaka bus stop model: A student observes gaps between buses at a stop in Mohakhali and fits an exponential with mean 6 minutes, lambda = 1/6 per minute. The simulation generates the next bus gap as X = -6 ln(1 - R). With R = 0.5, X = 6 ln 2, about 4.16 minutes; with R = 0.9, X = 6 ln 10, about 13.8 minutes. Passenger waits computed from these gaps match the observed ones closely, which is part of validation.

Real-life example 2, a mobile repair shop: The owner has no fitted distribution, just a notebook of 200 past repair times grouped into 30-minute bins. The simulation uses the empirical continuous inverse transform from that table. It is honest to the data and quick to build. Later, if the shop grows and more data arrives, the modeler can fit a lognormal and compare results.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that ln of a number between 0 and 1 is negative, and dropping the minus sign, which produces negative times. Mixing up rate and mean in the exponential formula. Overlapping or wrongly sized digit ranges in table lookup. Using the formula for the wrong side of the triangular split point. Assuming the empirical method can produce values beyond the observed maximum.

What exams ask: Derive the inverse transform formula for exponential, uniform, Weibull or a given simple CDF. Generate a few variates from given random numbers. Build a cumulative table and random-digit assignment for a discrete distribution. Generate from an empirical continuous table with interpolation. Prove why the inverse transform gives the right distribution.

Recap: The inverse transform turns U(0,1) numbers into any distribution by solving F(X) = R. Exponential: X = -ln(1 - R)/lambda. Uniform: X = a + (b - a)R. Discrete and empirical: look up the cumulative table, interpolating for continuous data. It is exact, uses one R per value and keeps the order of R, which helps later tricks. When F has no usable inverse, as for the normal, the next lesson's methods take over.
key_points: A random variate is one generated value of a random variable, built from U(0,1) numbers.
Inverse transform: solve F(X) = R, so X = F-inverse(R); it works because P(R <= F(x)) = F(x).
Exponential: X = -ln(1 - R)/lambda; uniform: X = a + (b - a)R; Weibull: X = alpha(-ln(1 - R))^(1/beta).
Triangular uses two formulas, split at R = (c - a)/(b - a).
Discrete distributions: build a cumulative table and pick the first value with F(x) >= R.
Empirical continuous: locate the interval for R and interpolate linearly.
The normal has no closed-form inverse, so other methods (lesson 10) or numerical inverses are used.
lessons.tip: For every inverse formula you learn, test it with R = 0.5: the answer must be the median. For an exponential with mean 2, -2 ln(0.5) is about 1.39, the median, not the mean. This catches sign and rate errors instantly.
lessons.task: Using R values from a calculator, generate 10 exponential gaps with mean 3 minutes using X = -3 ln(1 - R). Add them up to get 10 arrival times. Then mark them on a line from 0 to 30 minutes and look at how clumpy the arrivals are.

quiz.q: What is the inverse transform formula for an exponential with rate lambda?
quiz.explain: Solving 1 - e^(-lambda X) = R gives X = -ln(1 - R)/lambda.

quiz.q: Demand values 0, 1, 2, 3 have cumulative probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.8, 1.0. With R = 0.62, demand is...
quiz.explain: 0.62 is above 0.4 and at most 0.8, so it maps to 2.

quiz.q: Uniform on [2, 8] with R = 0.35 gives...
Why can't the inverse transform be applied easily to the normal distribution?
options: Its CDF has no closed-form inverse
quiz.explain: The normal CDF cannot be written with simple functions, so its inverse is approximated numerically or other methods are used.

quiz.q: Repair-time intervals have cumulative probabilities 0.66 at 1.5 hours and 1.00 at 2.0 hours. With R = 0.83, X is...

lessons.title: Random Variate Generation II: Rejection, Convolution and the Normal
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to pick a random point inside the shape of Bangladesh on a map, so that every square kilometre is equally likely. There is no easy formula for that shape. But there is a lazy trick: draw a rectangle around the map, throw random darts at the rectangle, and keep only the darts that land inside the border. Darts in the Bay of Bengal or in India are thrown away. The kept darts are perfectly uniform over Bangladesh. That throw-and-keep idea is acceptance-rejection, the main tool when the inverse transform of lesson 9 fails. This lesson covers it, plus convolution, the special methods for the normal and Poisson, and composition.

When the inverse transform is not enough: The inverse transform needs a CDF you can invert. For the normal, gamma and beta distributions you cannot write the inverse with simple functions. Sometimes the inverse exists but is slow to compute. And for some distributions there is a natural description, like a sum of simpler variables, that suggests a faster method. So simulation libraries carry several methods and pick the best for each distribution.

Acceptance-rejection, the idea: We want X with density f(x) on an interval. Find a simpler density g(x) that we can already generate, and a constant c >= 1 such that f(x) <= c g(x) everywhere; c g(x) is a roof over f. Then repeat: generate a candidate Y from g, generate a uniform R, and accept Y as X if R <= f(Y) / (c g(Y)); otherwise reject and try again. The accepted values have exactly the density f. In the map analogy, g is the rectangle, f is the shape, and the test with R decides whether the dart is inside.

Efficiency: Each try is accepted with probability 1/c. So on average a variate costs c tries, each needing two uniform numbers. If c = 1.5, you need on average 1.5 tries; if c = 10, you need 10, which is wasteful. The art is choosing g so that c g(x) hugs f(x) closely. The simplest choice is a flat roof: g uniform on the interval and c g equal to the maximum height of f.

Acceptance-rejection worked: Take the density f(x) = 6x(1 - x) on [0, 1], a beta(2, 2) shape that looks like a hill with its top at x = 0.5, where f(0.5) = 1.5. Use g uniform on [0, 1] (g = 1) and c = 1.5. The accept test R2 <= f(Y) / 1.5 simplifies to R2 <= 4Y(1 - Y). Try 1: R1 = 0.2 gives Y = 0.2; 4 x 0.2 x 0.8 = 0.64; R2 = 0.7 is greater than 0.64, so reject. Try 2: R1 = 0.6 gives Y = 0.6; 4 x 0.6 x 0.4 = 0.96; R2 = 0.5 is at most 0.96, so accept X = 0.6. On average 2 of every 3 tries are accepted, since 1/c = 2/3. Values near the middle are accepted more often than values near 0 or 1, which builds the hill shape.

Why it works, in words: Picking Y uniformly and then accepting with probability proportional to f(Y) is like picking a random point under the roof and keeping it only if it is also under the curve f. Points under f are uniformly spread over the area under f, so their x-coordinates have density proportional to f. Because f has total area 1, the proportion is exact.

Poisson by multiplying uniforms: A neat special method uses the link with exponential gaps (lesson 6). The number of arrivals in one unit of time is Poisson with mean lambda. Arrivals happen whenever the sum of exponential gaps stays at most 1. Since each gap is -ln(R) / lambda, the condition sum of gaps <= 1 becomes product of R's >= e^(-lambda). Algorithm: set N = 0 and P = 1; repeat: generate R, set P = P x R; if P < e^(-lambda), output N and stop; otherwise N = N + 1 and continue.

Poisson worked: Generate demand with lambda = 2, so e^(-2) is about 0.1353. R1 = 0.62: P = 0.62, not below 0.1353, so N = 1. R2 = 0.48: P = 0.2976, not below, so N = 2. R3 = 0.39: P = 0.1161, below 0.1353, so stop and output N = 2. This method needs about lambda + 1 uniforms per variate, fine for small lambda. For large lambda (say above 15), libraries use other methods, or approximate with a normal of mean and variance lambda.

Convolution, adding simpler variables: Many distributions are sums of independent simpler ones. Generating each part and adding is called the convolution method. An Erlang with k phases is the sum of k independent exponentials. A binomial(n, p) is the sum of n Bernoulli(p) trials: generate n uniforms and count how many are below p. A triangular(0, 1, 2) is the sum of two independent U(0, 1). It is intuitive and easy to code, but costs k or n uniforms per value.

Erlang worked: A 3-step service, each step exponential with mean 2 minutes. With R1 = 0.2, R2 = 0.5, R3 = 0.7, the steps are -2 ln(0.2), about 3.22, -2 ln(0.5), about 1.39, and -2 ln(0.7), about 0.71, for a total of about 5.32 minutes. Shortcut: -2 ln(R1 x R2 x R3) = -2 ln(0.07) gives the same 5.32, with just one logarithm. The mean of many such totals is 6 minutes.

Normal by the sum of 12 uniforms: An old approximate trick uses the central limit theorem. Each U(0, 1) has mean 0.5 and variance 1/12. The sum of 12 has mean 6 and variance 1. So Z = (R1 + R2 + ... + R12) - 6 is approximately standard normal. It is easy to remember and fine for teaching, but it can never produce values beyond -6 or +6 and its tails are too thin, so real software does not use it for serious work.

Normal by Box-Muller: The exact classic method, published by Box and Muller in 1958. Take two independent uniforms R1 and R2. Compute Z1 = sqrt(-2 ln R1) cos(2 pi R2) and Z2 = sqrt(-2 ln R1) sin(2 pi R2). Z1 and Z2 are two independent standard normal variables. The idea: in two dimensions, a pair of independent normals has a random direction (uniform angle 2 pi R2) and a squared distance from the centre that is exponential, which is where -2 ln R1 comes from.

Box-Muller worked: R1 = 0.1758, R2 = 0.1489. First sqrt(-2 ln 0.1758) = sqrt(3.477), about 1.865. The angle is 2 pi x 0.1489, about 0.936 radians, with cosine about 0.593 and sine about 0.805. So Z1 is about 1.865 x 0.593, about 1.11, and Z2 is about 1.865 x 0.805, about 1.50. To get a normal with mean 10 and standard deviation 2, use X = 10 + 2Z: X1 is about 12.21 kg and X2 is about 13.00 kg. The polar method of Marsaglia is a variant that avoids computing sine and cosine by using acceptance-rejection on a circle.

Other distributions from the normal: Once you have standard normals, other distributions follow. Lognormal: X = e^(mu + sigma Z). Chi-square with k degrees of freedom: sum of k squared standard normals. Correlated normal pairs, useful when two inputs move together, such as rainfall in two neighbouring districts: Z1 and rho Z1 + sqrt(1 - rho^2) Z2 have correlation rho.

Composition: Some distributions are mixtures: with probability p1 draw from f1, with probability p2 from f2, and so on. Generate one uniform to choose the component, then generate from it. Example: at a pharmacy, 70 percent of prescriptions are simple with exponential service time of mean 1 minute, 30 percent are complex with mean 4 minutes. Draw R; if R <= 0.7 use the simple formula, otherwise the complex one. The overall mean is 0.7 x 1 + 0.3 x 4 = 1.9 minutes, but the shape has a much longer tail than a single exponential with mean 1.9.

Checking generated variates: Whatever method you use, check the output. Generate, say, 10,000 values, draw a histogram and lay the true density over it. Compare the sample mean and variance with the theoretical ones. For the beta(2, 2) example, the mean should be near 0.5 and variance near 0.05. A sign error or a wrong constant shows up instantly as a shifted or squashed histogram. Bugs in variate generators are silent: the simulation runs happily and gives wrong answers. A formal check is also possible: apply the chi-square or KS test from lesson 8, but now against the target distribution instead of the uniform. Many teams keep these checks as small automatic tests that run every time the generator code changes, so a careless edit is caught before it spoils weeks of results.

Real-life example 1, garment quality control: A factory models the stitch strength of seams as normal with mean 50 newtons and standard deviation 5. The simulation uses Box-Muller to generate strengths and counts how many seams fall below the 40-newton limit, about 2.3 percent in theory (two standard deviations below the mean). The engineers compare that with the rejects they actually see, a quick validation check, then simulate what happens if a new thread reduces the standard deviation to 4.

Real-life example 2, a ride-sharing demand model: A ride app models requests in each 5-minute block in a Dhaka zone as Poisson with lambda = 2 at midday. The simulation uses the multiply-uniforms method. Trip lengths are a composition: 60 percent short trips (exponential, mean 3 km) and 40 percent longer trips (lognormal). Each part uses the simplest correct method, and the combined model reproduces the app's real distribution of trip lengths.

Common mistakes: Choosing a roof c g(x) that does not fully cover f(x), which silently gives the wrong distribution. Forgetting that each rejection consumes random numbers, which matters when synchronising random numbers across designs. Using the sum-of-12 method in serious work. Applying Box-Muller with ln(0). Forgetting to scale: X = mu + sigma Z, not mu + Z.

What exams ask: Explain acceptance-rejection with a sketch and compute its efficiency 1/c. Generate a few values from a given density by acceptance-rejection with given random numbers. Generate Poisson values by the multiply-uniforms method. Generate Erlang or binomial values by convolution. Apply Box-Muller to given R1 and R2. Explain composition with an example.

Recap: When the inverse transform fails, use other tools. Acceptance-rejection throws candidates from an easy density under a roof c g(x) and keeps them with probability f/(c g); efficiency is 1/c. Poisson comes from multiplying uniforms until the product drops below e^(-lambda). Convolution adds simpler variables (Erlang, binomial). Box-Muller turns two uniforms into two exact normals. Composition mixes distributions. Always check output with histograms and moments. Next lesson puts random variates to work in Monte Carlo simulation.
key_points: Acceptance-rejection: draw Y from g, accept if R <= f(Y)/(c g(Y)); efficiency is 1/c tries per value.
The roof c g(x) must cover f(x) everywhere, and the tighter it fits, the fewer rejections.
Poisson(lambda): multiply uniforms until the product falls below e^(-lambda); the count before that is N.
Convolution: Erlang = sum of exponentials, binomial = sum of Bernoullis; -mean x ln(R1 R2 R3) gives an Erlang-3.
Box-Muller: Z1 = sqrt(-2 ln R1) cos(2 pi R2), Z2 = sqrt(-2 ln R1) sin(2 pi R2), then X = mu + sigma Z.
Composition picks a component of a mixture with one uniform, then generates from it.
Always check generated values with a histogram and their sample mean and variance.
lessons.tip: Draw every method once as a picture: the roof over the hill for rejection, a staircase of products for Poisson, a circle with an angle for Box-Muller. Pictures make the formulas easy to rebuild in the exam.
lessons.task: Take 12 random numbers from a calculator, add them and subtract 6. Repeat 5 times. You now have 5 approximately standard normal values. Turn them into heights with mean 160 cm and standard deviation 8 cm using X = 160 + 8Z, and check whether they look like real classmates' heights.

quiz.q: In acceptance-rejection with constant c, the probability of accepting a candidate is...
quiz.explain: On average c tries are needed per accepted value, so each try succeeds with probability 1/c.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 6x(1 - x) with a uniform proposal and c = 1.5, the accept test is R2 <= ...
Poisson with lambda = 2: products of uniforms are 0.62, 0.2976, 0.1161. e^(-2) is 0.1353. Output?
quiz.explain: The product first drops below 0.1353 at the third uniform, so N = 2.

quiz.q: Box-Muller turns two uniforms into...
quiz.explain: Z1 and Z2 from Box-Muller are independent N(0, 1).

quiz.q: Which method is the natural way to generate an Erlang variable?
quiz.explain: An Erlang with k phases is the sum of k independent exponentials.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo Simulation I: Estimating with Randomness
lessons.content:
Imagine a pond of an odd shape in the middle of a square field, and you want its area. No formula fits the shape. So you stand at the edge and throw 1,000 small stones at random over the whole field. Afterwards you count: 300 stones fell in the water. If the field is 100 square metres, the pond is about 300/1000 of it, roughly 30 square metres. You just estimated an area using nothing but randomness and counting. That is Monte Carlo simulation. It is the static kind of simulation from lesson 2: no clock, no queue, just many random trials and an average.

What Monte Carlo is: Monte Carlo simulation is a family of methods that estimate a number by repeated random sampling. The recipe is always the same: describe the quantity you want as an expected value (an average over randomness), generate many random samples, compute the quantity for each sample, and average. By the law of large numbers (lesson 4), the average approaches the true value as the number of samples grows. The name came from Ulam and von Neumann in the 1940s, after the Monte Carlo casino, because the method relies on chance.

Why it is useful: Many important numbers are averages that are hard or impossible to compute exactly: the probability that a project finishes on time, the expected loss of a bank portfolio, the area of a complicated shape, an integral in 20 dimensions, the chance of winning a card game. Monte Carlo turns all of these into the same simple job: simulate, count, average. It needs no clever mathematics, only a model of one random trial and a good random number generator.

Estimating pi with darts: The classic first example. Take the square from 0 to 1 on both axes and the quarter circle of radius 1 inside it, centred at the origin. The square has area 1 and the quarter circle has area pi/4, about 0.785. Throw a random dart: generate R1 and R2, and treat (R1, R2) as a point. It is inside the quarter circle if R1 squared plus R2 squared is at most 1. The fraction of darts inside estimates pi/4, so 4 times that fraction estimates pi.

Pi worked: Suppose 1,000 darts are thrown and 787 land inside. The estimate is 4 x 787/1000 = 3.148, close to 3.1416 but not exact. A different seed might give 3.12 or 3.17. The estimate is random; its quality is measured by its standard error. Each dart is a Bernoulli trial with p = pi/4, so the fraction has standard deviation sqrt(p(1 - p)/n). For pi = 4 times the fraction, the standard error is 4 sqrt(0.1685/n). With n = 10,000 that is about 0.016; with n = 1,000,000 it is about 0.0016.

The square-root law: Look at those numbers. Going from 10,000 to 1,000,000 darts, 100 times more work, made the error only 10 times smaller. That is the fundamental rule of Monte Carlo: the error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n). To halve the error you need 4 times as many samples; to get one more correct decimal digit you need 100 times as many. Monte Carlo gets rough answers quickly and precise answers very slowly. This is why variance reduction (lesson 12) is so valuable: reducing the variance is like getting free samples.

Integration, the hit-or-miss method: To estimate the integral of a function f(x) on [0, 1] where 0 <= f(x) <= 1, throw random points (R1, R2) into the unit square and count hits where R2 <= f(R1). The fraction of hits estimates the area under the curve, which is the integral. For f(x) = x squared, the true integral is 1/3. With 5 example points (0.3, 0.05), (0.6, 0.5), (0.8, 0.4), (0.2, 0.1), (0.9, 0.7): check 0.05 <= 0.09 hit, 0.5 <= 0.36 miss, 0.4 <= 0.64 hit, 0.1 <= 0.04 miss, 0.7 <= 0.81 hit. That is 3 hits out of 5, an estimate of 0.6, terrible because 5 is a tiny n, but the method is clear.

Integration, the sample-mean method: A better method. The integral of f on [0, 1] equals the average value of f(X) when X is U(0, 1). So generate R1, ..., Rn, compute f of each, and average. For x squared with R = 0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.9, 0.5, the squares are 0.01, 0.16, 0.49, 0.81, 0.25; their average is 1.72/5 = 0.344, already close to 0.333 with only 5 numbers. On a general interval [a, b], the integral is (b - a) times the average of f(a + (b - a)R).

Why sample-mean beats hit-or-miss: Hit-or-miss throws away information: it only records whether a point is under the curve, not by how much. The sample-mean method uses the actual height of f. Mathematically, the sample-mean estimator always has variance no larger than the hit-or-miss estimator for the same n. For x squared on [0, 1], the variance of one sample-mean term is 1/5 - 1/9 = 4/45, about 0.089 (standard deviation about 0.30), while one hit-or-miss term has variance (1/3)(2/3), about 0.222. So with 10,000 samples the sample-mean standard error is about 0.003.

Buffon's needle: In 1777, Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, posed this: drop a needle of length l onto a floor with parallel lines a distance d apart, with l <= d. The probability that the needle crosses a line is 2l/(pi d). With l = d, that is 2/pi, about 0.637. So by dropping many needles and counting crossings, you can estimate pi: pi is about 2 times the number of drops divided by the number of crossings. It is one of the earliest Monte Carlo experiments, done with real needles long before computers.

When Monte Carlo beats formulas, many dimensions: For a smooth one-dimensional integral, classic numerical methods like Simpson's rule (deep-cse-3-4) are much more accurate than Monte Carlo for the same work. But in many dimensions, grid methods explode: 10 points per dimension in 10 dimensions is 10^10 grid points. Monte Carlo's error is 1/sqrt(n) regardless of the number of dimensions. That is why physics, finance, computer graphics (path tracing in deep-cse-5-2) and machine learning use Monte Carlo for high-dimensional averages.

Monte Carlo for probabilities: Any probability is an expected value of an indicator (1 if the event happens, 0 if not). Example: what is the chance that the sum of three dice is more than 15? Simulate three dice many times and count. The exact answer is 10/216, about 0.046, which you can check by listing outcomes, and the Monte Carlo estimate with 100,000 trials will usually be within about 0.0013 of it (two standard errors). For problems where listing outcomes is impossible, like the chance of a full house in a 5-card hand with special house rules, Monte Carlo is the practical way.

How many samples do I need: Turn the square-root law around to plan a study. For a 95 percent confidence level, the half-width of the interval is about 1.96 times the standard error, so to reach a target half-width h you need n = (1.96 sigma / h) squared, where sigma is the standard deviation of one trial. For pi from darts, one trial of 4 times the indicator has sigma = 4 x sqrt(0.1685), about 1.64. To be within 0.01 of pi with 95 percent confidence: n = (1.96 x 1.64 / 0.01) squared, about 103,600 darts. For the sample-mean integral of x squared, sigma is about 0.298; to be within 0.001 you need about 341,000 samples. In practice sigma is unknown before you start, so run a small pilot of, say, 1,000 trials, estimate sigma from it, and then compute n. This pilot-then-plan habit saves hours of wasted computing and stops you from publishing a number that looks precise but is not.

The Monte Carlo workflow: Step 1, define the random inputs and their distributions. Step 2, define the output computed from one set of inputs. Step 3, generate n independent sets of inputs and compute n outputs. Step 4, report the average, and also the standard error s/sqrt(n) or a confidence interval (lesson 24). Step 5, if the error is too large, increase n by the square of the factor you want to improve, or use variance reduction. Always report precision; a Monte Carlo number without an error estimate is only half an answer.

Random walks, another classic: Monte Carlo is not only about areas. A random walk is a path built from random steps, like a drunk man who takes each step left or right with equal chance. Simulating thousands of walks answers questions that are hard by hand: how far from the start is he after 100 steps on average (about the square root of 100, so 10 steps, measured as root-mean-square distance), or how likely is he to reach a wall 20 steps away before 400 steps. Random walks model share prices, the spread of a smell in a room, and the movement of molecules, and they are the simplest bridge from static Monte Carlo to the dynamic simulations of the coming lessons.

Pseudo-code: count = 0; repeat n times: x = random(); y = random(); if x*x + y*y <= 1 then count = count + 1; end; piEstimate = 4 * count / n. Six lines, and it runs millions of times per second on a laptop. The same skeleton, with a different trial inside the loop, solves almost every Monte Carlo problem in this course.

Real-life example 1, a cricket tournament: Bangladesh's chance of reaching a semi-final depends on many matches, each with its own win probability, plus net run rate ties. Listing all combinations is tedious. A Monte Carlo model plays the whole group stage 100,000 times with random results based on estimated probabilities and counts how often Bangladesh qualifies. If it happens in 23,140 of 100,000 runs, the estimate is about 23 percent with a standard error of about 0.13 percentage points. TV analysts' qualification charts are often produced this way.

Real-life example 2, a rice farmer's income: A farmer's income depends on yield per bigha (affected by rainfall and pests) and the market price at harvest, both uncertain. An NGO advisor models yield as normal and price as triangular from past years, simulates 10,000 seasons and reports average income and the chance that income falls below the cost of seeds, fertiliser and labour. That chance of loss, say 18 percent, is far more useful for planning crop insurance than a single average income.

Common mistakes: Reporting the Monte Carlo average without its error. Using too few samples and trusting the second decimal place. Expecting the error to fall linearly with n. Using hit-or-miss when sample-mean is easy. Using a poor random generator, which can bias results in ways no amount of samples fixes. Forgetting that inputs may be correlated, such as yield and price falling together in a flood year.

What exams ask: Define Monte Carlo simulation and give an example. Estimate pi or an integral with given random numbers by hit-or-miss and sample-mean. Explain the 1/sqrt(n) error law and compute how many samples are needed for a target error. Describe Buffon's needle. Explain why Monte Carlo is preferred for high-dimensional problems.

Recap: Monte Carlo estimates a number by writing it as an average over randomness, sampling many times and averaging. Pi from darts, integrals by hit-or-miss or the better sample-mean method, probabilities by counting. The error falls only as 1/sqrt(n), so 4 times the samples halve the error, but this rate does not get worse with dimension. Always report the error. Next lesson applies Monte Carlo to real risk problems and shows tricks that reduce variance.
key_points: Monte Carlo estimates a quantity by writing it as an expected value, sampling randomly many times and averaging.
Pi estimate: 4 x fraction of random points with x^2 + y^2 <= 1 in the unit square.
Error shrinks like 1/sqrt(n): 4 times the samples halve the error, 100 times give one more digit.
Sample-mean integration (average of f(R)) has lower variance than hit-or-miss.
Buffon's needle: crossing probability 2l/(pi d) lets random drops estimate pi.
Monte Carlo's error rate does not depend on dimension, so it wins for high-dimensional problems.
Always report the standard error s/sqrt(n) or a confidence interval with a Monte Carlo estimate.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see a Monte Carlo result, ask: how many samples, and what is the standard error? If you cannot answer, you cannot trust the number. Make that question automatic.

It is faster for one-dimensional smooth integrals

lessons.title: Monte Carlo II: Risk, Reliability and Variance Reduction
lessons.content:
A contractor promises to finish a school building in 13 weeks, because that is what you get by adding up the most likely time for each step. Then the rains come early, one supplier is late, and it takes 17 weeks. Was he unlucky, or was the promise wrong from the start? Monte Carlo can answer that before the first brick is laid. This lesson uses Monte Carlo for real decisions under uncertainty: project schedules, the reliability of systems made of parts, and money risk. Then it shows tricks called variance reduction, which give the same accuracy with far fewer samples.

Risk analysis, the big idea: Most planning uses single numbers: this task takes 4 days, this machine costs 2 lakh taka, sales will be 1,000 units. Each of those is really a random variable. When you combine random variables, the result is random too, and its average is often NOT what you get by combining the averages. Monte Carlo risk analysis replaces each uncertain input by a distribution, simulates the whole plan thousands of times and reports the full distribution of the outcome: its mean, its spread and the probability of bad outcomes.

Project schedule, the setup: A small software project has four tasks. Task A (requirements) comes first. Then tasks B (backend) and C (app) run in parallel. Task D (testing) starts only after both B and C finish. Durations in days are triangular, from expert estimates (minimum, most likely, maximum): A is (3, 4, 8), B is (4, 6, 10), C is (3, 5, 11), D is (2, 3, 5). The project length is A + max(B, C) + D.

The single-number plan: Using the most likely values, A + max(B, C) + D = 4 + max(6, 5) + 3 = 13 days. Many managers would promise 13 days. Using the mean of each triangular (a + c + b)/3 gives A = 5, B = 6.67, C = 6.33, D = 3.33, and the path through B gives 15.0 days. Even that is too optimistic, as we will see.

The Monte Carlo result: Simulating 200,000 projects, each with random A, B, C and D drawn by the inverse transform of lesson 9, gives an average length of about 15.7 days. The chance of finishing within the promised 13 days is only about 6 percent. The chance of taking more than 18 days is about 11 percent. So the promise of 13 days was almost certain to fail. The extra 0.7 days beyond 15.0 come from the parallel tasks: the project waits for the slower of B and C, and the average of a maximum is larger than the maximum of the averages. This is called merge bias, and only simulation or careful probability reveals it.

Using the distribution: With the simulated outcomes sorted, you can read off percentiles. If the 80th percentile is, say, 17 days, the manager can promise 17 days and be right about 4 times in 5. You can also find which task most often lies on the slow path, which tells you where an extra developer helps most. This is the Monte Carlo upgrade of the PERT method you may meet in Software Project Management (deep-cse-6-11).

Reliability of a system: A system made of parts works or fails depending on how the parts are connected. In series, all parts must work: three parts each with reliability 0.95 give 0.95 x 0.95 x 0.95, about 0.857. In parallel (redundancy), the system fails only if all parts fail: two pumps each with reliability 0.9 give 1 - 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.99. Real systems mix series and parallel in complicated networks, and parts may share causes of failure. Monte Carlo handles all of this: in each trial, draw whether each part works (a Bernoulli), apply the network logic, and count system successes.

Reliability over time: If each part's lifetime is random, say Weibull, Monte Carlo can draw the lifetimes, compute when the system first fails, and estimate the probability of surviving one year, or the mean time to failure. A water supply in a Chattogram housing complex with two pumps in parallel feeding one main pipe in series can be studied this way, including repair times, to decide whether a third pump is worth buying.

Financial risk, the idea: Banks and investors simulate the value of a portfolio under many random futures, with returns drawn from fitted distributions and correlations between assets. From thousands of simulated futures they estimate measures like value at risk: the loss that will not be exceeded with, for example, 99 percent probability over the next 10 days. The model is only as good as its assumptions; the 2008 financial crisis showed that underestimating how assets crash together can make such numbers dangerously optimistic.

Monte Carlo in a spreadsheet: You do not need code. In a spreadsheet, one row is one trial. Columns use RAND() for uniform numbers and formulas for each input (for example, an exponential is =-LN(1-RAND())*mean). Another column computes the output. Copy the row down 5,000 times, then use AVERAGE, STDEV and PERCENTILE on the output column. Press recalculate to get a fresh set of trials. This is how many business analysts in Dhaka do quick risk studies.

Why variance reduction: From lesson 11, the error of a Monte Carlo estimate is sigma/sqrt(n). You can shrink it by raising n, slowly and expensively, or by lowering sigma, the variability of what you average. Variance reduction techniques (VRTs) change how samples are generated so that the estimator has smaller variance for the same n. Halving sigma is as good as 4 times the samples.

Common random numbers: When comparing two designs, such as 3 tellers vs 4 tellers, run both with the same random numbers for the same purposes: customer 17 arrives at the same time and wants the same service time in both runs. Then the difference in results comes from the design, not from luck. Mathematically, Var(X - Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) - 2 Cov(X, Y), and using the same random numbers makes Cov positive, shrinking the variance of the difference. This needs synchronisation, which is why separate random number streams for arrivals and services (lesson 7) matter. Lesson 24 uses CRN with a paired-t test.

Antithetic variates, the idea: Within one design, pair each run using random numbers R with a partner run using 1 - R. If one run gets unusually short service times, its partner gets unusually long ones, so their average is closer to the truth. Average the pair, and treat each pair as one observation. It works when the output moves in one direction as the inputs grow, which is common, and it works best with the inverse transform because larger R always means larger value.

Antithetic worked: Estimate the integral of e^x on [0, 1], whose true value is e - 1, about 1.718. One sample e^R has variance about 0.242. With two independent samples averaged, the variance is 0.242/2, about 0.121. With an antithetic pair, the average of e^R and e^(1-R), the two terms are strongly negatively correlated (covariance about -0.234), so the variance of the pair's average is (0.242 - 0.234)/2, about 0.0039. Same cost of two function evaluations, about 31 times less variance. Results are rarely this dramatic in queue models, but reductions of 20 to 50 percent are common.

Control variates, briefly: If you know the exact mean of some quantity that is correlated with your output, use the known error in that quantity to correct your estimate. Example: in a queue simulation the true mean service time is known (say 4 minutes). If a run happened to draw service times averaging 4.3 minutes, its waiting time is probably too high, so adjust it downward by an amount estimated from the data. The adjusted estimator has lower variance.

Importance sampling, briefly: When the event you care about is rare, like a dam overflowing once in 1,000 years or a network losing packets one time in a million, plain Monte Carlo wastes almost all samples on boring cases. Importance sampling draws more samples from the region that matters and corrects by weighting each sample by the ratio of the true density to the sampling density. Done well, it gives huge gains for rare events; done badly, it can make the variance worse, so it needs care.

Which technique when: Use common random numbers whenever you compare designs; it is cheap and almost always helps. Try antithetic variates when the output clearly rises or falls with the random inputs, such as total project time with task times. Use control variates when you know the exact mean of some input, such as the service time distribution you chose yourself. Keep importance sampling for rare events where plain sampling would almost never see the event. And measure: run a pilot with and without the technique and compare the variances, because a technique that helps in one model can do nothing in another.

Seeds and reproducibility: Every Monte Carlo study should record its seeds. CRN and antithetic variates are only possible because pseudo-random numbers can be replayed. A good report says: 10,000 trials, seed 12345, standard error 0.02, so that anyone can rerun and check.

Real-life example 1, a bridge construction schedule: An engineering firm building a small bridge in Sylhet has 25 tasks with expert three-point estimates, some depending on monsoon weather. Monte Carlo with 10,000 trials shows the 50th percentile finish is week 30 and the 90th percentile is week 36, while the deterministic plan said week 27. The firm schedules the risky river-bed work before the monsoon and quotes 34 weeks with a penalty clause it can live with.

Real-life example 2, a solar mini-grid: An NGO plans a solar mini-grid for an island village. Daily sunshine, battery health and village demand are uncertain. A Monte Carlo model simulates 1,000 random years and estimates the fraction of evenings with power cuts for battery sizes of 20, 30 and 40 kWh. Using common random numbers, all three sizes face the same weather years, so the comparison is sharp even with fewer trials. The NGO picks 30 kWh, where cut evenings drop below 2 percent at an affordable cost.

Common mistakes: Adding most-likely values and calling it the plan. Assuming the mean of a maximum equals the maximum of means. Ignoring correlations between inputs (bad weather slows many tasks at once). Using CRN but letting random numbers fall out of step between designs. Applying antithetic variates where the output does not move monotonically with inputs. Reporting a single number with no percentiles.

What exams ask: Explain Monte Carlo risk analysis with a project or inventory example. Compute series and parallel reliability. Explain merge bias. Describe common random numbers and antithetic variates and why they reduce variance, using Var(X - Y) and Cov. Outline how to do Monte Carlo in a spreadsheet.

Recap: Monte Carlo risk analysis replaces single-number guesses with distributions and reports the whole spread of outcomes, revealing effects like merge bias that make plans late. It handles reliability of complex systems and financial risk. Variance reduction lowers sigma instead of raising n: common random numbers sharpen comparisons, antithetic variates pair R with 1 - R, control variates correct with a known mean, and importance sampling targets rare events. Next lesson leaves static Monte Carlo behind and starts the core of the course: discrete-event simulation.
key_points: Risk analysis replaces single-number estimates with distributions and simulates the whole plan many times.
Adding most-likely task times underestimates projects; parallel paths create merge bias (mean of max > max of means).
Read percentiles from simulated outcomes to set promises like an 80 percent safe deadline.
Series reliability multiplies part reliabilities; parallel fails only if all parts fail; Monte Carlo handles complex networks.
Variance reduction lowers sigma: halving sigma equals 4 times the samples.
Common random numbers make Cov(X, Y) positive, shrinking Var(X - Y) when comparing designs.
Antithetic variates pair R with 1 - R; for e^x on [0,1] variance fell from about 0.121 to 0.0039 for two evaluations.
lessons.tip: Whenever someone gives you a plan with one number, ask what the 90th percentile would be. Thinking in percentiles instead of single numbers is the most practical thing this lesson teaches.
lessons.task: In a spreadsheet, put three columns for task times using =4+2*RAND(), =3+4*RAND() and =5+RAND(). Add a total column = first + MAX(second, third). Copy down 1,000 rows. Compare AVERAGE of the total with 5 + max(5, 5.5), and look at PERCENTILE(total, 0.9).
