lessons.title: Multi-Server and General Queues
lessons.content:
Walk into two banks. In the first, each of the two tellers has a separate line, and you must guess which will move faster; often you pick wrong and watch the other line zoom past. In the second, there is one snake line and the person at the front goes to whichever teller is free. Which bank serves you faster on average? And what if the bank replaced its two tellers with one teller who works twice as fast? Queuing theory answers these questions with numbers, and the answers surprise many people. This lesson covers multi-server queues, queues with general service times, and how to put a price on waiting.

The M/M/c model: Poisson arrivals at rate lambda, c identical servers each with exponential service rate mu, one shared FIFO line, infinite capacity. Utilisation per server is rho = lambda / (c mu), and stability needs rho < 1. The offered load a = lambda / mu is the average number of busy servers. The state is still the number in system n, and it is still a birth-death process, but now the death rate depends on n: with n customers and n < c, n servers are busy, so the departure rate is n mu; once n >= c, all c servers are busy and the rate is c mu.

The Erlang C formula: Solving the balance equations gives P0 = 1 / [sum for k = 0 to c - 1 of a^k / k! + a^c / (c! (1 - rho))]. The probability that an arriving customer has to wait, called Erlang's C formula after the Danish telephone engineer A. K. Erlang, is C = [a^c / (c! (1 - rho))] P0. Then Lq = C rho / (1 - rho), Wq = Lq / lambda, W = Wq + 1/mu and L = Lq + a. You do not need to memorise P0 for exams if a formula sheet is given, but you should know how to use it step by step.

Worked, two tellers with one shared line: lambda = 10 customers per hour, each teller serves mu = 6 per hour (10 minutes each), c = 2. Offered load a = 10/6, about 1.667, rho = 10/12, about 0.833. P0 = 1 / [1 + 1.667 + 1.667^2 / (2 x 0.167)] = 1 / [1 + 1.667 + 8.333] = 1/11, about 0.091. Erlang C = 8.333 x 0.091, about 0.758, so about 76 percent of customers have to wait. Lq = 0.758 x 0.833 / 0.167, about 3.79. Wq = 3.79 / 10 hours, about 22.7 minutes. W = 22.7 + 10, about 32.7 minutes.

Separate lines compared: Now split the same customers into two separate lines, each with its own teller, customers choosing randomly and never switching. Each line is an M/M/1 with lambda = 5 and mu = 6, rho = 0.833. Wq = rho / (mu - lambda) = 0.833 / 1 hour, 50 minutes! W = 60 minutes. Same staff, same customers, same utilisation, yet the average wait more than doubles. The reason: with separate lines, one teller can sit idle while the other line has people waiting. The shared line never wastes a free teller when someone is waiting. This is why banks, airports and passport offices in Bangladesh increasingly use a single snake line or a token system.

One fast server compared: What about one teller who serves 12 per hour (5 minutes each)? That is M/M/1 with lambda = 10 and mu = 12: Wq = 25 minutes, W = 30 minutes. Compared with two slow tellers in a shared line, the single fast server gives slightly longer waiting in line (25 vs 22.7 minutes) but shorter total time (30 vs 32.7 minutes), because service itself is quicker. There is also a risk difference: if the one fast teller falls sick, service stops; with two tellers it only slows. Numbers inform the decision, but the decision also weighs risk.

Adding a third server: With c = 3 and the same lambda = 10 and mu = 6, rho = 10/18, about 0.556. The Erlang C probability of waiting drops to about 0.30, and Wq to about 2.2 minutes. From 2 to 3 tellers, waiting falls from 22.7 to 2.2 minutes, a tenfold improvement for 50 percent more staff. Near high utilisation, one extra server has a huge effect; at low utilisation it barely matters. Simulation and formulas both show this sharp curve.

M/G/1 and general service: Exponential service is rarely realistic. The M/G/1 model keeps Poisson arrivals and one server but allows any service distribution with mean 1/mu and standard deviation sigma. The Pollaczek-Khinchine (P-K) formula gives Lq = (lambda^2 sigma^2 + rho^2) / (2 (1 - rho)). Then Wq = Lq / lambda, W = Wq + 1/mu, L = Lq + rho. Only the mean and the variance of service time matter, not the full shape.

P-K worked: lambda = 10 per hour, mean service 5 minutes (mu = 12 per hour, rho = 0.833). Case 1, exponential service: sigma = 5 minutes = 1/12 hour, so lambda^2 sigma^2 = 100/144, about 0.694, and Lq = (0.694 + 0.694) / (2 x 0.167), about 4.17, Wq = 25 minutes, exactly the M/M/1 answer as it should be. Case 2, a trained server with sigma = 2 minutes: lambda^2 sigma^2 = 100 x (2/60)^2, about 0.111; Lq = (0.111 + 0.694) / 0.333, about 2.42; Wq about 14.5 minutes. Case 3, constant service (M/D/1), sigma = 0: Lq = 0.694 / 0.333, about 2.08; Wq = 12.5 minutes.

M/D/1 halves the queue: Compare case 1 and case 3: Lq for constant service is exactly half of the M/M/1 value. This is a general result: at the same utilisation, removing all service variability halves the queue. Reducing variability partly, as in case 2, gives part of the benefit. This is the mathematical reason behind standard procedures, checklists, pre-filled forms and automated machines: they cut the variance of service time, and that cuts waiting without adding any staff.

Why variance matters, intuition: A single very long service holds up everyone behind it. With high variance, such long services are more common, and the people stuck behind them add up. The P-K formula weighs lambda^2 sigma^2 directly, so doubling the standard deviation of service roughly quadruples that part of the queue. When a manager says our average service is only 5 minutes, ask also: how variable is it?

Arrival variability matters too: The same logic applies to arrivals. Scheduled arrivals (appointments) are less variable than Poisson, and queues shrink. For G/G/1 queues, a widely used approximation by Kingman says Wq is roughly [(ca^2 + cs^2) / 2] x [rho / (1 - rho)] x mean service time, where ca and cs are the coefficients of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) of interarrival and service times. For M/M/1 both are 1 and the formula is exact. The message is the same: waiting = variability x utilisation x time.

Networks of queues: Many systems are chains or networks: a hospital patient goes to registration, then a doctor, then maybe the lab, then the pharmacy. Jackson networks are networks of M/M/c stations with Poisson outside arrivals and random routing. Jackson's theorem (1957) shows that, in steady state, each station behaves like an independent M/M/c queue with its own total arrival rate, found by solving flow-balance equations: the arrival rate to a station equals outside arrivals plus the flows routed in from other stations. Real networks with non-exponential service, blocking between stations or priorities break these assumptions, and simulation takes over.

Cost models, choosing the number of servers: Waiting has a cost: lost customers, unhappy patients, idle trucks, lost production. Servers have a cost: wages, machines. A simple model: total cost per hour = (cost per server per hour) x c + (waiting cost per customer per hour) x L. With lambda = 10, mu = 6, server cost 150 taka per hour and waiting cost 200 taka per hour per customer in the system: c = 2 gives L about 5.45 and total about 300 + 1,091 = 1,391 taka per hour; c = 3 gives L about 2.04 and total about 450 + 408 = 858; c = 4 gives L about 1.74 and total about 600 + 348 = 948. The best choice is 3 servers. Deciding the waiting cost is often the hardest part, and it is a management judgement, not mathematics.

Real-life example 1, a hospital emergency department: A district hospital in Mymensingh sees about 8 emergency patients per hour at night, each needing about 20 minutes of a doctor (mu = 3 per hour). With 3 doctors, rho = 8/9, about 0.89: very high, long waits likely. With 4 doctors, rho = 0.67. Erlang C gives a first estimate; a simulation then adds priority for critical cases, doctors who leave for ward calls and a time-varying arrival rate. The formulas set the right range; the simulation sets the final number.

Real-life example 2, call centre staffing: A mobile operator's call centre must answer 80 percent of calls within 20 seconds. Calls arrive at about 600 per hour in the evening, each lasting about 3 minutes (mu = 20 per hour per agent), so the offered load is 30 agents' worth. Using Erlang C repeatedly for c = 31, 32, 33 and so on, planners find the smallest c that meets the target, then add agents for breaks and training. Workforce management software does exactly this for every half hour of the day.

Common mistakes: Computing rho as lambda / mu instead of lambda / (c mu) for c servers. Assuming separate lines are as good as a shared line. Using M/M/c formulas when service has low variability, overestimating waits. Forgetting that P-K needs the variance, not just the mean. Putting waiting cost on Lq when the problem means time in the whole system, or the reverse. Treating formula results as exact for systems with balking, priorities or time-varying arrivals.

What exams ask: Compute P0, Erlang C, Lq, Wq, W and L for an M/M/c system. Compare one shared line with separate lines, or c slow servers with one fast server. Apply the P-K formula for M/G/1 and M/D/1. Explain why variability increases waiting. Find the optimal number of servers with a cost model. Explain Jackson networks in words.

Recap: M/M/c uses the Erlang C formula; one shared line beats separate lines (22.7 vs 50 minutes wait in our example) because no server idles while others queue. Near high load one extra server cuts waits dramatically. The P-K formula for M/G/1 shows that service variability drives waiting; constant service halves the queue. Kingman's approximation sums it up: waiting grows with variability, utilisation and service time. Cost models balance staff cost against waiting cost. Next lesson applies simulation to a different kind of system: inventory.
key_points: M/M/c: rho = lambda/(c mu) < 1; Erlang C gives the probability of waiting, then Lq = C rho/(1 - rho).
Two tellers with one shared line: Wq about 22.7 minutes; the same tellers with separate lines: 50 minutes.
One fast server has a shorter total time but less resilience than several slower servers.
Near high utilisation, one extra server cuts waiting dramatically (22.7 to 2.2 minutes from 2 to 3 servers).
Pollaczek-Khinchine: Lq = (lambda^2 sigma^2 + rho^2)/(2(1 - rho)); only mean and variance of service matter.
Constant service (M/D/1) halves the M/M/1 queue: reducing variability reduces waiting.
Cost model: choose c to minimise server cost x c + waiting cost x L.
lessons.tip: When comparing designs, always compute utilisation first. If it is above about 0.85, expect long, sensitive waits; if it is below about 0.5, servers are probably idle too much. That one number frames the whole discussion.
lessons.task: Visit or recall a place with several counters and separate lines (a super shop, a fuel station). Note how often one counter is idle while another line has people. Write a short paragraph explaining with this lesson's numbers why a single shared line would help.

quiz.q: For an M/M/c queue with lambda = 10, mu = 6 and c = 2, the utilisation per server is...
quiz.explain: rho = lambda/(c mu) = 10/12, about 0.833.

quiz.q: Why does one shared line beat separate lines with the same servers?
options: Servers work faster in a shared line
A server never sits idle while customers are waiting elsewhere
quiz.explain: With separate lines, one server can be idle while the other line has a queue.

quiz.q: In the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula, which service-time property besides the mean affects Lq?
quiz.explain: Lq depends on lambda^2 sigma^2, so the variance of service matters.

quiz.q: Compared with M/M/1 at the same utilisation, the M/D/1 queue length Lq is...
quiz.explain: Constant service removes service variability, halving Lq.

quiz.q: Server cost 150 taka per hour and waiting cost 200 taka per hour per customer. Total costs are about 1,391, 858 and 948 for 2, 3 and 4 servers. The best choice is...
quiz.explain: 3 servers give the lowest total cost, about 858 taka per hour.

lessons.title: Inventory Systems Simulation
lessons.content:
A pharmacy owner in Rajshahi faces the same question every week: how many boxes of paracetamol, saline and insulin should I keep? Too few and a patient walks away empty-handed, maybe to a rival shop, maybe without medicine they need. Too many and money sits on shelves, medicines expire and the godown fills up. Demand is random, suppliers take days to deliver, and every order has a cost. An inventory system is a system that stores goods to meet uncertain demand, and simulation is one of the best tools to design its rules. This lesson shows the basic costs, the classic formula, ordering policies, a hand simulation and how simulation compares policies.

What an inventory system is: Goods come in through orders and go out through demand. The stock on hand rises with deliveries and falls with sales. Key elements: demand (how much customers want per day, usually random), lead time (days between placing an order and receiving it, sometimes also random), the review method (check stock continuously or at fixed times), and the ordering policy (when to order and how much). Examples are everywhere: a grocery shop's rice, a garment factory's fabric and buttons, a hospital's blood bank, a fuel station's diesel tank, even a phone's battery stock at a service centre.

The three costs: Ordering cost K is a fixed cost for each order, regardless of size: paperwork, transport, the time to call the supplier. It pushes you to order rarely and in big amounts. Holding cost h is the cost of keeping one unit in stock for one period: storage space, money tied up that could earn interest, spoilage, expiry, theft. It pushes you to keep stock low. Shortage cost p is the cost of not having a unit when a customer wants it: lost profit, lost goodwill, emergency purchase or, in a hospital, harm to a patient. It pushes you to keep stock high. Good policies balance these three.

Backorders versus lost sales: When stock runs out, some customers wait for the next delivery (backorder), like a customer who pre-orders a new phone. Others go elsewhere (lost sale), like a patient who needs medicine today. The model must choose, because the two give different results: backorders are filled from the next delivery, lost sales simply vanish. A pharmacy in a town with many rivals is mostly a lost-sales system.

The EOQ formula: If demand were constant and known, the classic Economic Order Quantity (Harris, 1913) gives the best order size: Q* = square root of (2 D K / H), where D is annual demand, K the ordering cost and H the holding cost per unit per year. Example: a shop sells 1,200 bottles of a syrup per year, ordering costs 500 taka per order and holding costs 20 taka per bottle per year. Q* = square root of (2 x 1,200 x 500 / 20) = square root of 60,000, about 245 bottles. That means about 4.9 orders per year. Ordering cost per year is about 2,449 taka and holding cost is also about 2,449 taka, total about 4,899. At the EOQ, the two costs are always equal: a neat check.

Why EOQ is not enough: Real demand is random, lead times vary, shortages happen, prices change with quantity, shelf life is limited. EOQ assumes all of these away. It gives a good starting order size, but it cannot tell you how much safety stock to hold against random spikes or what the shortage rate will be. This is where simulation comes in: keep all the randomness, try a policy, measure the costs. More analytical inventory theory is covered in the Operations Research course (deep-cse-6-10).

The (s, S) policy: Review stock periodically, say every evening. If the inventory position (stock on hand plus stock already ordered but not yet arrived) is at or below a reorder point s, order enough to bring it up to a level S. Otherwise do nothing. Example: s = 4, S = 10: if the evening position is 3, order 7. Using inventory position, not just shelf stock, prevents ordering twice for the same gap while an order is on the way. The (s, S) policy is simple and very often close to optimal.

Other common policies: The (s, Q) policy orders a fixed quantity Q whenever the position falls to s, like EOQ with a reorder point. The order-up-to or (R, S) policy checks every R days and always orders up to S, whatever the stock: a shop that orders every Saturday. The reorder point s is usually set as average demand during the lead time plus safety stock. Safety stock protects against randomness; more randomness or longer lead time needs more safety stock.

The pharmacy hand simulation, setup: A pharmacy sells boxes of a common antacid. Daily demand is random: 0 boxes with probability 0.10, 1 with 0.20, 2 with 0.35, 3 with 0.25, 4 with 0.10; mean 2.05 per day. Unmet demand is lost. Policy (4, 10): check in the evening; if inventory position is 4 or less, order up to 10. Lead time 2 days: an order placed on day 2 evening arrives on day 5 morning. Costs: holding 2 taka per box per night, ordering 50 taka per order, shortage 20 taka per box lost. Start with 8 boxes. Demands for 10 days, generated from random numbers by inverse transform (lesson 9): 3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 3, 0, 2, 4, 3.

The table, days 1 to 5: Day 1: start 8, demand 3, sell 3, end 5; position 5 is above 4, no order. Day 2: start 5, demand 2, end 3; position 3 is 4 or less, so order 7 (to reach 10), due day 5. Day 3: start 3, demand 4, sell only 3, lose 1, end 0; position is 0 + 7 on order = 7, no new order. Day 4: start 0, demand 1, lose 1, end 0; position 7, no order. Day 5: the 7 boxes arrive, start 7, demand 2, end 5; position 5, no order.

The table, days 6 to 10: Day 6: start 5, demand 3, end 2; position 2, order 8, due day 9. Day 7: start 2, demand 0, end 2. Day 8: start 2, demand 2, end 0. Day 9: 8 boxes arrive, start 8, demand 4, end 4; position 4, order 6, due day 12. Day 10: start 4, demand 3, end 1. End-of-day stock over 10 days: 5, 3, 0, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 4, 1, total 22 box-nights.

The costs: Holding = 22 x 2 = 44 taka. Ordering = 3 orders x 50 = 150 taka. Shortage = 2 lost boxes x 20 = 40 taka. Total = 234 taka for 10 days, 23.4 taka per day. Also useful: the fill rate. Total demand was 24 boxes and 22 were sold, so the fill rate is 22/24, about 91.7 percent. A manager might find 2 lost sales in 10 days acceptable for an antacid but not for insulin.

Why one run is not enough: The 10-day table used one particular sequence of demands. A different sequence gives a different cost. To compare policies, we must simulate many long runs, as lesson 24 will explain. With a computer, each run can cover a full year of 365 days and be repeated 200 times. The hand table is for understanding the logic; the computer is for answers.

Comparing policies by simulation: Running 200 replications of 365 days for each of four policies, with the same demand distribution and costs, gave average daily costs of about 27.2 taka for (3, 8), 24.3 for (4, 10), 23.9 for (6, 12) and 22.2 for (6, 15). Among these, (6, 15) is cheapest: holding a bit more stock and ordering a bit more at a time pays off, because each order costs 50 taka and each lost box 20 taka. A real study would search more pairs of s and S, and use common random numbers so that every policy faces the same demand days (lesson 24), making the comparison sharper.

The newsvendor problem: Some goods are useful for one period only: newspapers, Eid sweets, fresh fish, Pohela Boishakh decorations. You order once, then demand happens. A sweet shop buys a batch of special doi for 60 taka per pot and sells at 100 taka; leftovers are thrown away at the end of the day. Underage cost (one pot too few) Cu = 100 - 60 = 40 taka of lost profit. Overage cost (one pot too many) Co = 60 taka. The best order is the demand level where the probability of demand being at or below it equals Cu / (Cu + Co) = 40/100 = 0.4, called the critical ratio.

Newsvendor worked: Suppose demand is equally likely to be any whole number from 80 to 120 pots. The 0.4 point is about 80 + 0.4 x 40 = 96 pots. Computing the expected profit for each order quantity confirms it: ordering 90 gives about 3,466 taka, 96 gives about 3,508, 100 gives about 3,488 and 110 gives about 3,266. Notice the best order is below the average demand of 100, because a leftover pot costs more than a missed sale. With Monte Carlo, the same method works for any demand distribution, even one estimated from past sales data.

Real-life example 1, hospital blood bank: Blood units expire after about 35 to 42 days, demand is random, and a shortage can cost a life. Hospitals simulate collection drives, demand by blood group and expiry together to set target stock levels, balancing wasted expired units against shortages. Simulation can also test rules like issuing the oldest unit first.

Real-life example 2, a garment factory: An export garment factory in Gazipur needs buttons, zippers and thread for many orders. Imported items have long and variable lead times of 3 to 8 weeks. Running out stops a production line of hundreds of workers. Planners simulate demand from the order book and lead-time variability to decide safety stocks, often finding that reducing lead-time variability with a reliable supplier saves more than holding more stock.

Common mistakes: Using stock on hand instead of inventory position for reorder decisions, which causes double orders. Ignoring lead time. Forgetting the difference between lost sales and backorders. Judging a policy from one short run. Comparing average cost only, without looking at the fill rate or shortages for critical items. Using EOQ when demand is very uncertain or seasonal.

What exams ask: Define ordering, holding and shortage costs. Compute EOQ and the annual cost. Explain (s, S), (s, Q) and periodic review policies. Simulate an inventory system by hand for several days given demand random numbers, lead time and costs. Compute average cost and fill rate. Solve a simple newsvendor problem with the critical ratio.

Recap: Inventory systems balance ordering, holding and shortage costs under random demand and lead time. EOQ gives a starting order size for constant demand. Policies like (s, S) use the inventory position and a reorder point. Hand simulation of a pharmacy for 10 days gave a cost of 23.4 taka per day and a fill rate of about 92 percent; many long computer runs compare policies fairly. The newsvendor critical ratio decides one-time orders. Next lesson moves from discrete events to continuous change.
key_points: Inventory costs: ordering cost K per order, holding cost h per unit per period, shortage cost p per unit short.
EOQ: Q* = sqrt(2DK/H); at EOQ, annual ordering and holding costs are equal.
(s, S) policy: if inventory position <= s, order up to S; use position, not shelf stock.
Hand simulation tracks each day: arrivals, demand, sales, lost sales, end stock, orders and costs.
One 10-day run is not enough; compare policies with many long replications.
Newsvendor: order where P(demand <= q) = Cu/(Cu + Co), the critical ratio.
Lost sales and backorders give different models; choose based on real customer behaviour.
lessons.tip: In hand inventory tables, write one column for each of: arrivals, start stock, demand, sold, lost, end stock, on order, order placed. Most mistakes come from mixing start and end stock or forgetting what is already on order.
lessons.task: Redo the pharmacy table with policy (6, 12) and the same 10 demands and costs. Compute total cost and fill rate, and compare with the (4, 10) result of 234 taka. Which seems better over these 10 days?

quiz.q: Which cost pushes a manager to order rarely and in large amounts?
quiz.explain: A fixed cost per order is spread over more units when orders are large.

quiz.q: Annual demand 1,200, ordering cost 500 taka, holding 20 taka per unit per year. EOQ is about...
In an (s, S) policy with s = 4 and S = 10, the inventory position is 3. How much is ordered?
quiz.explain: Order up to S: 10 - 3 = 7.

quiz.q: Why use inventory position instead of shelf stock to decide orders?
options: It includes stock already ordered, preventing duplicate orders
quiz.explain: Position = on hand + on order, so a gap is not ordered twice.

quiz.q: A newsvendor has Cu = 40 and Co = 60. The critical ratio is...

lessons.title: Continuous Simulation
lessons.content:
So far our systems jumped: a customer arrives, a service ends, stock drops by 3 boxes. Between events, nothing changed. But many things change smoothly all the time. A cup of tea cools minute by minute. The water level in a tank rises while the tap runs. A disease spreads through a town day by day. Rain fills the Padma and the river level climbs. For these, we use continuous simulation: the state is described by quantities that change continuously, and the rules are written as rates of change. This lesson shows how a computer imitates smooth change with small steps, and how to avoid the classic traps.

What continuous simulation is: The state variables (temperature, water volume, number of infected people) change continuously with time. The model says how fast each one changes, given the current state. In mathematics this is a differential equation, dx/dt = f(x, t): the rate of change of x depends on x itself and maybe on time. Derivatives and differential equations were covered in Calculus & Differential Equations (deep-cse-1-4). A continuous simulation solves these equations numerically, step by step, because most real models have no neat formula answer.

Why we need it: Many important systems are naturally continuous: physical processes (heat, motion, fluid flow, electric circuits), chemical reactions, populations of animals or bacteria, epidemics, economies, climate. Discrete-event simulation would need an event for every tiny change, which makes no sense. Continuous models also capture feedback well: the more people infected, the faster new infections come, until there are few people left to infect.

The tea example, model: A cup of tea at 85 degrees Celsius sits in a room at 25 degrees. Newton's law of cooling says the tea cools at a rate proportional to the temperature difference: dT/dt = -k (T - 25). Take k = 0.1 per minute. At the start, the difference is 60 degrees, so the tea cools at 0.1 x 60 = 6 degrees per minute. As it cools, the difference shrinks and cooling slows. This equation has an exact answer, T(t) = 25 + 60 e^(-0.1 t), which lets us check our numerical method.

Euler's method: The simplest way to step forward. If we know T now and the rate now, assume the rate stays the same for a short step h, and move: T(new) = T(now) + h x rate(now). Then recompute the rate and repeat. It is like walking in the dark: look at the slope under your feet, take a small step in that direction, look again. Numerical Methods (deep-cse-3-4) covers Euler and better methods in detail.

Euler worked for tea: With step h = 1 minute. Minute 0: T = 85, rate = -0.1 x 60 = -6. Minute 1: T = 85 - 6 = 79; rate = -0.1 x 54 = -5.4. Minute 2: T = 79 - 5.4 = 73.6; rate = -4.86. Minute 3: 68.74. Minute 4: 64.37. Minute 5: 60.43. The exact value at minute 5 is 25 + 60 e^(-0.5), about 61.39. Euler is about 1 degree low after 5 minutes, because it uses the fast early cooling rate for the whole step even though the rate keeps slowing.

Step size matters: At minute 10, the exact temperature is about 47.07. Euler with h = 1 gives about 45.92 (error about 1.15). With h = 0.1 it gives about 46.96 (error about 0.11): ten times smaller step, about ten times smaller error. With h = 5 it gives 40.0 (error about 7). With h = 20, Euler does something absurd: in one step the tea drops by 20 x 6 = 120 degrees, to minus 35 degrees, colder than the room it is cooling toward. Too big a step can make a simulation unstable and produce nonsense. Small steps cost more computing time; choosing h is a trade-off between accuracy and speed.

Better methods: Euler's error per unit time shrinks only in proportion to h. The Runge-Kutta methods look at the slope at several points inside each step and combine them. The classic fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) uses four slope evaluations per step and its error shrinks like h^4: halve the step and the error drops about 16 times. Most simulation tools use RK4 or adaptive methods that automatically take smaller steps where things change fast and bigger steps where they are calm.

The water tank: A tank is filled by a pipe at 20 litres per minute, and water leaks out at a rate of 0.1 times the current volume per minute (more water, more pressure, faster outflow). dV/dt = 20 - 0.1 V. Starting empty, with h = 1: V goes 0, 20, 38, 54.2, and so on. The tank does not fill forever: it approaches an equilibrium where inflow equals outflow, 20 = 0.1 V, so V = 200 litres. Finding equilibria by setting the rate to zero is a quick check on any continuous model. Water tank models are used for reservoirs, dams like Kaptai, and even for blood sugar in the body.

Logistic growth: A population of bacteria, fish in a pond or users of a new app grows faster when it is bigger, but space and food are limited. The logistic model: dN/dt = r N (1 - N/K), where r is the growth rate and K is the carrying capacity. Take r = 0.5 per day, K = 1,000 and N = 10 at the start. Euler with one-day steps: day 1, 10 + 0.5 x 10 x 0.99 = 14.95; day 2, about 22.31; day 3, about 33.22. Early growth is nearly exponential; later it slows and N levels off near 1,000. The resulting S-shaped curve appears in app adoption, mobile phone spread in Bangladesh and many other places.

Predator-prey: The Lotka-Volterra model links two populations, for example tigers and deer in the Sundarbans. Deer grow on their own but are eaten; tigers die out without food but grow when deer are plentiful. With two coupled equations, a simulation shows cycles: deer increase, then tigers increase, then deer fall, then tigers fall, then deer recover, and so on. The real Sundarbans is much more complex, but the model teaches that populations can oscillate naturally without any outside cause.

The SIR epidemic model: Split a population of N people into Susceptible S (can catch the disease), Infected I and Recovered R. Each day, new infections = beta x S x I / N and recoveries = gamma x I. So dS/dt = -beta S I / N, dI/dt = beta S I / N - gamma I, dR/dt = gamma I. Take N = 1,000, beta = 0.3 per day (contact and transmission rate), gamma = 0.1 per day (illness lasts about 10 days), starting with S = 990, I = 10, R = 0.

SIR worked: Day 1: new infections = 0.3 x 990 x 10 / 1,000 = 2.97; recoveries = 0.1 x 10 = 1. So S = 987.03, I = 11.97, R = 1. Day 2: new infections about 3.55, recoveries about 1.20; S about 983.49, I about 14.32, R about 2.20. Continuing with daily steps, infections peak around day 28 with about 316 people sick at once, then fall. In the end only about 53 people never catch it. The ratio beta/gamma = 3 is the basic reproduction number R0: each sick person infects about 3 others at the start. If R0 is below 1, the outbreak dies out.

What SIR teaches policy: Halving contacts (beta = 0.15, R0 = 1.5) gives a much lower and later peak, so hospitals are not overwhelmed at once: the idea of flattening the curve used during COVID-19. Vaccination moves people from S to R before the outbreak; once enough are immune, R0 times the fraction susceptible falls below 1 and the disease cannot spread, which is herd immunity. Real epidemic models add age groups, exposed but not yet infectious people, travel between districts and randomness, but the core is still these equations.

Flattening in numbers: Run the same simulation with beta = 0.15, keeping everything else the same. The peak now comes around day 66 instead of day 28, and only about 71 people are sick at the same time instead of about 316, more than four times fewer. By the end about 403 people never catch the disease, compared with about 53 before. Nothing about the virus changed; only how often people met. This is why simulation results were shown to governments during COVID-19: a model lets leaders see the effect of a rule like closing schools or limiting gatherings before trying it on real people, although the exact numbers always depend on uncertain inputs like beta.

Combined simulation: Some systems mix both kinds of change. A steel furnace heats continuously (continuous), but batches of metal are loaded and unloaded at specific times (discrete events). A battery drains continuously, but a phone switches modes at events. Combined simulation lets continuous variables trigger events (when temperature reaches 1,500 degrees, start pouring) and events change continuous variables (adding cold metal drops the temperature). Tools like AnyLogic and Simulink support this mix.

Real-life example 1, flood forecasting: The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre in Bangladesh uses continuous hydrological and hydraulic models of rivers. Rain and upstream inflow enter as rates; water levels and flows change continuously along the river network. Solved numerically with small time steps, the models forecast water levels at many stations days ahead, giving people time to move animals and belongings to safety.

Real-life example 2, a car's cruise control: Engineers simulate a car's speed with a differential equation including engine force, air drag and road slope. A controller adjusts the throttle to keep the speed at 80 km/h. Simulating thousands of hills and wind conditions before building anything finds a controller that is smooth and stable. The same approach designs drone stabilisers and robot arms (deep-cse-8-5).

Common mistakes: Taking too large a step and getting unstable nonsense like negative temperatures or populations. Not checking against a known exact solution or equilibrium. Mixing units in rates (per minute vs per hour). Forgetting that Euler always lags behind changing rates. Treating a deterministic SIR result as exact for a small town where randomness matters a lot.

What exams ask: Differentiate discrete and continuous simulation. Write a differential equation for a described system. Apply Euler's method for a few steps by hand. Explain the effect of step size. Describe RK4 briefly. Set up and step the SIR model, and define R0. Explain combined simulation with an example.

Recap: Continuous simulation models smooth change with differential equations and solves them numerically. Euler's method steps forward with the current rate; smaller steps are more accurate but slower, and too large steps become unstable. RK4 is far more accurate. Tea cooling, water tanks, logistic growth, predator-prey and SIR epidemics are classic models; equilibria and exact solutions help check them. Next lesson looks at two other styles: system dynamics and agent-based simulation.
key_points: Continuous simulation tracks state variables that change smoothly, using differential equations dx/dt = f(x, t).
Euler's method: x(new) = x(now) + h x rate(now); simple but always lags behind a changing rate.
Tea cooling with h = 1 gives 60.43 at 5 minutes vs exact 61.39; smaller steps reduce error.
Too large a step makes the simulation unstable (h = 20 gives tea at -35 degrees).
RK4 uses four slopes per step; its error shrinks like h^4.
SIR model: infections beta S I/N, recoveries gamma I; R0 = beta/gamma decides whether an outbreak grows.
Combined simulation mixes continuous change with discrete events.
lessons.tip: Before trusting a continuous simulation, set the rates to zero and solve for the equilibrium by hand, then check the simulation settles there. It catches sign errors and unit errors in seconds.
lessons.task: Use Euler with h = 1 day to step the SIR model for days 1 to 4 with beta = 0.15 instead of 0.3 (keep N = 1,000, gamma = 0.1, S = 990, I = 10). Compare I on day 4 with the beta = 0.3 case and explain what halving contacts does.

quiz.q: Which situation is best modelled by continuous simulation?
options: Temperature of tea cooling over time
quiz.explain: Temperature changes smoothly; the others are naturally discrete events.

quiz.q: Euler's method for dT/dt = -0.1(T - 25), T = 85, h = 1. T after one step is...
What happens if the Euler step size is far too large?
options: The result can become unstable and absurd
quiz.explain: With h = 20 the tea drops to -35 degrees, colder than the room.

quiz.q: In the SIR model with beta = 0.3 and gamma = 0.1, R0 is...
quiz.explain: R0 = beta / gamma = 0.3 / 0.1 = 3.

quiz.q: A tank fills at 20 L/min and leaks at 0.1 V per minute. The equilibrium volume is...
quiz.explain: Set 20 - 0.1 V = 0, so V = 200 litres.

lessons.title: System Dynamics and Agent-Based Simulation
lessons.content:
Why does Dhaka traffic get worse even after a new flyover opens? Why do neighbourhoods sometimes split into groups when no one wants strong separation? Why do flocks of birds move as one without a leader? These questions are not about a single queue or a single equation. They are about whole systems with loops of cause and effect, and about many individuals following simple rules. Two simulation styles were built for exactly this: system dynamics, which looks at stocks and flows from above, and agent-based modelling, which builds the system from the individuals up. This lesson explains both and when to use which.

System dynamics, what it is: System dynamics (SD) was created by Jay Forrester at MIT in the late 1950s to study companies, cities and later the whole world. It describes a system with stocks (things that accumulate, like water in a tank, people in a city, money in a bank account) and flows (rates that fill or drain the stocks, like births per year or deposits per month). Under the hood, SD is continuous simulation (lesson 20): each stock changes by inflow minus outflow. What SD adds is a way of thinking and drawing that focuses on feedback loops and delays.

Stocks and flows worked: A university has 6,000 students. Each year it admits 2,000 new students (inflow), and each year about one quarter of current students graduate (outflow = students / 4). Year 1: 6,000 + 2,000 - 1,500 = 6,500. Year 2: 6,500 + 2,000 - 1,625 = 6,875. The stock keeps growing but more slowly. Setting inflow equal to outflow gives the equilibrium: 2,000 = S / 4, so S = 8,000 students. The administration can see years ahead how many classrooms and teachers they will need, and how fast they will get there.

Feedback loops: A feedback loop is a chain of causes that comes back to where it started. A reinforcing loop (also called positive feedback) amplifies change: more users of a messaging app make it more useful, which brings more users. Bank interest grows savings, which earns more interest. A balancing loop (negative feedback) pushes toward a goal: when a room is hotter than the AC setting, the AC cools harder; as it cools, the AC works less. Most real behaviour comes from several loops interacting: growth from reinforcing loops, limits from balancing loops.

Delays: Delays between cause and effect create overshoot and oscillation. You turn the shower knob, the water is still cold, so you turn more; then it becomes too hot. A shop orders more stock because shelves are empty, but delivery takes two weeks, so it orders again; then too much arrives at once. Farmers plant more of a crop when its price is high, but harvest comes months later when everyone has planted it and the price crashes. SD models make these delays explicit so their effects can be studied.

Causal loop diagram, Dhaka traffic: A causal loop diagram (CLD) draws variables connected by arrows marked plus (same direction) or minus (opposite direction). Consider: road capacity plus leads to travel speed; travel speed plus leads to attractiveness of driving; attractiveness of driving plus leads to number of cars; number of cars minus leads to travel speed. Building a flyover raises capacity and speed at first, which makes driving more attractive, so more people drive, which slows traffic again. This loop is called induced demand, and it is why new roads alone rarely cure congestion; better public transport like the metro rail changes the loop by giving an alternative.

System archetypes: SD researchers noticed that the same loop structures appear again and again, and named them archetypes. Limits to growth: a reinforcing loop drives growth until a balancing loop, like limited land or water, stops it; a new tea stall booms until the lane is full of rivals. Fixes that fail: a quick fix solves the symptom but feeds the problem later, like pumping more groundwater in Dhaka, which lowers the water table and makes the next shortage worse. Tragedy of the commons: each fishing boat in the Bay of Bengal gains by catching more, but together they shrink the fish stock everyone depends on, which is why hilsa fishing bans exist during breeding season. Spotting an archetype tells you where to act.

SD strengths and limits: SD is excellent for strategic, big-picture questions: policies over years, the effect of delays, why a fix fails. It is fast to run and easy to explain with diagrams. But it treats people as averages in a stock: it cannot say which individual waits, where exactly someone lives, or how a specific network of friends spreads a rumour. For that, we need a model built from individuals.

Agent-based modelling, what it is: In agent-based modelling (ABM), the system is made of many agents, each with its own state (location, age, money, health, opinion) and simple rules for behaviour (move toward food, buy if price is low, copy friends' opinions). Agents interact with each other and with an environment, often a grid or a map. The simulation advances in steps; at each step every agent looks around and acts. We then watch what patterns appear at the level of the whole system.

Emergence: The key idea of ABM is emergence: global patterns that arise from local rules, without anyone planning them. No single bird leads a flock; each bird follows three rules (stay close to neighbours, avoid crashing, match their direction), and flocking emerges. Craig Reynolds showed this in 1986 with his Boids model, and similar rules are used to animate crowds in films and games. Traffic jams can appear on a highway with no accident: one driver brakes slightly, the next brakes a bit more, and a jam wave moves backward through the cars.

Schelling's segregation model: In 1971 the economist Thomas Schelling placed two kinds of agents on a grid, with some empty cells. Each agent is happy if at least a certain fraction of its neighbours, say 30 percent, are of its own kind; otherwise it moves to a random empty cell. Even with this mild preference, where every agent would be happy in a mixed neighbourhood, the grid quickly organises into large single-kind clusters. Individual intentions and collective results can be very different. This is a lesson for city planners and for anyone who thinks a pattern must mean someone wanted it.

The Game of Life: John Conway's Game of Life (1970) is a grid where each cell is alive or dead. Each step, every cell counts its 8 neighbours. A live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours survives; a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours becomes alive; all other cells die or stay dead. A row of 3 live cells, the blinker, flips between horizontal and vertical forever. A 5-cell shape called the glider moves diagonally across the grid. From four simple rules come still shapes, oscillators, moving objects and even patterns that work like a computer. It shows how simple local rules can produce rich behaviour.

Agents versus averages: Run the SIR epidemic of lesson 20 as an agent-based model of 1,000 people, each infected person meeting random others each day. The average behaviour looks like the smooth equations, but individual runs differ. Sometimes the first few sick people recover before passing the disease on, and the outbreak dies out by luck even though R0 = 3. For simple models like this, the chance of such early fade-out starting from one case is about 1/R0, roughly one run in three. The equations, which only track averages, can never show this. When numbers are small, like the first cases in a village, randomness and individuals matter and ABM or stochastic simulation is the safer choice.

Building an ABM: Define the agents and their attributes. Define the environment (grid, network, map). Write the rules: what each agent senses, decides and does. Decide the update order: all at once or one by one in random order (the order can change results). Initialise, run many steps, and measure system-level outputs like the fraction segregated or average travel time. Because rules include randomness, run many replications, just as in DES. Tools include NetLogo (great for learning), Mesa in Python, and AnyLogic.

ABM strengths and limits: ABM captures individual differences, local interactions, networks, geography and adaptation. It can explain how patterns arise, not just describe them. But it needs many assumptions about behaviour that are hard to check, many parameters, and lots of computing for millions of agents. Validation is harder (lesson 23): a model that reproduces a pattern does not prove its rules are the real ones. Keep agent rules as simple as the question allows.

Choosing DES, SD or ABM: Use discrete-event simulation when the system is a process with entities flowing through resources and queues: banks, factories, hospitals, networks; questions are operational, minutes to months. Use system dynamics for aggregate, strategic questions with feedback and delays: policy over years, market growth, population, supply chains at a high level. Use agent-based modelling when individual differences and interactions matter and you care how patterns emerge: epidemics in social networks, evacuation crowds, markets of traders, land use. Many real studies combine styles: an ABM of passengers inside a DES of a metro station, for example.

Real-life example 1, Rohingya camp planning: Humanitarian groups working in the camps near Cox's Bazar have used agent-based models to study how a disease might spread among households living close together, and how placement of water points and health centres changes walking distance and crowding. Each agent is a person with a household, age and daily movement. The models help compare plans, while planners remember their uncertain assumptions.

Real-life example 2, a garment company's growth: A garment company in Narayanganj uses a system dynamics model of orders, workers, training and quality. More orders need more workers; new workers are less skilled, which lowers quality, which loses future orders after a delay. The model shows that growing too fast can create a boom-and-bust cycle, and that investing in training smooths it out: a lesson hard to see without simulation.

Common mistakes: Using SD when individual differences are the whole point, or ABM when a simple stock model would do. Drawing causal loop diagrams without checking the sign of each link. Forgetting delays. In ABM, adding rules until the model fits the data, then believing it explains reality. Running an ABM once and treating random patterns as results. Ignoring update order.

What exams ask: Define stocks, flows and feedback loops; distinguish reinforcing and balancing loops. Draw a causal loop diagram for a given situation. Compute a stock over a few periods. Define agent, environment and emergence; describe Schelling's model or the Game of Life rules. Compare DES, SD and ABM and choose one for a scenario.

Recap: System dynamics models stocks and flows with feedback loops and delays, giving a top-down view for strategic questions. Agent-based modelling builds the system from individuals with simple rules, and patterns emerge, as in flocking, Schelling segregation and the Game of Life. DES suits operational processes, SD aggregate policy, ABM interacting individuals, and they can be combined. Next lesson goes back to data: how to choose good input distributions.

Reinforcing loops amplify change; balancing loops push toward a goal; delays cause overshoot and oscillation.
Causal loop diagrams show cause-effect links with plus and minus signs, like induced demand in Dhaka traffic.
Agent-based models are built from individual agents with states and simple rules interacting locally.
Emergence: global patterns (flocking, jams, segregation) arise from local rules without central planning.
Game of Life rules: survive with 2 or 3 neighbours, birth with exactly 3, otherwise die or stay dead.
Choose DES for process flows, SD for aggregate strategy with feedback, ABM for interacting individuals.

lessons.title: Input Modeling
lessons.content:
A simulation is like a cooking pot: whatever goes in decides what comes out. If you feed a perfect bank simulator with wrong service times, it will give confident, precise and completely wrong answers. Simulation people say garbage in, garbage out. Input modeling is the job of choosing the probability distributions and parameters that drive the model: interarrival times, service times, demand sizes, breakdown times, travel times. It is often the most time-consuming part of a simulation study and one of the most important. This lesson gives the four steps: collect data, identify a distribution family, estimate its parameters, and test the fit.

Step 1, collecting data: Go to the real system and measure. Time 100 customers' arrivals at a bank counter with a stopwatch or from the token machine's log. Record repair times from a factory's maintenance book. Download trip times from a ride-sharing app's database. Data collection sounds simple but is full of traps, and many experienced modellers say it takes more time than writing the model itself.

Data traps: The period may be unusual: measuring a bank on the day before Eid gives an extreme, not normal, load. Data may be recorded wrongly: a clerk writes the time a form was closed in the system, not when the customer left. Different types may be mixed: a hospital's consultation times mix quick follow-ups and long first visits, which might need separate distributions. Rounding hides detail: times written only to the nearest 5 minutes. Censoring: a reneging customer's wait is only known to be at least some value. Always talk to the people who collected the data before trusting it.

Step 2, identifying a family, using histograms: Draw a histogram: divide the range into intervals of equal width and count how many observations fall in each. Look at the shape. A peak at zero and a long right tail suggests exponential. A symmetric bell suggests normal. A hump with a long right tail and no values below zero suggests gamma, Weibull or lognormal. A flat shape suggests uniform. Choosing interval width matters: too few intervals hide the shape, too many make it jagged. A rule of thumb is about the square root of the number of observations.

Using physical reasoning: The process itself suggests a family. Arrivals from many independent people: Poisson process, exponential gaps (lesson 6). Times that are the sum of several similar steps: Erlang or gamma. Times that are the product of many small factors, like repair times: often lognormal. Time to failure of parts that wear out: Weibull. Number of defects in a batch: binomial or Poisson. Count of customers per hour: Poisson. Combining the picture with the reasoning gives a good candidate.

Summary statistics help: Compute the sample mean, standard deviation and the coefficient of variation (CV = standard deviation / mean). An exponential distribution has CV = 1. If service times have CV around 0.5, exponential is a poor fit; gamma or lognormal with lower spread may fit better. If CV is close to 0, times are nearly constant. A normal distribution can give negative values; for times with small means and large spread, that is a warning sign.

Step 3, estimating parameters, the idea of MLE: Once a family is chosen, find its parameter values from data. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable. For many common distributions the MLE has a simple formula. For the exponential, the MLE of the rate is 1 / sample mean. For the Poisson, the MLE of lambda is the sample mean. For the normal, the MLE of the mean is the sample mean and of the variance is the average squared deviation. More complex families like gamma and Weibull need numerical methods, which tools do automatically.

MLE worked, exponential: Ten service times at a mobile recharge booth, in minutes: 2.1, 4.5, 0.8, 6.2, 3.0, 1.4, 5.5, 2.7, 3.9, 1.9. Sum = 32.0, sample mean = 3.2 minutes. If we assume exponential, the rate estimate is 1/3.2 = 0.3125 per minute. But check: the sample standard deviation is about 1.78, so CV is about 0.56, far from 1. That hints exponential may not be right, and we should try a gamma or lognormal too. Ten points is also very few; we would want at least 50 to 100 before deciding.

Step 4, goodness-of-fit tests: A test asks whether the data could plausibly have come from the fitted distribution. The null hypothesis is that the distribution fits. A large test statistic means the data look too different, and we reject. A small one means we have no evidence against the fit; this does not prove the fit is perfect, only that it is not obviously wrong. With huge data sets, tests reject even good-enough fits because tiny differences become detectable; with small data sets, they accept almost anything. Use tests together with plots and judgement.

Chi-square test worked: A bank counted arrivals in 100 one-minute intervals: 0 arrivals in 10 intervals, 1 in 30, 2 in 24, 3 in 20, 4 in 9 and 5 in 7. Total arrivals = 0 + 30 + 48 + 60 + 36 + 35 = 209, so the estimated Poisson mean is 2.09 per minute. Expected counts with Poisson(2.09), grouping 4 or more together: 12.4, 25.9, 27.0, 18.8 and 15.9. The chi-square statistic sums (observed - expected)^2 / expected over the cells: about 0.45 + 0.67 + 0.34 + 0.07 + 0.00, about 1.53.

Reading the chi-square result: Degrees of freedom = number of cells - 1 - number of estimated parameters = 5 - 1 - 1 = 3. The critical value at the 5 percent level with 3 degrees of freedom is 7.81. Since 1.53 is far below 7.81, we do not reject: Poisson arrivals are a reasonable model. Cells should have expected counts of at least about 5, which is why we grouped 4 and 5 together. This is the same chi-square test used for random numbers in lesson 8, now applied to real data.

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test: The KS test compares the empirical CDF of the data (the fraction of observations at or below each value) with the fitted CDF, and takes the largest vertical gap D. It needs no grouping into cells, which is good for small samples of continuous data. For large n, the 5 percent critical value is roughly 1.36 / square root of n: about 0.136 for 100 observations. If D is larger, reject. When parameters are estimated from the same data, the standard critical values are too generous, and adjusted tables should be used.

Q-Q plots: A quantile-quantile plot puts the sorted data on one axis and the matching quantiles of the fitted distribution on the other. If the fit is good, the points lie near a straight 45-degree line. Curvature at the ends shows that the tails are wrong, for example data with more long times than the fitted distribution predicts. Q-Q plots are often more informative than a single test number, because they show where the misfit is. Tail behaviour matters a lot in queues, since rare long services cause long waits.

When there is no data: For a new system that does not exist yet, like a new metro station, there is nothing to measure. Ask experts for the minimum, most likely and maximum values and use a triangular distribution. If a counter clerk says a form takes at least 2 minutes, usually 4, and at most 10, use triangular(2, 4, 10), whose mean is (2 + 4 + 10)/3, about 5.33 minutes. The beta distribution is a smoother alternative. Then run sensitivity analysis: change these guesses and see whether the decision changes. If it does, collecting real data is worth the cost.

Empirical distributions: If no standard family fits, use the data directly. An empirical distribution samples from the observed values, or interpolates between them. It always matches the data, but cannot produce values outside the observed range, so rare extreme events never happen in the simulation. Some tools combine an empirical body with a fitted tail.

Nonstationary inputs: Arrival rates often change with time: a bank is quiet at 10 a.m., packed at 1 p.m. on salary day, quiet again at 3. Using one average rate for the whole day hides the rush and badly underestimates waiting. Model a nonstationary Poisson process with a rate that changes by hour, estimated from data for each period. Generate it by thinning: generate arrivals at the maximum rate and keep each one with probability equal to the current rate divided by the maximum.

Correlated inputs: Inputs are not always independent. A large order at a factory takes long in cutting and long in sewing; treating the two times as independent underestimates variation. Daily demand for umbrellas is high for several days in a row during monsoon. Ignoring correlation can make a system look much calmer than it is. Advanced methods model these links, but the first step is simply to check for them with scatter plots and autocorrelation.

Real-life example, a city bus depot: A transport planning team in Chattogram models bus arrivals at a depot. Data from GPS trackers show travel times with a long right tail due to traffic jams; a lognormal fits well, and a Q-Q plot confirms the tail. The arrival rate differs strongly by hour, so they use 18 hourly rates. Repair times come from the workshop log, which mixes minor and major repairs, so they split them into two types with separate distributions. Each choice is documented so that others can check it.

Tools: Input analysers such as the Arena Input Analyzer, ExpertFit, Stat::Fit and Python libraries like scipy.stats and fitter fit many families at once and rank them by test statistics. Useful, but never accept the top-ranked family blindly; check the plots and the physical reasoning, and prefer a simpler family if it fits almost as well.

Common mistakes: Assuming exponential everywhere because the formulas are easy. Using only the mean and ignoring variability. Fitting the normal to times that cannot be negative. Collecting data on an unusual day. Using one rate for a whole day with rush hours. Trusting a test result without looking at the plot. Mixing different types of jobs into one distribution.

What exams ask: State the steps of input modeling. Explain how to choose a distribution from a histogram. Find MLEs for the exponential and Poisson distributions from data. Perform a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, including degrees of freedom. Describe the KS test and Q-Q plots. Explain what to do when no data are available.

Recap: Input modeling turns real data into distributions for the simulation: collect data carefully, identify a family with histograms, summary statistics and physical reasoning, estimate parameters by MLE (exponential rate = 1/mean, Poisson lambda = mean), and test fit with chi-square, KS and Q-Q plots. Without data, use expert triangular estimates plus sensitivity analysis. Watch for time-varying and correlated inputs. Next lesson asks whether the model itself is right: verification and validation.
key_points: Garbage in, garbage out: wrong input distributions give precise but wrong results.
Four steps: collect data, identify a family, estimate parameters, test the fit.
Histograms, physical reasoning and the coefficient of variation (CV = 1 for exponential) guide the family choice.
MLE: exponential rate = 1/sample mean; Poisson lambda = sample mean.
Chi-square: sum of (O - E)^2/E; df = cells - 1 - estimated parameters; expected counts at least about 5.
KS uses the largest gap between empirical and fitted CDFs; Q-Q plots show where the fit fails.
No data: use triangular(min, mode, max) from experts and test sensitivity; model time-varying rates separately.
lessons.tip: Always draw a picture before trusting a number. A histogram and a Q-Q plot take a minute and often reveal mixed data, wrong units or bad tails that a single test statistic hides.
