lessons.title: Verification and Validation
lessons.content:
Imagine an engineer shows a hospital director a beautiful animated simulation: patients walking, doctors moving, graphs rising. The model says adding one doctor will cut waiting by 40 percent. Should the director spend the money? Only if two things are true: the program does what the modeller intended, and what the modeller intended matches the real hospital closely enough for this decision. Checking the first is called verification; checking the second is called validation. Together they decide whether a model deserves trust. This lesson explains both, with practical techniques and a worked comparison against real data.

The two questions: Verification asks: did we build the model right? Is the computer program a correct implementation of the conceptual model, free of bugs and logical errors? Validation asks: did we build the right model? Does the conceptual model, and so the program, represent the real system accurately enough for the purpose of the study? A perfectly verified program can still be invalid, if its assumptions are wrong. A model with a valid design can still give wrong answers, if the code has bugs. Both are needed.

Where they fit: Picture three boxes: the real system, the conceptual model (assumptions, flowcharts, distributions on paper) and the computer program. Validation links the real system and the conceptual model. Verification links the conceptual model and the program. Calibration, adjusting parameters so the model matches the real system, goes on inside validation. All of this happens throughout the study, not only at the end (lesson 3), because finding a wrong assumption early is far cheaper than finding it after the report.

Verification technique 1, good programming practice: Write the model in small modules: arrival generator, server logic, statistics collection. Test each one alone. Use clear names and comments. Have a second person read the code in a structured walkthrough, explaining every line. Many bugs are found simply by explaining code aloud. Use version control so changes can be traced. These are ordinary software engineering habits (deep-cse-6-11 discusses them at project scale), and they matter even more when the output is a number someone will act on.

Verification technique 2, trace and animation: Run the model for a few events and print the full state after each: clock, event type, queue length, server status, statistics so far. Compare with a hand simulation like the tables in lessons 13 and 14. Animation does the same visually: if a customer walks through a wall, skips the queue, or two customers are served by one teller at once, you see it immediately. Animation is also excellent for showing the model to managers.

Verification technique 3, known answers: Set inputs so that the model becomes a system with a known exact answer. Make arrivals and service exponential with one server and compare with the M/M/1 formulas: with lambda = 10 and mu = 12 per hour, average wait in queue should be near 25 minutes and utilisation near 0.833 (lesson 17). Check Little's law between time-averaged L and customer-averaged W. If the full model has 5 counters, test it with M/M/c and Erlang C. Agreement within confidence intervals is strong evidence the event logic is right.

Verification technique 4, extreme and degenerate tests: Push inputs to the edges and check that outputs move sensibly. Zero arrivals: no customers, no waiting, server idle 100 percent. Arrival rate larger than service capacity: queue should keep growing. Service time almost zero: waits should almost vanish. One customer only: their time in system should equal their service time. Double the number of servers: waiting should fall, not rise. Also check continuity: a small change in input should give a small change in output, not a sudden jump.

Verification technique 5, consistency checks: Customers entering minus customers leaving should equal customers still in the system at the end. Total busy time of a server cannot exceed the run length. Probabilities used in routing should add to 1. Every random input should use its own stream so that changing one does not shift others (lesson 7). These conservation checks are cheap to code and catch many silent bugs.

Validation, face validity: Show the model's logic, animation and outputs to people who know the real system well: bank managers, nurses, factory supervisors. Ask whether the behaviour looks reasonable. They notice things modellers miss: tellers take a 20-minute prayer break at 1 p.m.; ambulance patients skip registration; the pharmacy closes at 9. Face validity is the first step of the widely used three-step approach of Naylor and Finger (1967): build a model with high face validity, test its assumptions empirically, and compare its input-output transformations with the real system.

Validating assumptions: Check structural assumptions: does the real queue really work FIFO, or do VIP clients jump ahead? Do customers really choose the shortest line? Check data assumptions with the input modeling methods of lesson 22: do arrival times really fit the chosen distribution, and is the period of data representative? Write every assumption in a list, with its source and how it was checked. This list is often the most useful document in the whole study.

Validating input-output transformations: The strongest test: run the model with inputs from a real period and compare outputs with what actually happened in that period. If a bank's real arrival records from five days are fed into the model, the model's average wait for each day can be compared with the real measured average wait. If the model's results are close enough for the purpose, it gains credibility; if not, find out why.

Input-output validation worked: Five days at a bank branch. Real average waits in minutes: 5.1, 6.3, 4.8, 5.9, 5.0 (mean 5.42). Model, driven by each day's real arrivals: 5.6, 6.8, 5.5, 6.2, 5.4 (mean 5.90). Differences (model minus real): 0.5, 0.5, 0.7, 0.3, 0.4; mean 0.48, standard deviation about 0.148. A paired t statistic = 0.48 / (0.148 / square root of 5), about 7.2, far above the 5 percent critical value 2.776 with 4 degrees of freedom. So the model overestimates waits by about half a minute, around 9 percent, and this is not chance.

What to do with that result: Statistically different does not automatically mean useless. Ask whether a 9 percent overestimate could change the decision. If the bank wants to know whether waits will exceed 15 minutes after a change, a half-minute bias hardly matters. If it is choosing between two designs that differ by one minute, it matters a lot. Next, look for the cause: perhaps real tellers speed up when the line is long, which the model ignores. Adding that behaviour and recalibrating may remove the bias.

Calibration: Calibration means adjusting parameters, within realistic bounds, so that the model matches real outputs. It is iterative: compare, adjust, compare again. The danger is overfitting: tuning many knobs until the model matches the past exactly, but for the wrong reasons, so it fails on new situations. Good practice is to calibrate on one set of data (say, January) and validate on a different set (say, March) that was not used for tuning. This is the same idea as training and test data in machine learning (deep-cse-6-14).

Sensitivity analysis: Change each uncertain input a little, one at a time, and watch the output. If raising the mean service time by 10 percent changes the average wait by 40 percent, that input is critical and deserves the most careful data and validation. If the decision stays the same across the whole plausible range of an input, its exact value matters little and you can stop worrying about it. Sensitivity analysis tells you where to spend validation effort, and it gives decision makers an honest picture: here is what we are sure of, and here is what depends on guesses.

The Turing test for models: Give experts two sets of reports, one from the real system and one from the model, without saying which is which. If they cannot tell them apart better than by guessing, that supports validity. If they can, ask how they knew: their explanation often points directly at what the model is missing. The name comes from Alan Turing's test for machine intelligence.

Validity depends on purpose: No model is valid in general; it is valid for a purpose. A model of a bank built to choose the number of tellers may be useless for designing the lobby layout. The statistician George Box said all models are wrong, but some are useful. Always state the purpose, the range of conditions tested, and the known weaknesses. For important decisions, an independent group may review the model and formally accept it for use, called accreditation.

Credibility: Even a valid model is useless if decision makers do not believe it. Involve them early, show the animation, explain assumptions in plain language, show validation results honestly, including weaknesses. Managers who helped define a model trust it far more than one delivered as a black box.

Real-life example 1, an airport security model: Before a new terminal opens, planners at a busy international airport, such as the new Terminal 3 at Hazrat Shahjalal, validate their security checkpoint model against data from the existing terminal: hourly passenger counts, lane opening schedules and measured queue times. Only after the model reproduces the old terminal's peaks within an agreed tolerance do they trust its predictions for the new one.

Real-life example 2, a failed model: A company built a detailed warehouse simulation that matched average throughput perfectly. But it was never validated at peak days; the real warehouse used overtime and temporary workers during Eid sales, which the model did not include. Its recommendation to cut staff failed badly in the first festival season. The average was valid; the peak behaviour, the part that mattered, was not.

Documenting V and V: Write down every verification test and validation comparison: what was tested, the expected result, the actual result and what was changed afterwards. A short V and V report lets a new team member or an outside reviewer see why the model can be trusted, and it saves weeks when the model is updated next year with new data. Without it, even a good model is hard to defend in a meeting.

Common mistakes: Treating a bug-free program as a valid model. Validating only on averages and not on peaks or tails. Calibrating and validating on the same data. Hiding assumptions. Declaring a model valid in general rather than for a purpose. Skipping verification because the animation looks right.

What exams ask: Define verification and validation and draw their relationship with the real system, conceptual model and program. List verification techniques. Explain the Naylor-Finger three-step approach. Describe face validity, input-output validation and the Turing test. Explain calibration and the risk of overfitting. Perform a simple paired comparison between model and real output.

Recap: Verification checks the program matches the conceptual model, using modular code, walkthroughs, traces, animation, known answers like M/M/1, extreme tests and conservation checks. Validation checks the model represents the real system for its purpose: face validity, tested assumptions and input-output comparison with real data, plus careful calibration on separate data. Our bank model overestimated waits by about 9 percent: significant, but whether it matters depends on the decision. Next lesson analyses outputs properly.
key_points: Verification: did we build the model right (program matches conceptual model)?
Validation: did we build the right model (model represents the real system for its purpose)?
Verification techniques: modular code, walkthroughs, traces, animation, known answers (M/M/1), extreme tests, conservation checks.
Naylor-Finger: high face validity, empirically tested assumptions, input-output comparison with real data.
Paired comparison of model vs real days can reveal bias, such as a 0.48-minute overestimate.
Calibrate on one data set and validate on another to avoid overfitting.
A model is valid for a purpose and range, never in general; credibility needs involved decision makers.
lessons.tip: Keep an assumptions table from day one: assumption, source, how checked, effect if wrong. It makes validation, reporting and later updates much easier, and managers trust it.
lessons.task: Take the single-server simulator from lesson 15. Run three extreme tests: zero arrivals, arrival rate twice the service rate, and service time near zero. Write down what each output should be before running, then compare.

quiz.q: Checking that a program correctly implements the conceptual model is called...
quiz.explain: Verification asks whether we built the model right.

quiz.q: Which is a validation technique?
options: Comparing model output with real system data for the same period
quiz.explain: Input-output comparison with real data checks the model against reality.

quiz.q: A simulator set to M/M/1 with lambda = 10 and mu = 12 per hour gives average queue wait near 25 minutes. This helps...
options: Prove the real system is M/M/1
quiz.explain: Matching a known exact answer is evidence the code is correct.

quiz.q: Why calibrate on one data set and validate on another?
options: To avoid a model tuned to the past for the wrong reasons
quiz.explain: Separate data reveals overfitting from calibration.

quiz.q: Experts cannot tell model reports from real reports. This is...
quiz.explain: It is named after Turing's test of indistinguishability.

lessons.title: Output Analysis
lessons.content:
You run your bank simulation once and it says the average wait is 26.1 minutes. You run it again with a different seed and it says 23.2. Which is right? Neither and both: each run is one random sample of what could happen. A simulation with random inputs produces random outputs, and a single number from a single run can mislead badly. Output analysis is the statistics of simulation results: how many runs to do, how long, how to throw away misleading early data, how to put an honest error bar on an answer, and how to compare two designs fairly. This lesson uses the probability and statistics from deep-cse-2-6 on simulation output.

Why one run is not enough: Every run uses a different stream of random numbers, so outputs vary. If you report one run, you might happen to report a lucky or unlucky one. Worse, within one run, observations are not independent: if customer 50 waited long, customer 51 probably waited long too, because they were in the same queue. So the standard formulas for confidence intervals, which assume independent data, cannot be used directly on individual customers' waits from one run. The fixes in this lesson all work around this problem.

Terminating versus steady-state: A terminating simulation has a natural end: a bank open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., a one-day exam registration, a single cricket match crowd, a 30-day monsoon inventory period. Each run starts in a defined condition (the bank opens empty) and ends at a defined event. A steady-state (non-terminating) simulation studies long-run behaviour of a system that runs continuously: a 24-hour data centre, a mobile network, a continuous factory. The question is what happens in the long run, ignoring how it started. The type decides which analysis method to use.

Replications for terminating systems: Run the model n independent times, each with different random numbers, from the same starting conditions. From each replication take one summary number, such as that day's average wait. These n numbers are independent and identically distributed, so ordinary statistics apply. This is called the method of independent replications. The one-day average waits are the data points, not the individual customer waits inside each day.

Confidence interval formula: With n replication results, compute the sample mean x-bar and the sample standard deviation s. The 95 percent confidence interval is x-bar plus or minus t times s / square root of n, where t is the Student t value with n - 1 degrees of freedom at 0.975. For n = 10, t is 2.262. The term t s / square root of n is called the half-width. It tells how precisely the simulation has estimated the true long-run mean.

Confidence interval worked: Ten replications of the tea stall model from lesson 15 gave average waits in minutes: 24.6, 25.0, 24.8, 26.1, 23.2, 25.7, 24.1, 25.4, 26.3, 24.8. Sum = 250.0, so x-bar = 25.0. The sample standard deviation is about 0.93. Half-width = 2.262 x 0.93 / square root of 10, about 0.67. The 95 percent confidence interval is about 24.33 to 25.67 minutes. The M/M/1 formula says 25 minutes exactly, which lies inside: the simulation agrees with theory.

How to read a confidence interval: If we repeated this whole procedure (10 replications, compute interval) many times, about 95 percent of the intervals would contain the true mean. It does not mean individual customers wait between 24.3 and 25.7 minutes: individual waits range from 0 to over an hour. It is about the long-run average only. A narrow interval means a precise estimate of the average, not that the system is predictable.

How many replications: Suppose the manager wants the half-width to be at most 0.5 minutes. Since half-width shrinks like 1 / square root of n, we need about n = (t x s / 0.5)^2. Using s = 0.93 and the normal value 1.96 as a first guess gives about 13.4, so start with 14. With t values: n = 15 gives half-width 2.145 x 0.93 / square root of 15, about 0.52, still slightly too wide; n = 16 gives 2.131 x 0.93 / 4, about 0.50. So about 16 replications are needed. To halve the half-width, you need about four times as many replications.

Steady-state and initial bias: For steady-state systems, a run must start somewhere, usually empty and idle. But an empty bank is not typical of its long-run behaviour: early customers wait less than they would in steady state. Data from this warm-up period bias the average downward. The fix is to delete the warm-up: run the model, throw away statistics collected before some time d, and only keep data after it. Choosing d too short leaves bias; too long wastes computing time.

Welch's method for warm-up: Make several replications, say 5. For each time period (for example, each hour), average the output across the replications. Then smooth this averaged curve with a moving average over a few neighbouring periods. Plot it. The curve rises (or falls) at the start and then flattens around a level with small wiggles. The warm-up ends where the curve becomes flat. Pick d a little after that point to be safe. It is a visual method, simple and widely used.

Replication-deletion approach: For steady-state systems, the easiest method combines the above: decide the warm-up d with Welch's method, then make n independent replications, each of length d plus a long enough data collection period, delete the warm-up from each, and take each replication's average after d as one data point. Then use the same confidence interval formula as for terminating systems. Each replication pays the warm-up cost again, which is the price of simplicity.

Batch means: An alternative for steady-state is one very long run. After deleting warm-up once, divide the remaining output into k large batches, say 20 batches of 5,000 customers each, and take each batch's average. If batches are long enough, their averages are nearly independent, and they can be treated like replications to form a confidence interval with k - 1 degrees of freedom. Batch means pays the warm-up cost only once, but choosing batch size needs care: too small and the batches are still correlated, making the interval too narrow and falsely confident.

The autocorrelation trap: Suppose you take 10,000 individual customer waits from one run and compute s / square root of 10,000 as if they were independent. Because consecutive waits are positively correlated, this badly underestimates the true uncertainty, often by a factor of several times. Your interval looks very precise, but would miss the true mean far more than 5 percent of the time. This is one of the most common and most dangerous mistakes in simulation studies. Always build intervals from replications or batch means, never from correlated raw observations.

Comparing two designs: Often the question is not what the wait is, but which design is better: policy A or B, 3 tellers or 4, a token system or not. Run both, compute the difference in performance and build a confidence interval for that difference. If the interval does not contain zero, the difference is statistically significant. If it contains zero, the simulation has not shown a real difference: either the difference is small or more replications are needed.

Common random numbers (CRN): To compare designs fairly, give both the same random arrivals and service demands, so that each replication tests both designs under the same luck. If day 3 has a rush of customers, both designs face that rush. Then compute the difference for each replication, which removes much of the shared randomness. This is a variance reduction technique, related to those in lesson 12, and needs separate random number streams for each input so the inputs stay aligned (lesson 7).

Paired-t worked: Eight replications with CRN comparing average waits (minutes) for policy A, the current single queue, and policy B, with an extra express counter. A: 18.2, 21.5, 17.9, 24.0, 19.6, 22.3, 20.1, 23.4. B: 16.9, 20.8, 16.5, 22.1, 18.7, 21.0, 19.2, 21.6. Differences A - B: 1.3, 0.7, 1.4, 1.9, 0.9, 1.3, 0.9, 1.8. Mean difference 1.275, standard deviation about 0.43. With t = 2.365 for 7 degrees of freedom, half-width = 2.365 x 0.43 / square root of 8, about 0.36. Interval: about 0.92 to 1.63 minutes. Zero is outside, so B really reduces waiting, by about 1.3 minutes.

Why CRN helped: If we had ignored the pairing and treated A and B as two independent samples, their standard deviations of about 2.3 and 2.1 would give a half-width around 2.4 minutes. The interval for the difference would be roughly -1.1 to 3.6, containing zero: no conclusion. The pairing removed day-to-day variation shared by both designs, leaving only the real difference. The same eight runs gave a clear answer instead of a shrug.

Many designs at once: With 5 or 10 alternatives, comparing all pairs at 95 percent each raises the chance that at least one comparison is wrong. The Bonferroni correction makes each individual interval wider, for example 99 percent each for 5 comparisons, so the overall confidence stays about 95 percent. Specialised ranking and selection procedures can pick the best design with a guaranteed probability. Optimisation over many designs is the topic of the next lesson.

Real-life example: A telecom operator's network team simulates a new routing rule for its core network. Each replication covers a busy day, with CRN for traffic patterns. The rule's 95 percent interval for reduction in dropped calls is 0.8 to 1.6 percent, entirely above zero, so the change goes ahead. Another rule's interval, -0.3 to 0.9 percent, includes zero; they run more replications before deciding, rather than trusting one promising run.

Beyond the mean: Averages are not the whole story. A bank may care more about the fraction of customers who wait over 15 minutes, or the 90th percentile of waiting time, than about the average. These can be estimated the same way: from each replication take the fraction of customers waiting over 15 minutes as that replication's single number, then build a confidence interval across replications. Percentiles and tail measures need more replications than means, because rare events give fewer data. Report the measures that match the real decision, and show a histogram of waits so managers see the spread, not just the centre.

What exams ask: Explain why a single run is insufficient. Distinguish terminating and steady-state simulations. Compute a confidence interval from replication data. Calculate the number of replications for a target half-width. Explain warm-up, Welch's method, replication-deletion and batch means. Perform a paired-t comparison with CRN and interpret it.

Recap: Simulation outputs are random, and observations within a run are correlated. For terminating systems, use independent replications and a t confidence interval: our 10 runs gave 25.0 plus or minus 0.67 minutes, matching theory. Precision improves like 1 / square root of n. For steady-state, delete warm-up (Welch) and use replication-deletion or batch means. Compare designs with paired differences and common random numbers. Next: using simulation to optimise and a final capstone.
key_points: One run is one random sample; observations within a run are correlated, so raw-data intervals are wrong.
Terminating simulations have a natural end; steady-state simulations study long-run behaviour.
Independent replications: one summary per run; CI = mean +/- t x s / sqrt(n).
Ten runs gave 25.0 +/- 0.67 minutes; a half-width of 0.5 needed about 16 runs.
Half-width shrinks like 1/sqrt(n): halving it needs about four times as many runs.
Warm-up deletion with Welch's method; replication-deletion or batch means for steady state.
Compare designs with paired differences and common random numbers; zero outside the interval means a real difference.
lessons.tip: Report every simulation number with its confidence interval and the number of replications, like 25.0 +/- 0.67 minutes (10 replications, 95 percent). A number without an error bar invites wrong decisions.
lessons.task: Using the simulator from lesson 15, make 5 replications and compute the 95 percent confidence interval for average wait (t = 2.776 for 4 degrees of freedom). Then make 20 replications (t = 2.093) and compare the half-widths. Does the ratio match 1/sqrt(n)?

quiz.q: Why can't individual customer waits from one long run be treated as independent data?
options: There are too many of them
quiz.explain: A customer behind a long-waiting customer usually waits long too.

quiz.q: Ten replications have mean 25.0 and s = 0.93; t = 2.262. The half-width is about...
To halve the confidence interval half-width, you need about...
quiz.explain: Half-width shrinks like 1/sqrt(n), so n must grow 4 times.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of Welch's method?
options: Finding where the warm-up period ends
quiz.explain: It plots smoothed averages across replications to see when output settles.

quiz.q: A paired-t interval for A - B is 0.92 to 1.63 minutes. The conclusion is...
quiz.explain: Zero is outside and A - B is positive, so B's waits are lower.

lessons.title: Simulation Applications and Capstone
lessons.content:
You now have a full toolbox: random numbers and distributions, Monte Carlo, discrete-event logic, queuing formulas, inventory and continuous models, system dynamics and agents, input modeling, verification and validation, and output analysis. This last lesson puts the toolbox to work. First, how simulation is used to find the best design, not just to evaluate one. Then digital twins and the many fields where simulation is used today. Then a complete capstone study of a metro rail ticket counter in Dhaka, step by step, followed by the ethics of using models to make decisions, and a map of where to go next.

Simulation optimisation, the idea: A simulation answers what if: if we have 3 counters, the wait is about 7 seconds. Managers usually want what is best: how many counters, what reorder level, which schedule. Simulation optimisation wraps a search method around the simulation. The search proposes a design, the simulation evaluates it with replications, the search uses the result to propose a better design, and so on. The difficulty is that each evaluation is noisy and can be slow, so the search must be clever with few evaluations and careful about randomness.

Search methods: For a handful of options, simply simulate them all and compare with the statistical methods of lesson 24, using ranking and selection procedures to pick the best with a guaranteed probability. For many options, use metaheuristics: genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, tabu search, or scatter search, as in the commercial OptQuest engine used by many tools. Response surface methods fit a smooth curve to the simulation results and search on the curve. Analytical optimisation methods, which simulation optimisation often borrows from, are covered in Operations Research (deep-cse-6-10).

A short history: Modern simulation grew with the computer. In the late 1940s, Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann used random sampling on early computers at Los Alamos, and the method was named Monte Carlo. In 1961 Geoffrey Gordon at IBM created GPSS, one of the first languages for discrete-event simulation. In the 1960s Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard in Norway built SIMULA to write simulations, and in doing so invented classes and objects, the ideas behind object-oriented programming used in most languages today. Since then, simulation has moved from mainframes to laptops and the cloud, but the core ideas in this course have stayed the same.

Digital twins: A digital twin is a simulation model connected to a real system by live data, kept in step with it. Sensors on machines, GPS on buses or meters in a power grid feed the model continuously. The twin can show the current state, predict the next hours and test decisions before applying them: what happens if we reroute these trucks now? Factories, ports, power grids, and even cities build digital twins. They combine everything in this course with data engineering and system design (deep-cse-6-13) and often machine learning for prediction.

Application areas: Manufacturing: line balancing, buffer sizes, maintenance planning. Healthcare: emergency departments, operating theatre schedules, bed planning, epidemic response. Transport: traffic signals, ports, airports, railways, ride-sharing. Telecom and computing: network capacity, cloud autoscaling, data centre design, parallel job scheduling (deep-cse-7-5). Supply chains and retail: inventory, warehouses, delivery routes. Finance: risk with Monte Carlo. Defence and emergency planning: evacuation, disaster response. Robotics and AI: robots and reinforcement learning agents are trained in simulated worlds before facing the real one (deep-cse-8-4, deep-cse-8-5). Games and films: physics and crowd simulation.

Capstone, the problem: Note: the numbers in this capstone are invented for teaching, not real data from Dhaka Mass Transit Company. A metro station in Dhaka has ticket vending machines for single-journey tickets. At the evening peak, passengers needing tickets arrive at about 120 per hour. Each purchase takes on average 45 seconds, so one machine can serve about 80 per hour. The station has 2 machines and complaints about queues. Management asks: how many machines are needed so that average waits stay under 30 seconds, including on special days with 180 passengers per hour?

Step 1, formulate and plan: Following lesson 3, write down the objective (average wait under 30 seconds and few passengers waiting over 2 minutes), the alternatives (2, 3 or 4 machines; also a promotion for rechargeable cards that reduces ticket buyers by 30 percent), the performance measures (mean wait, fraction waiting over 2 minutes, machine utilisation), the scope (only the ticket area, from arrival at the machines to leaving with a ticket) and the time frame (a 3-hour evening peak, a terminating simulation).

Step 2, a quick analytical estimate: Before building anything, use queuing formulas (lesson 18) as an M/M/c approximation. With lambda = 120 per hour and mu = 80 per hour per machine: 2 machines give utilisation 0.75 and average wait about 58 seconds; 3 machines give utilisation 0.5 and about 7 seconds; 4 give about 1.3 seconds. At 180 per hour: 3 machines give utilisation 0.75 and about 34 seconds; 4 machines give about 6 seconds. This takes ten minutes and already says 2 machines are not enough and 3 might be borderline on special days.

Step 3, input modeling: Data from the station's gates and machine logs show something the formula ignored: passengers do not arrive smoothly; they come in bursts when each train arrives, every few minutes, and the rate changes through the evening. Service times are not exponential: most purchases take 30 to 50 seconds, but some take 2 minutes when a note is rejected. A lognormal fits the service times, checked with a Q-Q plot (lesson 22). Arrivals are modelled as batches after each train plus a nonstationary background rate.

Step 4, build, verify and validate: Build a discrete-event model with events for train arrival, passenger arrival at machines, purchase start and purchase end. Verify it: set Poisson arrivals and exponential service and check that waits match the M/M/c values above; run extreme tests; check that passengers in minus passengers out equals passengers still inside. Validate it: run with one week's real arrival data for the current 2 machines and compare predicted queue lengths with CCTV counts. Show the animation to station staff for face validity.

Step 5, experiments and output analysis: For each design, run 30 replications of the 3-hour peak with common random numbers so that all designs face the same trains and passengers. Suppose, in our invented case, the bursts make waits much worse than the smooth formula: with 3 machines the average wait is about 25 seconds on normal days but about 70 seconds on special days, with many passengers waiting over 2 minutes right after each train. With 4 machines, the special-day average falls to about 15 seconds. Paired confidence intervals show the 3-versus-4 difference is clearly real on special days but small on normal days.

Step 6, recommendation: Using the cost of a machine, the value of passengers' time, and the card promotion option, the team might recommend: 3 machines permanently, a fourth machine or a staffed counter opened on special event days, and a card promotion that, by reducing ticket buyers by 30 percent, makes 3 machines comfortable even on most special days. The report shows each result with confidence intervals, lists assumptions, and states that the model was validated only for evening peaks. This is how a real study turns the course's tools into a decision.

Lessons from the capstone: The quick formula was useful but too optimistic because it missed burst arrivals: always check assumptions against data. Simulation showed not just averages but who waits and when. Common random numbers made the comparison sharp. And the final answer combined numbers with judgement about costs, risk and passenger experience.

Ethics and responsibility: Simulation results influence money, safety and people's lives: how many nurses a hospital hires, how a city evacuates before a cyclone, which areas get buses. Be honest about uncertainty: give intervals, not single numbers. Do not tune a model to produce the answer your client wants. State assumptions clearly, especially those about people's behaviour. Check whether the model's averages hide unfair outcomes: a design that minimises average wait might make elderly or disabled passengers wait much longer. Protect any personal data used as input. A model gives authority to a decision; that authority must be earned.

Communicating results: The best model fails if its message is lost. Lead with the answer in one sentence, such as: three machines are enough on normal days, four on special days. Then show one clear chart of waiting time for each option with error bars, and keep the technical details in an appendix. Use the language of the people deciding: seconds of waiting and taka per month, not utilisation and degrees of freedom.

When not to simulate: If a simple formula answers the question well enough, use it. If there is no data and no expert knowledge, a simulation is just guesswork with decoration. If the decision is small and cheap to reverse, try it in reality. If the deadline is tomorrow, a rough calculation beats an unfinished model. Simulation is powerful but costly; use it when the stakes are high and the system is too complex for formulas.

Where to go next: For optimising decisions mathematically, study Operations Research (deep-cse-6-10). For handling the large data sets that feed models, Data Science (deep-cse-6-14). For running millions of replications or huge agent models fast, Parallel and High Performance Computing (deep-cse-7-5). For agents that learn from simulated environments, Reinforcement Learning (deep-cse-8-4), and for simulated robots, Robotics (deep-cse-8-5). Tools worth learning: Python with SimPy and Mesa, NetLogo for agent models, and a commercial tool like AnyLogic or Arena if your workplace uses one.

Course recap, part 1: A model is a simplified representation of a system; simulation runs a model over time to study behaviour (lessons 1 to 3). Randomness is generated with good pseudo-random numbers, tested, and transformed into any distribution by inverse transform, acceptance-rejection or special methods (lessons 4 to 10). Monte Carlo estimates quantities by repeated sampling, with error shrinking like 1 / square root of n and variance reduction to speed it up (lessons 11 and 12).

Course recap, part 2: Discrete-event simulation moves a clock from event to event using an event list, with time-weighted statistics (lessons 13 to 15). Queuing theory gives exact answers for simple systems, Little's law everywhere, and shows how utilisation and variability drive waiting (lessons 16 to 18). Inventory, continuous, system dynamics and agent-based models cover other kinds of systems (lessons 19 to 21). Input modeling, verification and validation, and output analysis make results trustworthy (lessons 22 to 24).

What exams ask: Explain simulation optimisation and name search methods. Define a digital twin. Describe application areas with examples. Outline a full simulation study for a given scenario, from problem formulation to recommendation. Discuss ethical issues and when simulation is not appropriate.

Final word: Simulation is a way of thinking: when a system is too complex to solve on paper, build a small world inside the computer, let it run many times, measure carefully, and be honest about what you know and what you do not. With that habit, you can study queues at a tea stall, epidemics in a city, robots learning to walk, or the metro station you ride every day.
key_points: Simulation optimisation wraps a search method (ranking and selection, metaheuristics) around noisy simulation evaluations.
A digital twin is a simulation kept in step with a real system through live data.
Simulation is used in manufacturing, healthcare, transport, telecom, supply chains, finance, robotics and AI.
Capstone: quick M/M/c estimates first, then input data, DES model, verification, validation, replications with CRN.
Burst arrivals after each train made waits much worse than the smooth formula predicted: always check assumptions.
Ethics: report uncertainty, state assumptions, avoid tuning to a desired answer, check fairness, protect data.
Do not simulate when a formula suffices, there is no data, or the decision is cheap to reverse.
lessons.tip: Start every study with a ten-minute back-of-the-envelope estimate using formulas. It frames the right range, catches silly simulation bugs, and tells you whether the full model is even needed.
lessons.task: Pick a queue you know (a school canteen, a bus counter, a hospital ticket counter). Write a one-page simulation study plan following the capstone's six steps: objective, alternatives, measures, a quick formula estimate, the data you would collect, and how you would validate the model.

quiz.q: What does simulation optimisation add to an ordinary simulation?
options: A search method that proposes and evaluates designs to find the best
quiz.explain: It combines search with simulation evaluations of candidate designs.

quiz.q: A model connected to a real factory by live sensor data and kept in step with it is a...
quiz.explain: A digital twin mirrors the real system using live data.

quiz.q: In the capstone, why was the M/M/c estimate too optimistic?
options: Passengers arrived in bursts after each train
quiz.explain: Burst arrivals create queues that smooth Poisson arrivals do not.

quiz.q: Which is an ethical practice in simulation studies?
options: Reporting only the single best run
Tuning the model to the client's preferred answer
Reporting confidence intervals and stating assumptions
quiz.explain: Honesty about uncertainty and assumptions earns the model its authority.

quiz.q: When is simulation usually NOT the right tool?
options: When a simple formula already answers the question well
When the system is complex and random
quiz.explain: If a formula suffices, simulation adds cost without benefit.
